questions.q: Soft-tissue attenuation of ultrasound is approximately:
questions.x: Attenuation rises about 0.5 dB per cm per MHz in soft tissue - the reason penetration falls as frequency rises.

questions.q: Cortical bone appears as a bright line with a dark band behind it mainly because:
o: Bone transmits sound faster than soft tissue
The large acoustic impedance mismatch at the bone surface reflects and absorbs nearly all the beam
Reverberation occurs within the marrow cavity
questions.x: The impedance mismatch at soft tissue-bone interfaces reflects most of the beam; the little that enters is absorbed, producing clean shadowing.

questions.q: Equidistant repeating bright lines deep to a strong reflector are called:
questions.x: Echoes bouncing repeatedly between the reflector and the transducer are registered as progressively deeper, equally spaced lines.

questions.q: A short, tapering bright trail behind a small highly reflective object such as a needle tip or foreign body is:
questions.x: Comet-tail is a short form of reverberation from closely spaced reflectors; it usefully marks needles, calcifications and foreign bodies.

questions.q: Narrow anechoic bands seen deep to the curved edges of a tendon or cyst wall result from:
o: Refraction (edge) shadowing as the beam bends at the curved interface
questions.x: At curved boundaries the beam is refracted away, leaving a hypoechoic band - do not mistake it for a tear or vessel.

questions.q: Ultrasound coupling gel is essential because it:
o: Eliminates the air gap whose impedance mismatch would reflect virtually the entire beam
questions.x: Air reflects almost 100% of the beam; gel provides impedance matching between probe and skin.

questions.q: Tissue harmonic imaging improves the image by:
o: Receiving echoes at harmonic multiples of the transmitted frequency, reducing near-field artifact and improving contrast
questions.x: Harmonics build with depth, so near-field clutter and side-lobe artifact are reduced and tissue contrast improves.

questions.q: For reliable color Doppler flow measurement, the angle between beam and vessel should ideally be kept:
questions.x: Doppler shift varies with the cosine of the insonation angle; above 60 degrees velocity errors grow rapidly and flow may not be detected.

questions.q: For superficial small structures such as finger flexor tendons or digital nerves, the best probe choice is a:
questions.x: Hockey-stick probes combine high frequency (resolution) with a small footprint that couples well on fingers, the wrist and the ankle.

questions.q: All else being equal, needle visibility on ultrasound improves with:
o: Bevel facing away from the probe
questions.x: A larger shaft presents a bigger specular reflector; echogenic surface texturing further improves visibility at steep angles.

questions.q: In an out-of-plane (short-axis) needle approach, the most reliable way to confirm tip position is:
o: Small test injections (hydrolocation) while sliding the probe along the needle
Freeze the image and remeasure depth
questions.x: Out-of-plane shows only a bright dot that may be the shaft; hydrolocation and probe sliding trace the needle to its true tip.

questions.q: The ALARA principle in diagnostic ultrasound refers to:
o: Keeping exposure As Low As Reasonably Achievable, while monitoring the mechanical and thermal indices
questions.x: ALARA balances diagnostic benefit against potential bioeffects; MI and TI on screen quantify cavitation and heating risk.

questions.q: The mechanical index (MI) on the display estimates the probability of:
questions.x: MI relates to peak rarefactional pressure and the likelihood of inertial cavitation; the thermal index (TI) relates to heating.

questions.q: Increasing the dynamic range (log compression) of the grayscale image will:
o: Display more shades of gray with lower contrast
questions.x: Wider dynamic range compresses more echo amplitudes into the display, giving a softer, lower-contrast image with more gray shades.

questions.q: Which change will INCREASE the frame rate?
questions.x: Fewer scan lines per frame and shorter round trips mean more frames per second; narrow the width, reduce depth, use one focal zone.

questions.q: Which antidepressant is an evidence-based first-line option for neuropathic pain?
questions.x: SNRIs (duloxetine, venlafaxine) and tricyclics are first-line adjuvants for neuropathic pain; SSRIs are weak analgesics.

questions.q: A troublesome class effect of tricyclic antidepressants that limits their use in elderly patients is:
o: Anticholinergic effects - dry mouth, urinary retention, confusion and orthostasis
questions.x: Start low and go slow in older patients; amitriptyline and nortriptyline remain useful but anticholinergic burden drives falls and delirium.

questions.q: Before initiating long-term opioid therapy for chronic non-cancer pain, best practice includes:
o: Risk stratification (e.g., opioid risk tool), informed consent and baseline urine drug screening
questions.x: Document risk assessment, functional goals, consent and monitoring; avoid opioid-benzodiazepine combinations.

questions.q: A recognized LOCAL adverse effect of corticosteroid injection, especially with superficial injections, is:
o: Skin depigmentation and subcutaneous fat atrophy
questions.x: Superficial steroid placement can blanch skin and thin subcutaneous fat; deeper placement and water-soluble agents reduce the risk.

questions.q: A typical corticosteroid dose for a large joint such as the knee is:
questions.x: Large joints take roughly 40 mg triamcinolone or equivalent; small joints take 10-20 mg - the examiner manual quotes these ranges.

questions.q: Intra-articular hyaluronic acid (viscosupplementation) is most commonly used for:
questions.x: Viscosupplementation is an option for knee OA after analgesics and exercise; it is contraindicated in joint infection.

questions.q: In controlled diagnostic blocks, the placebo response rate that motivates comparative or placebo-controlled designs is approximately:
questions.x: Roughly a third of patients report relief from inactive injections, so single uncontrolled blocks over-diagnose the pain generator.

questions.q: During conventional (thermal) radiofrequency neurotomy, the target tip temperature is typically:
questions.x: Thermal neurotomy lesions at 80-85°C for 60-90 seconds; pulsed RF stays below 42- 45°C to avoid destruction.

questions.q: Radiofrequency lesion size increases with all of the following EXCEPT:
o: Higher tip temperature and longer lesion time
questions.x: Lesion diameter grows with gauge, active-tip length, temperature and time; a moving electrode cannot hold target temperature.

questions.q: Before a neuraxial (epidural) injection, the agent whose anticoagulant effect requires the longest interruption among the following is:
questions.x: Warfarin requires interruption and INR normalization before neuraxial procedures; NSAIDs and low-dose aspirin are lower risk and often continued for peripheral injections.

questions.q: The maximum recommended dose of plain lidocaine (without epinephrine) for infiltration is approximately:
questions.x: Plain lidocaine 4.5 mg/kg (about 300 mg); epinephrine permits up to about 7 mg/kg by slowing absorption.

questions.q: During resuscitation for local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST), which drug should be AVOIDED?
questions.x: Avoid vasopressin, calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers and large epinephrine doses; lipid emulsion and seizure control are the cornerstones.

questions.q: A contraindication to stellate ganglion block on the planned side is:
o: Contralateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy or prior contralateral pneumonectomy
questions.x: Block-related recurrent laryngeal or phrenic involvement on the only functioning side can compromise airway and ventilation.

questions.q: The Budapest (clinical diagnostic) criteria for CRPS require findings in which set of categories?
questions.x: Reported symptoms in three categories and observed signs in two, with no better alternative diagnosis, define clinical CRPS.

questions.q: "Yellow flags" in chronic low back pain assessment refer to:
o: Psychosocial factors such as fear-avoidance beliefs, catastrophizing and work dissatisfaction that predict chronicity
questions.x: Yellow flags predict poor outcome and chronicity; they are distinct from red flags (serious pathology) that mandate work-up before injection.

questions.q: During cervical medial branch block, correct injectate spread is seen:
o: Along the waist of the articular pillar, lifting the semispinalis capitis away from bone
questions.x: Spread along the pillar waist under the muscle confirms perineural placement; foraminal or anterior spread means the needle is malpositioned.

questions.q: The C7 medial branch differs from C3-C6 because its target lies:
o: At the pillar waist like the others
Higher, crossing the base of the C7 transverse process toward the apex of the superior articular process
questions.x: The C7 articular pillar is shallow and its medial branch runs higher; the C6-7 joint is blocked with C6 and C7 level targets.

questions.q: When counting cervical levels from below, the most useful caudal landmark is:
o: The prominent C7 spinous process (vertebra prominens)
questions.x: Confirm C7 (prominent, non-bifid, with a long spinous process) and count upward; confirm from above with the bifid C2.

questions.q: For ultrasound-guided cervical selective nerve root block, the safest initial bony contact for the needle is:
o: The posterior tubercle of the transverse process
questions.x: Resting on the posterior tubercle keeps the needle dorsal and away from the vertebral artery before advancing into the foramen's posterior aspect.

questions.q: Real-time visualization of injectate during cervical transforaminal injection is critical primarily to detect:
o: Intravascular uptake into radicular or vertebral vessels, which can cause cord or brain infarction
questions.x: Loss of injectate visualization on the static image suggests vascular uptake - stop, reposition, and use non-particulate steroid.

questions.q: The anterior boundary of the thoracic paravertebral space is the:
questions.x: The space is bounded anteriorly by parietal pleura (hence pneumothorax risk), posteriorly by the superior costotransverse ligament.

questions.q: A single-injection thoracic paravertebral block characteristically spreads:
o: Across the midline to both sides
questions.x: The wedge-shaped space communicates vertically, so one injection covers several ipsilateral dermatomes; anterior displacement of the pleura confirms placement.

questions.q: The key needle maneuver that prevents pleural puncture during intercostal or paravertebral block is:
o: Contacting the rib or transverse process first, then walking off in a controlled direction
questions.x: Bony contact gives depth certainty; walking caudally off the rib keeps the needle a controlled few millimeters deep to bone.

questions.q: For diagnostic lumbar medial branch blocks, the injectate volume should be:
questions.x: Large volumes overflow to adjacent structures and destroy specificity; small volumes anesthetize only the target nerve.

questions.q: For intra-articular lumbar facet injection under ultrasound, the needle enters the joint from the:
o: Inferior/posterior aspect of the joint gap seen in the paramedian oblique view
questions.x: The posterior joint gap is targeted; a slight give and capsular distension on injection confirm intra-articular placement.

questions.q: For S1-S3 lateral branch blocks, the sonographic target is:
o: The tissue immediately lateral to each posterior sacral foramen
questions.x: The lateral branches emerge from the posterior foramina and run inferolaterally; blocks here predict response to SI joint radiofrequency.

questions.q: During ultrasound-guided caudal epidural injection, the main limitation of ultrasound compared with fluoroscopy is:
o: The sacral cornua cannot be seen
Injectate spread and intravascular uptake inside the canal are difficult to confirm sonographically
The hiatus is too small to image
questions.x: Bone blocks the view of the canal contents; watch for turbulence and use Doppler, but fluoroscopy with contrast remains the gold standard for spread.

questions.q: In ultrasound-guided lumbar selective nerve root block, the needle should approach the foramen:
o: Dorsally, contacting the superior articular process/pars region before advancing toward the root
questions.x: A dorsal approach avoids the ventral radiculomedullary arteries (including the artery of Adamkiewicz territory) and the disc.

questions.q: On the paramedian sagittal oblique lumbar view, the "anterior complex" deep to the anechoic CSF consists of the:
o: Anterior dura, posterior longitudinal ligament and posterior vertebral body cortex
questions.x: The deep hyperechoic line fuses anterior dura, PLL and vertebral cortex; the posterior hyperechoic line is the flavum-posterior dura unit.

questions.q: A typical injectate volume for sacroiliac joint injection is:
o: About 1-1.5 mL, because the joint accepts only small volumes
questions.x: The SI joint holds little fluid; resistance or backflow along the needle track signals extra-articular placement.

questions.q: A technical limitation of ultrasound-guided SI joint injection is that:
o: Only the inferior recess is accessible; the superior and anterior joint cannot be reached under ultrasound
The joint cannot be seen at all
Doppler is unavailable at that depth
questions.x: The synovial lower pole is sonographically accessible and is the standard target; the rest of the joint is hidden behind the ilium.

questions.q: Pain from lumbar facet joints characteristically:
o: Is predominantly axial, radiating to the buttock and posterior thigh, usually not below the knee
questions.x: Facet referral is non-dermatomal and stays proximal; pain below the knee with neurological signs suggests radiculopathy instead.

questions.q: Cervicogenic headache most often originates from which structure, as confirmed by controlled blocks?
o: C2-3 zygapophysial joint (third occipital nerve territory)
questions.x: The C2-3 joint and its third occipital nerve are the commonest validated source; diagnostic TON blocks confirm it before radiofrequency.

questions.q: On a transverse midline lumbar scan, the spinous process produces:
o: A window to the thecal sac
A bright superficial line with dense shadowing that obscures deeper structures
questions.x: The spinous process blocks the midline view, which is why neuraxial scanning shifts to the paramedian oblique interlaminar window.

questions.q: Skin-to-dura distance measured on the paramedian oblique ultrasound view:
o: Correlates closely with MRI/needle depth and helps plan epidural or intrathecal needle length
questions.x: Ultrasound depth to the posterior dura predicts needle depth within a few millimeters - a useful pre-procedure measurement.

questions.q: For cervical sympathetic trunk (stellate) block at C6, correct injectate spread is:
o: Along the surface of the longus colli under the prevertebral fascia, descending toward C7-T1
questions.x: Spread caudally over the longus colli reaches the stellate ganglion at C7-T1 while the needle stays safely at C6.

questions.q: Hoarseness immediately after a stellate ganglion block indicates spread to the:
questions.x: Hoarseness means local anesthetic reached the recurrent laryngeal nerve; it is a side effect, not a sign of success - Horner syndrome is.

questions.q: The greater occipital nerve is the medial branch of the dorsal ramus of:
questions.x: The GON is the medial branch of the C2 dorsal ramus; C1 has essentially no sensory dorsal ramus distribution.

questions.q: The lesser occipital nerve, sometimes blocked with the greater occipital nerve for occipital neuralgia, arises from:
o: The ventral rami of C2-C3 via the cervical plexus, emerging behind the sternocleidomastoid
questions.x: Unlike the GON (dorsal ramus), the lesser occipital nerve is a ventral ramus cervical plexus branch ascending along the posterior SCM border.

questions.q: The suprascapular nerve provides the majority (about 70%) of sensory innervation to the:
questions.x: This dominant articular supply is why suprascapular block and radiofrequency can control chronic shoulder pain; the nerve has no cutaneous branch.

questions.q: On ultrasound of the intercostal space, the pleura is identified as:
o: A bright hyperechoic line that slides with respiration (lung sliding)
A dark band under the muscle
questions.x: The shimmering, respiration-phasic pleural line is the safety landmark - stay superficial to it at all times.

questions.q: The iliohypogastric nerve provides motor innervation to the:
o: Lower abdominal wall muscles (internal oblique and transversus abdominis)
questions.x: Ilioinguinal and iliohypogastric nerves (L1) motor-supply the lower abdominal wall and sense the suprapubic/inguinal skin.

questions.q: The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve supplies:
o: The cremaster muscle and the scrotum/labia majora
questions.x: The femoral branch supplies upper anterior thigh skin; the genital branch runs in the inguinal canal to the cremaster and scrotum/labia.

questions.q: Meralgia paresthetica is distinguished from lumbar radiculopathy clinically because it:
o: Is purely sensory - no motor deficit or reflex change - over the anterolateral thigh
questions.x: The LFCN carries no motor fibers; weakness, reflex loss or back pain should redirect the diagnosis toward L2-L3 radiculopathy.

questions.q: In the femoral triangle, the order of structures from LATERAL to MEDIAL is:
questions.x: NAVL from lateral to medial; the femoral nerve sits on the iliacus under the fascia iliaca, lateral to the pulsatile artery.

questions.q: In the subsartorial (adductor) canal, the saphenous nerve travels with the:
o: Great saphenous vein at the hip
questions.x: The nerve accompanies the femoral artery in the canal before becoming subcutaneous between sartorius and gracilis at the knee.

questions.q: At the subgluteal level, the sciatic nerve is scanned between which two bony landmarks?
questions.x: The ischial tuberosity-greater trochanter interval is the classic subgluteal window, with the nerve deep to gluteus maximus.

questions.q: The common peroneal (fibular) nerve is MOST vulnerable to compression where it:
o: Winds around the fibular neck, superficial and fixed against bone
questions.x: Its superficial course around the fibular neck explains compression palsies (crossing legs, casts, weight loss) presenting with foot drop.

questions.q: Distal to the tarsal tunnel, the tibial nerve divides into the:
questions.x: The plantar nerves supply the sole; entrapment causes burning plantar pain (tarsal tunnel syndrome).

questions.q: The sural nerve is most easily found on ultrasound:
o: Between the lateral malleolus and the Achilles tendon, beside the small saphenous vein
questions.x: Trace the small saphenous vein proximally - the sural nerve runs beside it in the posterolateral ankle.

questions.q: In the mid-forearm, the median nerve lies between the:
o: Flexor digitorum superficialis and flexor digitorum profundus
Flexor carpi radialis and palmaris longus
questions.x: Follow the nerve proximally from the wrist (the elevator technique) to confirm identity when anatomy is confusing.

questions.q: Sensation over the thenar eminence is preserved in carpal tunnel syndrome because the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve:
o: Is a branch of the ulnar nerve
Arises proximal to the wrist and passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum
questions.x: Thenar eminence numbness suggests proximal median neuropathy (e.g., pronator syndrome), not carpal tunnel syndrome.

questions.q: During dynamic scanning of the elbow in flexion, an ulnar nerve that displaces over the medial epicondyle demonstrates:
o: Ulnar nerve subluxation/dislocation - a cause of snapping and neuritis
A normal variant in every individual
questions.x: Dynamic flexion may reveal anterior nerve displacement (sometimes with the medial triceps), producing snapping and friction neuritis.

questions.q: In the spiral groove, the radial nerve is accompanied by the:
o: Profunda brachii (deep brachial) artery, between the lateral and medial heads of triceps
questions.x: The nerve hugs the humerus with the profunda brachii artery - humeral shaft fractures threaten both; confirm with Doppler.

questions.q: The posterior interosseous nerve may be compressed as it enters the supinator at the:
questions.x: PIN compression causes finger/thumb extension weakness without sensory loss - pure motor radial tunnel syndrome.

questions.q: The musculocutaneous nerve pierces which muscle before becoming the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm?
questions.x: It innervates coracobrachialis, biceps and brachialis, then emerges between biceps and brachialis as the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve.

questions.q: The axillary nerve travels through the quadrilateral space together with the:
questions.x: Quadrilateral space syndrome (athletes, posterior shoulder pain) compresses the nerve and artery here; the nerve supplies deltoid and teres minor.

questions.q: The ultrasound target for pudendal block is the interligamentous plane between the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments, using which pulsatile landmark?
o: Internal pudendal artery near the ischial spine
questions.x: Find the ischial spine, the two ligaments and the internal pudendal vessels on Doppler; the nerve lies medial to the artery.

questions.q: The superior hypogastric plexus, blocked for pelvic cancer pain, lies:
o: Anterior to the L5-S1 junction below the aortic bifurcation
questions.x: The plexus sits retroperitoneally over the L5-S1 disc and sacral promontory, relaying pelvic visceral pain.

questions.q: Lumbar sympathetic block for CRPS of the lower limb is performed at the anterolateral aspect of which vertebral level?
questions.x: The lumbar sympathetic chain runs anterolateral to the L2-L3 vertebral bodies; blockade warms the ipsilateral foot.

questions.q: The subscapularis tendon is best evaluated with the shoulder in:
o: External rotation, which stretches and exposes its insertion on the lesser tuberosity
questions.x: External rotation moves the tendon out from under the coracoid and tensions it for long- and short-axis assessment.

questions.q: To image the infraspinatus and posterior glenohumeral recess, the patient's hand is placed:
o: Across the chest onto the opposite shoulder
questions.x: This position opens the posterior recess for joint injection and presents infraspinatus and teres minor in long axis.

questions.q: The biceps tendon sheath is clinically important in shoulder ultrasound because it:
o: Communicates with the glenohumeral joint, so sheath fluid often signals joint effusion
questions.x: The sheath is an extension of the joint; fluid restricted to the sheath with a normal joint suggests primary biceps tenosynovitis.

questions.q: Acromioclavicular joint osteoarthritis on ultrasound typically shows:
o: Joint space narrowing with capsular hypertrophy and marginal osteophytes
questions.x: Bulging osteophytes and a hypertrophied capsule are typical; a large step-off suggests instability instead.

questions.q: The rotator interval contains the long head of biceps tendon stabilized by the:
questions.x: The biceps pulley (coracohumeral ligament, superior glenohumeral ligament, subscapularis and supraspinatus fibers) prevents medial subluxation.

questions.q: The annular ligament of the elbow is best seen surrounding the:
questions.x: It wraps the radial head within the radial notch of the ulna; look for tears with radial head instability.

questions.q: The anterior "sail sign" on elbow imaging indicates:
o: Displacement of the anterior fat pad by joint effusion
questions.x: Effusion lifts the anterior fat pad out of the coronoid fossa; with the posterior fat pad sign it flags occult fracture after trauma.

questions.q: When scanning the distal biceps tendon insertion, the structure immediately medial to it that must be avoided during injection is the:
questions.x: The tendon inserts on the radial tuberosity; the brachial artery and median nerve lie medially - map them before bicipitoradial bursa injection.

questions.q: The commonest site of superficial bursitis at the elbow is the:
questions.x: The olecranon bursa has no deep communication with the joint; aspirate cautiously and rule out septic bursitis and gout.

questions.q: The dorsal wrist ligament most commonly assessed with ultrasound after trauma is the:
questions.x: Scapholunate injury is the commonest cause of carpal instability; compare the dorsal ligament and scapholunate gap with the other side.

questions.q: De Quervain tenosynovitis involves which tendons in the first dorsal compartment?
o: Extensor pollicis longus and extensor indicis
Flexor carpi radialis and palmaris longus
Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis
Extensor digitorum and extensor digiti minimi
questions.x: Look for retinacular thickening, tendon sheath fluid and a septum dividing the compartment - inject the sheath, not the tendon.

questions.q: A trigger finger is caused by thickening of which structure?
o: A1 pulley at the metacarpal head, impeding flexor tendon gliding
questions.x: Ultrasound-guided release or steroid injection targets the thickened A1 pulley; watch the digital nerves on either side.

questions.q: The triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) is located on which side of the wrist?
o: Ulnar, between the distal ulna and the carpus
questions.x: TFCC tears cause ulnar-sided wrist pain and may accompany distal radioulnar joint instability.

questions.q: The anterior capsule of the hip is reinforced by which strong ligament, seen over the femoral neck?
questions.x: The iliofemoral ligament is the echogenic band over the anterior recess; effusion lifts it off the femoral neck.

questions.q: On hip ultrasound, the acetabular labrum normally appears as a:
o: Hyperechoic triangular fibrocartilage at the acetabular rim; hypoechoic clefts suggest a tear
questions.x: The labrum deepens the socket; basal clefts, intrasubstance hypoechoic foci or paralabral cysts indicate tears.

questions.q: The iliopsoas bursa is clinically relevant because it:
o: Lies posterior to the sciatic nerve
Communicates with the hip joint in about 15% of adults and may fill with joint effusion
questions.x: A distended iliopsoas bursa may be the first sign of hip joint disease; it lies between the tendon and the anterior capsule.

questions.q: The common hamstring origin evaluated with ultrasound attaches to the:
questions.x: Proximal hamstring tendinopathy and tears are assessed at the ischial tuberosity, beside the sciatic nerve.

questions.q: The pes anserine bursa lies between the pes anserine tendons and the:
o: Superficial medial collateral ligament / proximal tibia
questions.x: Sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus insert together; bursitis mimics medial joint line pain.

questions.q: The superficial medial collateral ligament of the knee inserts on the tibia approximately:
o: 5-7 cm below the joint line, deep to the pes anserine tendons
questions.x: Trace the long superficial MCL from the medial femoral epicondyle to its distal tibial insertion; grade tears by fiber disruption.

questions.q: Of the cruciate ligaments, which can be directly assessed with ultrasound?
o: The PCL, in the posterior knee with the knee flexed; the ACL is largely inaccessible
questions.x: The posterior window shows the PCL between femur and tibia; ACL assessment relies on secondary signs and other imaging.

questions.q: The normal quadriceps tendon on longitudinal scan has which architecture?
questions.x: Rectus femoris, combined vastus intermedius/medialis/lateralis laminae stack in three layers; delamination marks partial tearing.

questions.q: Proximal patellar tendinopathy (jumper's knee) shows:
o: Hypoechoic thickening of the deep proximal tendon, often with neovascularity on Doppler
questions.x: The deep fibers at the inferior patellar pole are affected first; Doppler neovascularity correlates with pain.

questions.q: Dynamic ultrasound for peroneal tendon instability is performed with:
o: Dorsiflexion and eversion stress, watching for anterior subluxation over the lateral malleolus
questions.x: A torn superior peroneal retinaculum lets brevis/longus snap over the fibula during dorsiflexion-eversion.

questions.q: Tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction is associated with which progressive foot deformity?
o: Acquired flatfoot (arch collapse with hindfoot valgus)
questions.x: Tenosynovitis progresses to tearing and loss of the medial arch - assess the tendon behind the medial malleolus dynamically.

questions.q: Non-insertional Achilles tendinopathy typically involves the tendon segment:
o: 2-6 cm above the insertion, the hypovascular watershed zone
questions.x: The watershed segment is the commonest degeneration site; insertional disease involves the retrocalcaneal bursa and enthesis instead.

questions.q: The axial resolution of a 12 MHz probe exceeds that of a 5 MHz probe because:
o: It has a longer spatial pulse length
Its shorter wavelength shortens the spatial pulse length
questions.x: Shorter wavelength means a shorter pulse, and axial resolution is about half the spatial pulse length.

questions.q: Elevational (slice-thickness) resolution depends on:
o: The number of scan lines only
The thickness of the beam in the dimension perpendicular to the image plane
questions.x: Elevational resolution is set by beam thickness out of the image plane; thin beams (lens focusing, 1.5D arrays) reduce partial-volume artifact.

questions.q: The twinkle artifact on color Doppler is characteristically seen behind:
o: Rough, strongly reflecting calcific foci or stones
questions.x: A shimmering mosaic of color behind a rough reflector - useful for confirming calcifications and stones, and sometimes needle tips.

questions.q: Diagnostic ultrasound machines assume an average soft-tissue sound speed of:
questions.x: Depth is calculated from echo delay assuming 1540 m/s; media with very different speeds (fat 1450) cause misregistration artifacts.

questions.q: Which structure produces the STRONGEST acoustic shadow?
questions.x: Bone and calcium reflect and absorb nearly everything; fluid shadows least and instead enhances through-transmission.

questions.q: Which tissue attenuates ultrasound the LEAST?
o: Fluid (e.g., a simple cyst or effusion)
questions.x: Fluid barely attenuates, which is why tissue behind a cyst or effusion looks brighter (posterior acoustic enhancement).

questions.q: When you switch from a 10 MHz to a 5 MHz probe you should expect:
o: Higher frame rate at any depth
Deeper penetration but coarser (lower) spatial resolution
questions.x: Lower frequency attenuates less, reaching deeper targets at the cost of resolution - the fundamental trade-off of probe selection.

questions.q: Color Doppler gain set too high produces:
o: Color blooming beyond the vessel walls with speckled background noise
questions.x: Reduce gain until color just fills the vessel without bleeding into surrounding tissue; then confirm true flow direction and anatomy.

questions.q: A displayed thermal index (TI) of 1.0 indicates an estimated worst-case temperature rise of about:
questions.x: TI models heating; MI models cavitation. Keep both as low as reasonably achievable while preserving diagnostic quality.

questions.q: Which statement about curvilinear (sector) probes is TRUE?
o: Their diverging beams widen the far field but reduce line density and lateral resolution with depth
They always operate at higher frequency than linear probes
questions.x: The wide far field suits deep abdominal/pelvic targets, but diverging scan lines spread out and lateral resolution degrades with depth.

questions.q: When an injection probe may contact non-intact skin or sterile fields, transducer reprocessing requires:
o: High-level disinfection (or a sterile cover with sterile gel)
Low-level wipe only, even for mucosal contact
Autoclaving the probe in every case
questions.x: Match disinfection level to contact risk: low-level for intact skin, high-level for non-intact skin/sterile fields, plus covers for injections.

questions.q: A proper pre-injection "time-out" includes verification of:
o: Patient identity, procedure, site and side, medication and allergy status
questions.x: The time-out is a scored safety step: right patient, right procedure, right site/side, right drug and dose, allergies checked.

questions.q: For a deep nerve target at 8-10 cm, which needle offers the best balance of visibility and steerability?
questions.x: Larger, stiffer shafts deflect less and reflect more sound; echogenic texturing keeps the tip visible at steep deep angles.

questions.q: Air should be purged from the syringe before an ultrasound-guided injection because injected air bubbles:
o: Appear as bright echoes with shadowing/reverberation that obscure the target
questions.x: Air-tissue interfaces scatter the beam; even small bubbles can hide the needle tip and target after injection begins.

questions.q: A practical drawback of power Doppler compared with color Doppler is that it:
o: Is less sensitive to slow flow
Is more susceptible to motion (flash) artifact and gives no flow direction
questions.x: Power Doppler trades direction information for sensitivity to slow flow, but patient or probe motion floods the image with flash artifact.

questions.q: Which class is generally NOT recommended for long-term management of fibromyalgia?
questions.x: Fibromyalgia responds to gabapentinoids, SNRIs, TCAs and exercise; opioids lack efficacy and worsen outcomes.

questions.q: Compared with gabapentin, pregabalin has:
o: More predictable (linear) absorption with bioavailability above 90%
questions.x: Gabapentin absorption is saturable and variable; pregabalin's linear kinetics simplify titration. Both are renally cleared.

questions.q: The lidocaine 5% patch is an accepted topical treatment for:
questions.x: The patch acts locally on sensitized cutaneous nociceptors with minimal systemic absorption - a core option for PHN.

questions.q: The capsaicin 8% patch relieves neuropathic pain by:
o: Activating TRPV1 receptors, producing reversible defunctionalization of epidermal C-fiber endings
questions.x: Initial burning is followed by weeks of reduced sensitivity from reversible nerve-ending defunctionalization.

questions.q: Ketamine, used intravenously in refractory CRPS and neuropathic pain, acts mainly as an:
questions.x: NMDA blockade dampens central sensitization and wind-up; psychotomimetic effects limit dosing.

questions.q: Escalating pain intensity despite increasing opioid doses, with pain spreading beyond the original site, suggests:
questions.x: OIH is managed by dose reduction or rotation and multimodal therapy, not reflex escalation.

questions.q: Ziconotide, used in intrathecal pumps for severe refractory pain, blocks:
o: N-type voltage-gated calcium channels in the dorsal horn
questions.x: Ziconotide is a conotoxin peptide for pump delivery; it has no opioid tolerance but a narrow therapeutic window.

questions.q: A late complication of long-term intrathecal opioid delivery is:
o: Catheter-tip granuloma, which can compress the spinal cord
questions.x: Granulomas form from high-concentration infusates; new neurological deficit in a pump patient mandates urgent imaging.

questions.q: Spinal cord stimulation for chronic back and leg pain places its electrode leads in the:
o: Posterior epidural space overlying the lower thoracic cord
questions.x: Leads stimulate the dorsal columns (gate-control mechanism) covering the painful dermatomes with paresthesia or subperception fields.

questions.q: The primary purpose of a diagnostic selective nerve root block before surgery is to:
o: Confirm which nerve root is the pain generator
questions.x: Small-volume blocks identify the symptomatic level; concordant relief guides the surgical or radiofrequency target.

questions.q: The false-positive rate of a single uncontrolled diagnostic medial branch block is approximately:
questions.x: Up to a third or more of single blocks are false positive; comparative or placebo-controlled blocks are the accepted remedy.

questions.q: During radiofrequency neurotomy near a mixed nerve, motor stimulation at 2 Hz is used to:
o: Verify a safe distance from motor fibers (no distal muscle contraction at threshold)
questions.x: Dissociation between sensory response at 50 Hz and absent motor response at 2 Hz reassures before lesioning.

questions.q: Sensory stimulation during radiofrequency electrode placement is typically performed at:
o: 50 Hz, seeking concordant sensation at low voltage (about 0.5 V or less)
questions.x: Low-threshold concordant sensation confirms proximity to the target sensory nerve before lesioning.

questions.q: For neuraxial (epidural or intrathecal) injections, solutions should be:
o: Combined with particulate steroid in all cases
questions.x: Preservatives such as benzyl alcohol are neurotoxic; check every vial used near the neuraxis.

questions.q: Post-dural puncture headache is caused by:
o: CSF leakage with loss of buoyancy and traction on pain-sensitive intracranial structures
questions.x: The headache is postural (worse upright); persistent cases are treated with an epidural blood patch.

questions.q: The lateral atlanto-axial (C1-2) joint receives its innervation from the:
questions.x: The C2 ventral ramus supplies the lateral C1-2 joint - relevant when targeting it for cervicogenic headache; the vertebral artery loops dangerously nearby.

questions.q: The cervical articular pillars visualized on a sagittal scan are formed by the stacked:
questions.x: Adjacent superior and inferior articular processes stack into the pillar; the groove between two peaks is the medial branch target.

questions.q: For cervical sympathetic trunk block under ultrasound, the needle is advanced:
o: In-plane from lateral to medial, passing posterior to the carotid sheath onto the longus colli
questions.x: The lateral in-plane approach keeps the carotid, jugular, thyroid and esophagus out of the needle path and lands on the longus colli surface.

questions.q: Because the third occipital nerve varies in its course across the C2-3 joint, the block is best performed by:
o: Depositing small aliquots at several points along the lateral margin of the C2-3 joint
questions.x: The nerve may cross the joint high or low; small volumes at the upper, middle and lower joint margin capture all variants.

questions.q: Facet (zygapophysial) tropism refers to:
o: Asymmetry between the orientation of the left and right facet joints
questions.x: Tropism alters the scan plane needed to open the joint gap and is associated with rotational instability and disc degeneration.

questions.q: Cooled radiofrequency for sacroiliac joint denervation was developed mainly to:
o: Avoid the need for diagnostic blocks
Create larger lesions that capture the variable courses of the S1-S3 lateral branches
questions.x: Lateral branch anatomy is variable; internally cooled electrodes produce larger, more predictable lesions than conventional RF.

questions.q: On ultrasound, the piriformis muscle is identified as it exits the pelvis through the:
questions.x: Scan from the lateral sacrum toward the greater trochanter; the muscle slides through the greater sciatic foramen with the sciatic nerve below it.

questions.q: For an ultrasound-guided ganglion impar block via the classic posterior route, the needle passes through the:
questions.x: The ganglion sits on the anterior surface of the sacrococcygeal junction; the needle crosses the sacrococcygeal ligament to reach it.

questions.q: The ligamentum flavum is thickest (3-5 mm) and most reliably targeted at which spinal region?
questions.x: Lumbar flavum is thick and paired, meeting in the midline - its fusion with the posterior dura forms the classic hyperechoic line.

questions.q: The posterior lumbar epidural space normally contains:
o: Fat and the internal vertebral venous plexus
questions.x: Epidural fat and valveless veins lie between the flavum and the dura - one reason intravascular uptake is common in epidural injection.

questions.q: In adults, the conus medullaris usually terminates at the level of:
questions.x: Knowing the conus ends at L1-L2 (and the dural sac at S2) frames safe levels for neuraxial procedures.

questions.q: Within the anechoic thecal sac on the paramedian oblique view, the cauda equina roots appear as:
o: Multiple small hyperechoic dots and linear echoes floating in CSF
questions.x: The roots shimmer and move with patient positioning - a useful confirmatory sign of the thecal sac level.

questions.q: Which neuraxial injection is best validated for ultrasound-only guidance?
questions.x: The sacral hiatus is superficial and sonographically accessible in most adults; other neuraxial injections still rely on fluoroscopy or loss-of-resistance.

questions.q: The L4-5 facet joint receives its innervation from the medial branches of:
questions.x: Each joint is supplied by the medial branch of its own level and the level above - hence two blocks per joint.

questions.q: The mamillo-accessory ligament, beneath which the lumbar medial branch runs, extends between the:
o: Mamillary process and accessory process at the transverse process base
questions.x: The nerve is trapped in this osteofibrous tunnel at the TP-SAP junction - the exact sonographic target.

questions.q: The sonographic target for thoracic medial branch block is the:
o: Superolateral corner of the transverse process
questions.x: Thoracic medial branches cross the superolateral TP corner before reaching the facet - block there, not at a lumbar-style junction.

questions.q: Even with ultrasound guidance for lumbar interlaminar epidural injection, loss-of-resistance or fluoroscopic confirmation is still required because:
o: The thecal sac cannot be seen
Ultrasound cannot reliably display the needle as it traverses the ligamentum flavum into the epidural space
questions.x: Bone windows let you see the dura but not the advancing needle; LOR or contrast confirmation remains mandatory.

questions.q: Provocation discography is performed primarily to:
o: Reproduce the patient's concordant pain and identify the symptomatic disc
questions.x: It is a diagnostic (provocative) test; concordant pain at low pressure with a negative control disc suggests discogenic pain.

questions.q: In about what proportion of individuals does the vertebral artery enter the transverse foramen at a level other than C6?
questions.x: Entry at C7, C5 or higher occurs in a meaningful minority - always trace the artery with Doppler at the actual level before cervical injections.

questions.q: Between C2 and C1, the vertebral artery is particularly vulnerable because it:
o: Loops laterally and posteriorly before entering the C1 transverse foramen, lying unprotected near the C1-2 joint
questions.x: This loop is the principal danger of posterior C1-2 (atlanto-axial) injections; stay midline and image the artery first.

questions.q: The phrenic nerve runs on the anterior surface of which muscle, at risk during interscalene and cervical sympathetic blocks?
questions.x: The phrenic nerve descends on the anterior scalene under the prevertebral fascia - identify it before blocking nearby.

questions.q: In the interscalene groove, the upper brachial plexus roots classically appear as:
o: A stack of hypoechoic round structures between the anterior and middle scalene muscles (the stoplight sign)
questions.x: Three stacked dark circles (C5-C7 roots) between the two scalenes are the hallmark of the interscalene level.

questions.q: At the supraclavicular level, the brachial plexus (trunks/divisions) is found:
o: Medial to the internal jugular vein
Clustered posterolateral to the subclavian artery, above the first rib
questions.x: The plexus huddles behind and lateral to the artery on the first rib - the corner pocket gives the densest, fastest block.

questions.q: The cords of the brachial plexus at the infraclavicular level are named according to their relationship to the:
questions.x: Lateral, posterior and medial cords are named for their positions around the axillary artery behind the pectoralis minor.

questions.q: In the axilla, the radial nerve is typically located:
o: Posterior to the axillary artery, near the conjoint tendon of latissimus dorsi and teres major
questions.x: The radial nerve is the deepest of the axillary nerves; the musculocutaneous nerve hides within the coracobrachialis instead.

questions.q: At the elbow crease, the median nerve lies:
questions.x: Find the pulsatile brachial artery in the antecubital fossa; the median nerve is the honeycomb structure on its medial side.

questions.q: The radial nerve divides into its superficial sensory branch and the posterior interosseous nerve near the:
o: Radiocapitellar joint at the level of the lateral epicondyle
questions.x: Trace the nerve from the spiral groove distally; the bifurcation lies just before the PIN enters the supinator.

questions.q: Medial winging of the scapula from serratus anterior weakness implicates injury to the:
questions.x: The long thoracic nerve (C5-C7) runs on the serratus fascia and is vulnerable to surgery, traction and neuralgic amyotrophy.

questions.q: The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) may be injured in the posterior cervical triangle (e.g., lymph node biopsy), producing weakness of the:
o: Trapezius, with lateral scapular winging and shoulder droop
questions.x: Trapezius weakness drops the shoulder and wings the scapula laterally - a recognized cause of posterior triangle pain.

questions.q: The ilioinguinal nerve provides sensation to the:
o: Skin over the inguinal crease, mons pubis and root of the penis/anterior scrotum or labia
questions.x: Knowing this territory separates ilioinguinal neuralgia from genitofemoral and iliohypogastric pain after hernia surgery.

questions.q: The femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve supplies the skin over the:
questions.x: The genital branch travels the inguinal canal; the femoral branch passes under the inguinal ligament to the upper anterior thigh.

questions.q: The obturator nerve provides motor innervation primarily to the:
questions.x: It exits the medial psoas border and traverses the obturator canal; blocks treat adductor spasticity and contribute to hip analgesia.

questions.q: A femoral nerve lesion characteristically produces:
o: Weak knee extension, a diminished knee jerk and anterior thigh/medial leg numbness
questions.x: The femoral nerve drives the quadriceps and senses the anterior thigh and, via the saphenous nerve, the medial leg.

questions.q: The posterior femoral cutaneous nerve supplies the skin of the:
o: Posterior thigh (with a strip toward the popliteal fossa)
questions.x: The PFCN emerges below the piriformis with the sciatic nerve and descends superficially over the posterior thigh.

questions.q: Superior cluneal nerve entrapment produces pain referred to the:
o: Iliac crest and buttock, often mimicking lumbar radiculopathy
questions.x: The superior cluneal nerves (L1-L3 dorsal rami) cross the posterior iliac crest - a treatable cause of pseudo-sciatica.

questions.q: In the popliteal fossa, the tibial nerve is found:
o: Superficial and slightly lateral to the popliteal vein and artery
questions.x: From superficial to deep: tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery - the nerve sits just under the fascia.

questions.q: On the dorsum of the ankle, the deep peroneal nerve accompanies the:
o: Dorsalis pedis artery, between the extensor hallucis longus and extensor digitorum longus tendons
questions.x: The nerve supplies the first web space; blocks use the artery as the Doppler landmark at the ankle crease.

questions.q: The superficial peroneal nerve supplies sensation to most of the:
o: Dorsum of the foot and toes, except the first web space
questions.x: It pierces the crural fascia in the distal lateral leg; entrapment causes dorsal foot paresthesia spared by the deep branch.

questions.q: The medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve runs beside which superficial vessel of the forearm?
questions.x: This medial cord branch travels with the basilic vein; it is at risk in elbow surgery and venipuncture.

questions.q: The intercostobrachial nerve, injured during axillary surgery, arises from the:
o: Lateral cutaneous branch of the second intercostal nerve (T2)
questions.x: It senses the medial upper arm and axilla; injury causes burning axillary pain after breast or axillary surgery.

questions.q: The celiac plexus is located:
o: Posterior to the pancreas within the lesser sac
Anterolateral to the aorta at the level of the celiac trunk origin (T12-L1)
questions.x: The plexus wraps the celiac trunk origin; the splanchnic nerves feed it through the diaphragmatic crura.

questions.q: The greater splanchnic nerve arises from which levels?
questions.x: Greater (T5-T9), lesser (T10-T11) and least (T12) splanchnic nerves pierce the crus to reach the celiac plexus.

questions.q: The lumbar plexus is embedded within which muscle?
questions.x: Femoral, obturator, LFCN and genitofemoral nerves all emerge from the psoas - the basis of the psoas compartment block.

questions.q: The sacral plexus forms on the anterior (pelvic) surface of which muscle?
questions.x: The plexus condenses into the sciatic nerve on the piriformis belly before exiting the greater sciatic foramen.

questions.q: Which is NOT a component of Horner syndrome?
questions.x: Sympathetic blockade constricts the pupil (miosis) with ptosis, anhidrosis and apparent enophthalmos; mydriasis is the opposite sign.

questions.q: An articular-sided partial-thickness supraspinatus tear appears on ultrasound as:
o: A hypoechoic/anechoic defect at the articular surface near the footprint
questions.x: Articular-sided (PASTA) lesions break the deep surface at the footprint; bursal-sided lesions break the superficial surface instead.

questions.q: Which ultrasound feature best supports a full-thickness (rather than partial-thickness) rotator cuff tear?
o: A small hypoechoic focus at the articular surface
A through-and-through tendon defect with the peribursal fat and deltoid sagging onto the humeral head
questions.x: Complete defects let the deltoid and peribursal fat drop onto the bare humeral head; the cartilage interface sign adds confidence.

questions.q: For an ultrasound-guided subdeltoid bursa injection, the needle is typically advanced:
o: In-plane from the lateral side, into the bursal plane between the deltoid and the supraspinatus
questions.x: Keep the needle in the bursal plane without crossing tendon; watch the injectate distend the bursa, not the deltoid muscle.

questions.q: Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) on ultrasound is associated with thickening and hyperemia of the:
questions.x: Capsular fibrosis centers on the rotator interval/CHL and the axillary recess; Doppler hyperemia marks the painful phase.

questions.q: Before injecting a joint that may be septic (hot, swollen, febrile patient), the priority is to:
o: Aspirate the joint fluid for cell count, Gram stain and culture - and withhold corticosteroid until infection is excluded
questions.x: Steroid into a septic joint is a catastrophe; aspiration is both diagnostic and therapeutic and comes first.

questions.q: The common flexor origin of the elbow attaches to the:
questions.x: Pronator teres and the wrist flexors share this origin; tendinosis here is golfer's elbow (medial epicondylosis).

questions.q: The tendon MOST affected in lateral epicondylosis is the:
questions.x: ECRB degenerates first at the common extensor origin; the condition is tendinosis (angiofibroblastic degeneration), not true tendinitis.

questions.q: The anterior bundle of the ulnar collateral ligament of the elbow, injured in throwing athletes, inserts on the:
o: Sublime tubercle of the coronoid process of the ulna
questions.x: Scan from medial epicondyle to the sublime tubercle; valgus stress dynamically opens a lax or torn ligament.

questions.q: The carpal tunnel contains the median nerve and how many flexor tendons?
questions.x: Four FDS, four FDP and the flexor pollicis longus share the tunnel with the nerve; the ulnar bursa is the common sheath.

questions.q: The flexor retinaculum (roof of the carpal tunnel) attaches on the radial side to the:
o: Tubercles of the scaphoid and trapezium
questions.x: Radial attachment is scaphoid-trapezium, ulnar is pisiform-hamate; the nerve flattens beneath this fibrous roof.

questions.q: The most common wrist ganglion arises dorsally from the region of the:
questions.x: Dorsal ganglions track to the scapholunate interval; ultrasound shows the stalk before aspiration.

questions.q: Intersection syndrome results from friction where the first dorsal compartment tendons (APL/EPB) cross over the:
o: Flexor tendons at the carpal tunnel
Second dorsal compartment tendons (ECRL and ECRB), proximal to the wrist
questions.x: Pain and crepitus sit 5-7 cm proximal to Lister's tubercle, distinct from De Quervain at the radial styloid.

questions.q: The gluteus medius tendon inserts predominantly on which facet of the greater trochanter?
questions.x: Gluteus minimus takes the anterior facet, gluteus medius the lateral and superoposterior facets - the key insertion map for trochanteric pain.

questions.q: The superoposterior facet of the greater trochanter is described as "bare" because:
o: No tendon inserts there; the subgluteus medius bursa separates it from the gluteus medius tendon
questions.x: The bare area is where the subgluteus medius bursa sits - the usual bursal injection target in trochanteric pain syndrome.

questions.q: The direct head of the rectus femoris originates from the:
questions.x: The reflected head arises just above the acetabulum; origin apophysitis and tears occur at the AIIS in adolescents and kickers.

questions.q: Adductor-related groin pain is assessed with ultrasound at the adductor longus origin on the:
questions.x: Scan the fibrocartilaginous enthesis on the pubic body; hypoechoic thickening and neovascularity mark enthesopathy.

questions.q: The biceps femoris tendon and the lateral collateral ligament insert together (conjoined) on the:
questions.x: This posterolateral corner complex stabilizes against varus and external rotation; the common peroneal nerve curves just behind it.

questions.q: Parameniscal cysts most often develop adjacent to:
o: Horizontal (cleavage) meniscal tears, which pump joint fluid to the periphery
questions.x: A cyst beside the meniscus is a red flag for an underlying tear - aspirating the cyst alone leads to recurrence.

questions.q: Prepatellar bursitis (housemaid's knee) involves the bursa located:
o: Between the skin and the anterior surface of the patella
questions.x: It is a superficial, occupational bursitis from kneeling; exclude sepsis before steroid injection.

questions.q: The deep infrapatellar bursa lies between the distal patellar tendon and the:
questions.x: Do not confuse it with the superficial infrapatellar bursa under the skin; deep bursitis mimics distal patellar tendinopathy.

questions.q: Osgood-Schlatter disease on ultrasound shows fragmentation and swelling at the:
questions.x: Traction apophysitis of the patellar tendon insertion in growing athletes; the adult analog is distal patellar tendinopathy.

questions.q: Anterior ankle impingement on ultrasound is suggested by:
o: Bone spurs on the anterior distal tibia and talar neck, with capsular thickening
questions.x: Anterior osteophytes and synovial thickening pinch in dorsiflexion - scan the anterior recess dynamically.

questions.q: Haglund deformity, contributing to retrocalcaneal bursitis, is:
questions.x: The bony prominence pumps against the retrocalcaneal bursa and Achilles insertion (pump bump).

questions.q: The plantar fascia is thickest and most commonly diseased at its origin from the:
questions.x: Measure the fascia on longitudinal scan at the calcaneal origin; fasciosis shows hypoechoic thickening beyond 4 mm.

questions.q: The sinus tarsi, containing the interosseous talocalcaneal ligaments, lies on which side of the hindfoot?
questions.x: Sinus tarsi syndrome follows inversion injuries; it sits between talus and calcaneus on the lateral hindfoot.

questions.q: Which knob adjusts the brightness of ALL echoes in the image equally?
questions.x: TGC compensates depth-specific attenuation; overall gain brightens or darkens the whole image - trim overall gain after setting TGC.

questions.q: Machine presets (nerve, MSK, vascular) primarily change:
o: A package of frequency, focus, compounding and Doppler defaults suited to the examination
questions.x: Presets are starting points - still fine-tune frequency, gain, focus and depth manually for each patient and target.

questions.q: Electronic beam focusing in an array transducer works by:
o: A mechanical lens in front of the crystals
Firing elements with small time delays so the wavefronts converge at a chosen depth
questions.x: Phased time delays focus (and steer) the beam electronically; each additional focal zone adds transmit cycles and slows the frame rate.

questions.q: Grating and side lobes produce:
o: Echoes from strong off-axis reflectors displayed as if they were on-axis (ghost images)
questions.x: Off-axis energy returns strong echoes from bone or needles that the machine misplaces into the main image - reposition the probe if a structure does not add up.

questions.q: The maximum pulse repetition frequency of a B-mode system is limited mainly by:
o: Imaging depth - deeper targets require longer round-trip listening time
questions.x: The next pulse cannot fire until the deepest echoes of the previous line return; deep imaging therefore lowers PRF and frame rate.

questions.q: The duty factor of a typical pulsed diagnostic ultrasound system is:
o: Less than 1% - the machine listens almost all the time
questions.x: Pulses last microseconds while listening occupies most of each cycle; the low duty factor keeps average intensity low.

questions.q: Setting a HIGH color Doppler scale (high PRF) will:
o: Filter out slow-flow signals and show only faster flow
questions.x: A high scale avoids aliasing in fast arteries but loses the slow venous and hyperemic tendon flow you often want to see.

questions.q: Aliasing on color Doppler appears as:
o: Color wrap-around/inversion in the center of the vessel (red turning to blue)
questions.x: Velocities above the Nyquist limit fold onto the opposite color; raise the scale, shift the baseline or improve the angle.

questions.q: The "walk-down" technique describes:
o: Sliding the probe along a nerve
Advancing the needle in small increments under continuous imaging, confirming the tip at each step
questions.x: Incremental advancement with tip confirmation at every step is the safest way to reach deep or awkward targets.

questions.q: Which factor does NOT meaningfully affect needle visibility?
questions.x: Visibility depends on gauge, angle, beam steering, coating and tissue echogenicity - not on the syringe.

questions.q: Recommended ergonomic practice for the scanning operator includes:
o: Neutral wrist position, elbow close to the body and the patient positioned at elbow height
questions.x: Work-related musculoskeletal strain is common in sonographers; neutral posture and correct patient height prevent it.

questions.q: Saving cine clips rather than still images is most valuable for documenting:
o: Dynamic events such as tendon subluxation, impingement and injectate spread
questions.x: Dynamic pathology and needle advancement only make sense in motion - record short clips during maneuvers and injections.

questions.q: After chlorhexidine-alcohol skin preparation for an injection, you should:
o: Insert the needle immediately while wet
Wipe the solution off at once
Allow the skin to dry completely for full antiseptic effect
questions.x: Alcohol-based antiseptics need contact and evaporation time; wet insertion dilutes antisepsis and can track solution into tissue.

questions.q: If the needle tip cannot be confidently identified during an injection, the correct action is to:
o: Stop, and re-establish tip visualization (probe slide/tilt, needle jiggle, hydrolocation) before advancing further
Convert to a blind landmark technique
questions.x: Continuous tip visualization is the core safety rule of every CIPS checklist; never advance an unseen needle toward a critical structure.

questions.q: Thermal bioeffects from diagnostic ultrasound are of greatest concern when imaging:
o: Tissue immediately adjacent to bone, which absorbs strongly and heats the periosteum
questions.x: Bone absorbs ultrasound avidly; avoid long dwell times at high thermal index over periosteum.

questions.q: On the WHO analgesic ladder, step 2 adds:
o: A weak opioid (e.g., tramadol, codeine) to non-opioid analgesia
questions.x: The ladder escalates non-opioid to weak opioid to strong opioid, with adjuvants available at every step.

questions.q: Tramadol's analgesic action combines weak mu-opioid agonism with:
questions.x: The monoaminergic component adds neuropathic efficacy but creates serotonin-syndrome and seizure risks, especially with antidepressants.

questions.q: Methadone requires extra caution among opioids because of:
o: QT prolongation and a long, variable elimination half-life causing delayed accumulation
questions.x: The analgesic effect fades long before the drug does; ECG monitoring and slow titration are essential.

questions.q: Buprenorphine differs from full opioid agonists because it is:
o: A partial mu agonist with a ceiling effect on respiratory depression
questions.x: The respiratory ceiling improves safety, but its high receptor affinity can precipitate withdrawal in patients taking full agonists.

questions.q: Naloxone in opioid overdose may need repeated dosing or infusion because:
o: Its half-life is shorter than most opioids it reverses
It does not enter the CNS
questions.x: Recurrent respiratory depression follows naloxone clearance whenever the offending opioid outlasts it.

questions.q: NSAID-induced renal impairment is mediated by:
o: Prostaglandin inhibition causing afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction
questions.x: Risk peaks with dehydration, CKD and concomitant ACE inhibitors/ARBs or diuretics - check renal function in older patients.

questions.q: The principal clinical advantage of COX-2 selective NSAIDs is:
o: Reduced gastrointestinal bleeding and no antiplatelet effect
questions.x: COX-2 selectivity spares gastric mucosa and platelet function; renal and cardiovascular cautions remain.

questions.q: Water-soluble (non-particulate) corticosteroids are preferred when injecting:
o: Superficial sites and foraminal regions, to reduce skin atrophy and embolic risk
questions.x: Particulate crystals cause depigmentation and fat atrophy superficially and can embolize radicular arteries; dexamethasone avoids both problems.

questions.q: A post-injection "steroid flare" typically presents as:
o: Increased pain 24-48 hours after injection, settling spontaneously
questions.x: Crystal-induced synovitis is self-limited - warn patients, treat with ice and simple analgesia, and distinguish it from infection.

questions.q: Systemic absorption after epidural corticosteroid injection can suppress:
o: The thyroid axis for a year
questions.x: HPA suppression and hyperglycemia are transient but real - one reason dose and frequency are limited.

questions.q: A commonly quoted annual ceiling for epidural steroid injections in one patient is about:
questions.x: Cumulative steroid load (bone density, HPA, glucose) argues for spacing; ongoing need beyond this warrants re-evaluation.

questions.q: Prolotherapy involves repeated injection of:
o: A proliferant such as hypertonic dextrose into ligaments and entheses
questions.x: The irritant provokes a healing response in chronically painful entheses; evidence is strongest for selected tendinopathies and SIJ dysfunction.

questions.q: Bone marrow aspirate concentrate (BMAC) is injected for:
o: Regenerative treatment of osteoarthritis and tendinopathy using the patient's own marrow-derived cells and growth factors
questions.x: Marrow is harvested from the iliac crest, concentrated and injected under ultrasound guidance - an office regenerative option alongside PRP.

questions.q: Cryoneurotomy differs from thermal radiofrequency in that it:
o: Freezes the nerve to about -70°C, producing Wallerian degeneration while preserving the perineurium, so the nerve regenerates
questions.x: The preserved connective-tissue scaffolding lets axons regrow over months - a reversible sensory block used for intercostal and occipital nerves.

questions.q: A typical pulsed radiofrequency protocol delivers:
o: Short pulses (e.g., 20 ms at 2 Hz) with pauses, keeping tip temperature at or below 42°C for 2-4 minutes
questions.x: The electric field, not heat, modulates dorsal horn and DRG signaling; tissue is not destroyed, so it suits DRG and peripheral nerves.

questions.q: On a sagittal cervical scan, the C2 level is recognized by:
o: The first bifid spinous process with the prominent drooping C2 inferior articular process
questions.x: The bifid C2 spinous process and its large inferior articular process anchor level counting from above; confirm C7 from below.

questions.q: The C8 nerve root exits the spinal canal between:
questions.x: Cervical roots exit above their same-numbered vertebra (C5 exits above C5); C8 is the exception, exiting between C7 and T1.

questions.q: Anterior narrowing of the cervical intervertebral foramen is usually caused by osteophytes from the:
questions.x: Uncovertebral spurs narrow the foramen anteriorly while facet hypertrophy narrows it posteriorly - the root is squeezed between them.

questions.q: The commonest levels for cervical disc herniation are:
questions.x: These mobile lower segments degenerate first; C6 and C7 radiculopathies dominate the clinical picture.

questions.q: A positive Spurling maneuver (neck extension with rotation toward the painful side) suggests:
questions.x: Reproduction of radiating arm pain is specific for root irritation; axial pain without radiation points elsewhere.

questions.q: The commonest levels for lumbar disc herniation are:
questions.x: The lower two segments bear the greatest load and motion; L5 and S1 radiculopathies predominate.

questions.q: A posterolateral L4-5 disc herniation typically compresses the:
questions.x: In the lateral recess the traversing root is compressed; only far-lateral (extraforaminal) herniations catch the exiting root.

questions.q: The lumbar multifidus muscle overlies which sonographic targets?
o: The facet joints, laminae and medial branches
questions.x: Multifidus and the erector spinae group cover the posterior elements; they are traversed or displaced in medial branch and ESP techniques.

questions.q: On ultrasound of the sacral hiatus, the sacrococcygeal ligament appears as:
o: A hyperechoic band stretched between the two sacral cornua over the anechoic canal
questions.x: The ligament plus the two cornua frame the classic 'frog-eye' hiatus view before puncture.

questions.q: A typical injectate volume for caudal epidural injection is:
questions.x: The capacious sacral canal accepts larger volumes, which also carry injectate up several lumbar levels.

questions.q: Without image guidance, the reported intra-articular success rate of sacroiliac joint injection is approximately:
questions.x: The irregular, deep joint defeats blind placement - image guidance is effectively mandatory, and even then only the inferior recess is reached.

questions.q: The widest lumbar interlaminar window for viewing the thecal sac is:
questions.x: The L5-S1 interlaminar gap is the largest and the easiest window for neuraxial sonoanatomy.

questions.q: On a thoracic scan, a transverse process is confirmed sonographically by its relation to the:
o: Rib, which articulates with it at the costotransverse joint
questions.x: Following a rib medially leads to its costotransverse joint and transverse process - the anchor for paravertebral and medial branch blocks.

questions.q: Piriformis syndrome is supported clinically by pain reproduced with:
o: The FAIR test (flexion, adduction and internal rotation of the hip)
questions.x: FAIR stretches the piriformis against the sciatic nerve; combine with muscle tenderness and exclusion of lumbar causes.

questions.q: During ganglion impar block, ideal injectate spread is seen:
o: In the midline presacral plane anterior to the sacrococcygeal junction
questions.x: The ganglion lies on the ventral surface of the junction; midline presacral spread without intravascular uptake confirms placement.

questions.q: The superior hypogastric plexus relays pain from which organs?
o: Pelvic viscera - bladder, uterus/prostate and rectum
questions.x: This is the target for cancer and chronic pelvic pain; the plexus lies over the L5-S1 disc below the aortic bifurcation.

questions.q: The most urgent imaging study for suspected epidural abscess after an injection is:
questions.x: Back pain with fever and new neurology after neuraxial injection is an emergency; early MRI and drainage prevent paralysis.

questions.q: Clopidogrel should be withheld for how long before high-risk neuraxial pain procedures?
questions.x: Platelet inhibition is irreversible; neuraxial work needs 5-7 drug-free days - coordinate with the prescriber and current guidance.

questions.q: Direct oral anticoagulants such as apixaban are typically withheld before high-risk (neuraxial) injections for:
questions.x: DOAC half-lives are short; timing depends on the drug, procedural bleeding risk and creatinine clearance - document the plan.

questions.q: Controlled-block studies show that chronic pain after whiplash injury most commonly originates from the:
o: Cervical zygapophysial (facet) joints, especially C2-3 and C5-6
questions.x: Facet joints account for the majority of chronic whiplash pain, which is why medial branch blocks dominate its workup.

questions.q: The three trunks of the brachial plexus are named:
questions.x: Roots form trunks (upper C5-6, middle C7, lower C8-T1), then divisions, cords and branches; the supraclavicular fossa shows the trunks.

questions.q: An interscalene block most characteristically spares sensation in the:
o: Ulnar hand and medial forearm (C8-T1 territory)
questions.x: The lower trunk sits deepest in the groove and is often missed - ulnar sparing is the classic interscalene gap.

questions.q: Axillary nerve block is most often added to suprascapular block for analgesia of:
o: The lateral shoulder/deltoid region and shoulder joint surgery
questions.x: Suprascapular plus axillary blocks cover most shoulder joint innervation - an opioid-sparing alternative to interscalene block.

questions.q: Reduced longitudinal gliding of the median nerve in carpal tunnel syndrome is assessed by:
o: Dynamic ultrasound during finger and wrist flexion-extension
questions.x: The nerve normally slides under the retinaculum; restricted gliding plus inlet swelling supports CTS.

questions.q: The deep motor branch of the ulnar nerve at the wrist curves around the:
questions.x: The motor branch dives between pisiform and hamate; ganglion cysts here cause pure motor ulnar palsy.

questions.q: Cheiralgia paresthetica (Wartenberg syndrome) involves entrapment of the:
o: Superficial radial sensory nerve between brachioradialis and ECRL
questions.x: Watch straps and tight bands compress the nerve where it becomes superficial in the distal forearm - 'handcuff neuropathy'.

questions.q: Proper digital nerves of the fingers accompany the:
o: Digital arteries along the lateral aspects of each finger
questions.x: Locate the pulsatile digital artery with the hockey-stick probe; the nerve lies beside it - the basis of digital blocks.

questions.q: The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is notable for:
o: Being absent in half of people
Always passing through the inguinal canal
Course variants in roughly a quarter of individuals, sometimes piercing the sartorius
questions.x: Variability explains failed blocks; scan from the ASIS along the sartorius and compare sides before injecting.

questions.q: A transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block anesthetizes which segments?
o: T10-L1 thoracolumbar nerves running between internal oblique and transversus abdominis
questions.x: The fascial plane between the two muscles carries the anterior rami supplying the anterolateral abdominal wall.

questions.q: A rectus sheath block places injectate:
o: Between the rectus muscle and the posterior rectus sheath, bathing the anterior cutaneous intercostal branches
questions.x: It treats midline abdominal wall pain and somatic causes of chronic abdominal pain.

questions.q: A quadratus lumborum (QL) block targets the fascial plane:
o: Around the quadratus lumborum muscle, spreading toward the thoracolumbar fascia and paravertebral region
questions.x: Anterior, posterior and lateral QL approaches give abdominal and hip analgesia by spread along the thoracolumbar fascia.

questions.q: A PECS II / serratus anterior plane block deposits injectate:
o: At the level of the serratus anterior over the ribs (between pectoralis minor/latissimus and serratus)
questions.x: The plane block covers the lateral cutaneous intercostal branches for breast and chest-wall analgesia.

questions.q: Injectate from an erector spinae plane block at T5 spreads mainly to affect:
o: The dorsal rami (and variably ventral rami) over several vertebral levels
questions.x: Craniocaudal spread along the plane explains multi-level posterior thoracic analgesia; ventral extension is variable.

questions.q: The fascia iliaca compartment block bathes the femoral nerve and which companion nerve?
questions.x: Both nerves lie under the fascia iliaca; large-volume injection lateral to the femoral artery covers both (obturator coverage is inconsistent).

questions.q: On ultrasound in the medial thigh, the anterior and posterior divisions of the obturator nerve are found between the:
o: Adductor longus/brevis and adductor brevis/magnus planes
questions.x: The divisions run sandwiched between adductor muscle layers - identify the fascial planes, then block each division.

questions.q: At mid-thigh, the sciatic nerve lies posterior to the femur between the biceps femoris and the:
questions.x: The 'hamstring channel' between biceps femoris laterally and adductor magnus deep-medially is the classic mid-thigh sciatic window.

questions.q: The "V" sign in distal popliteal scanning is formed by:
o: The tibial and common peroneal nerves joining to form the sciatic nerve
questions.x: Injecting within the common paraneural sheath at the junction gives fast, complete sciatic block with a small volume.

questions.q: A complete ankle block requires anesthesia of how many nerves?
o: 5 - tibial, sural, saphenous, deep peroneal and superficial peroneal
questions.x: The five terminal nerves around the ankle give complete foot anesthesia; ultrasound guides each small-volume block.

questions.q: At the medial ankle, the saphenous nerve accompanies the:
o: Great saphenous vein, anterior to the medial malleolus
questions.x: Trace the vein in front of the medial malleolus; the nerve beside it is the terminal sensory branch of the femoral nerve.

questions.q: The anterior approach to the cervical sympathetic trunk is performed at C6 rather than C7 because at C7:
o: The vertebral artery has usually not yet entered the foramen and the pleural dome is closer
questions.x: Working at C6 (Chassaignac tubercle) keeps the needle away from the unprotected artery and the lung apex while injectate descends to the ganglion.

questions.q: A retrocrural splanchnic nerve block differs from an antecrural celiac plexus block in that it targets the splanchnic nerves:
o: Before they pass through the diaphragmatic crura, at the T11-T12 vertebral level
questions.x: Retrocrural blocks hit the splanchnic nerves (with pneumothorax risk); antecrural blocks hit the celiac plexus around the celiac trunk.

questions.q: An objective sign of a successful lumbar sympathetic block is:
o: Ipsilateral foot skin temperature rise of about 2°C or more
questions.x: Sympathetic vasodilation warms the foot - the lower-limb analog of Horner syndrome after stellate block.

questions.q: Neurolytic superior hypogastric plexus block is most appropriate for:
o: Cancer-related pelvic pain poorly controlled by opioids
questions.x: Phenol or alcohol neurolysis of the presacral plexus reduces pelvic cancer pain and opioid burden.

questions.q: Sphenopalatine (pterygopalatine) ganglion block is used primarily for:
o: Cluster headache and other trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias
questions.x: The ganglion carries parasympathetic outflow to lacrimal and nasal glands; infrazygomatic and transnasal approaches block it.

questions.q: Radiofrequency treatment of the gasserian (trigeminal) ganglion is performed for:
questions.x: The ganglion sits in Meckel's cave; lesioning is done under fluoroscopy through the foramen ovale - ultrasound cannot see it.

questions.q: The transverse humeral ligament roofs the bicipital groove, spanning between the:
questions.x: The roofed groove holds the long head of biceps; tendon subluxation out of it signals pulley and subscapularis failure.

questions.q: Structures compressed in subacromial impingement pass beneath the coracoacromial arch; they include the supraspinatus tendon and the:
questions.x: The bursa cushions tendon glide under the arch; bursal thickening and fluid worsen the impingement cycle.

questions.q: In the formative (quiet) phase of calcific tendinitis, the deposit appears on ultrasound as:
o: A well-defined hyperechoic focus with posterior shadowing
questions.x: The painful resorptive phase is ill-defined with little shadowing and rich Doppler flow - and is the best moment for barbotage.

questions.q: Acute rupture of the long head of biceps shows which ultrasound sign?
o: An empty bicipital groove with the retracted muscle belly (Popeye sign)
questions.x: Confirm by scanning the retracted stump distally; associated rotator cuff pathology is common in older patients.

questions.q: A spinoglenoid notch paralabral cyst usually signals an underlying:
questions.x: Fluid escapes through the labral tear into the notch, where the cyst can compress the suprascapular nerve - aspirate cautiously.

questions.q: The roof of the cubital tunnel is formed by the:
o: Osborne fascia (arcuate ligament) bridging the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris
questions.x: Release targets this fascia; the tunnel floor is the medial collateral ligament and capsule - watch for nerve subluxation on flexion.

questions.q: The easiest elbow recess for ultrasound-guided aspiration or injection is the:
o: Anterior recess with the arm extended
Posterior (olecranon fossa) recess with the elbow flexed
questions.x: Flexion moves fluid posteriorly and opens the fossa; the needle enters above the olecranon, avoiding triceps tendon and ulnar nerve.

questions.q: Bicipitoradial bursitis produces pain in the:
o: Antecubital fossa, aggravated by resisted supination
questions.x: The bursa wraps the distal biceps tendon; distension compresses nearby structures and mimics an antecubital mass.

questions.q: The six dorsal wrist compartments are defined by septa of the:
o: Extensor retinaculum attaching to the radius and ulna
