questions.x: Numbering runs radial to ulnar; compartment anatomy directs injection of De Quervain (first) and intersection (second) syndromes.

questions.q: The extensor pollicis longus tendon changes direction at which landmark?
questions.x: EPL angulates around Lister's tubercle toward the thumb; friction here predisposes to rupture after distal radius fractures.

questions.q: The scaphoid is prone to avascular necrosis of its proximal pole after fracture because its blood supply is:
o: Retrograde, entering distally and flowing back toward the proximal pole
questions.x: Fracture interrupts this distal-to-proximal flow; suspect scaphoid injury with snuffbox tenderness and initially negative films.

questions.q: Hypothenar hammer syndrome injures which structure in Guyon's canal?
questions.x: Repetitive palm impact against the hamate damages the superficial palmar branch of the ulnar artery - check it with Doppler.

questions.q: Cam-type femoroacetabular impingement is caused by:
o: An aspherical bony bump at the femoral head-neck junction reducing the normal offset
questions.x: The cam lesion jams into the rim in flexion-internal rotation, damaging labrum and cartilage; pincer morphology is the acetabular counterpart.

questions.q: During ultrasound-guided hip joint injection from an anterolateral approach, the correct final needle position is:
o: Within the anterior synovial recess along the femoral neck, with capsular distension on injection
questions.x: Watch injectate lift the capsule off the neck; contact with cartilage or flow toward the femoral vessels means repositioning.

questions.q: Pain and weakness on resisted hip abduction implicates pathology of the:
questions.x: Resisted abduction and the Trendelenburg sign test the abductor mechanism - the clinical pair of trochanteric pain syndrome.

questions.q: Quadratus femoris muscle edema on imaging suggests which hip disorder?
o: Ischiofemoral impingement between the ischium and the lesser trochanter
questions.x: Narrowing of the ischiofemoral space (after surgery, dysplasia or degeneration) traps the quadratus femoris - a cause of deep buttock pain.

questions.q: The iliotibial band inserts distally on:
o: Gerdy's tubercle of the proximal tibia
questions.x: Friction occurs more proximally at the lateral femoral epicondyle; the insertion itself rarely hurts - scan both sites in runners.

questions.q: Iliotibial band friction syndrome develops where the band glides over the:
o: Lateral femoral epicondyle at about 30 degrees of knee flexion
questions.x: Compression peaks near 30 degrees of flexion; ultrasound shows band thickening and periband fluid in runners and cyclists.

questions.q: Injury of the medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL) most often follows:
o: A direct blow to the tibia
questions.x: The MPFL is the main medial restraint; scan it along the medial patellar border after a first dislocation.

questions.q: The bursa between the quadriceps tendon and the distal femur, communicating with the knee joint, is the:
questions.x: The suprapatellar pouch is the largest knee recess and the standard ultrasound-guided injection window from lateral or medial.

questions.q: Meniscal healing is limited because the inner two-thirds of the meniscus (white zone) is:
o: Essentially avascular, receiving nutrition from synovial fluid
questions.x: Only the peripheral third (red zone) is vascular; white-zone tears rarely heal - relevant to injection targets and cyst formation.

questions.q: The superficial deltoid ligament of the medial ankle runs from the medial malleolus to the:
o: Navicular, sustentaculum tali of the calcaneus and talus
questions.x: Its fan-shaped fibers resist eversion; deep fibers reach the medial talus - assess both layers after eversion injuries.

questions.q: A "high ankle sprain" primarily injures the:
questions.x: External rotation injuries tear the AITFL/syndesmosis; squeeze and external rotation tests are positive and widening appears on stress views.

questions.q: For ultrasound-guided subtalar joint injection, the standard window is the:
o: Lateral subtalar recess at the sinus tarsi
questions.x: The lateral sinus tarsi window shows the posterior facet recess - inject there for subtalar arthritis or coalition pain.

questions.q: The sesamoid bones beneath the first metatarsal head lie within the tendons of the:
questions.x: The medial and lateral sesamoids sit in the two FHB heads; sesamoiditis and fractures mimic metatarsalgia - compare sides.

questions.q: Ultrasound used in medical imaging consists of which type of wave?
questions.x: Diagnostic ultrasound is a longitudinal mechanical wave: tissue particles oscillate parallel to the direction of propagation, creating alternating zones of compression and rarefaction. It requires a medium and cannot travel through a vacuum, unlike electromagnetic radiation.

questions.q: For a 10 MHz transducer, the wavelength in soft tissue (assuming 1540 m/s) is approximately:
questions.x: Wavelength = speed / frequency = 1540 m/s / 10,000,000 Hz = 0.154 mm. Shorter wavelengths at higher frequency give better axial resolution but less penetration, which is why 10 MHz is reserved for superficial structures.

questions.q: Which structure acts as a specular reflector during an ultrasound scan?
questions.x: Specular reflectors are large, smooth interfaces (fascia, pleura, peritoneum, tendon surface) that reflect the beam like a mirror; the echo returns only when the beam is near-perpendicular. Red blood cells are Rayleigh scatterers instead.

questions.q: Rayleigh scattering from red blood cells is the physical basis of:
questions.x: Red blood cells are much smaller than the wavelength, so they scatter the beam in all directions (Rayleigh scattering). The weak scattered echoes returning from moving cells carry the frequency shifts that Doppler ultrasound converts into flow information.

questions.q: As ultrasound propagates through tissue, absorption converts acoustic energy primarily into:
questions.x: Absorption converts acoustic energy into heat and rises steeply with frequency; it is the dominant cause of attenuation in soft tissue. This heating underlies the thermal index displayed on the machine and is why prolonged scanning of sensitive tissues is avoided.

questions.q: The region of the beam between the transducer face and the natural focus is called the:
questions.x: The Fresnel (near) zone extends from the transducer face to the natural focus, where the beam is narrowest and resolution best; beyond it lies the diverging Fraunhofer (far) zone. The adjustable focal zone should sit at or just below the target.

questions.q: A linear-array transducer produces which image shape?
questions.x: Linear arrays fire groups of elements sequentially along a flat footprint, producing a rectangular image with a wide near field — ideal for vascular access and superficial nerve blocks. Curvilinear and phased arrays produce diverging sector images.

questions.q: Trapezoid imaging on a linear probe is used to:
questions.x: Trapezoid (wide-view) imaging steers the outer beams outward so the image widens with depth, enlarging the far field to keep diverging structures — such as a needle approaching from in-plane — within view.

questions.q: Which control increases the patient's acoustic exposure?
questions.x: Transmit power raises the amplitude of the emitted pulse, increasing acoustic exposure (mechanical and thermal indices rise). Gain and TGC only amplify the returning echoes electronically and have no effect on the energy delivered to tissue.

questions.q: After scanning intact skin, the transducer should be disinfected according to:
o: Immersion in glutaraldehyde for all probes
questions.x: Probe housings and acoustic lenses are damaged by many chemicals (including alcohol on some models). Low-level disinfection with a manufacturer-approved agent is required after intact-skin use; semi-critical uses need high-level disinfection and a sterile cover.

questions.q: Widening the color Doppler box has which effect?
questions.x: Each color line requires multiple pulses per line (ensemble length), so a larger color box demands many more pulses per frame and the frame rate falls. Keep the box narrow and shallow, just covering the vessel of interest, especially when guiding a needle.

questions.q: High persistence (frame averaging) on B-mode will:
questions.x: Persistence averages successive frames, suppressing speckle noise and smoothing the image, but at the cost of temporal resolution — moving needles and pulsating vessels appear blurred. Lower persistence is preferred during needle guidance.

questions.q: To best demonstrate acoustic shadowing and anisotropy, which feature should be turned OFF?
questions.x: Spatial compound imaging steers beams from multiple angles and averages the frames, which fills in shadowing and smooths angle-dependent anisotropy. Switching it off restores the shadowing and anisotropy cues that help confirm tendon and needle-tip identity.

questions.q: When the image of a target is suboptimal, the FIRST step is to:
o: Re-optimize depth, gain, focus and frequency
questions.x: Systematic optimization — depth so the target fills the mid-screen, gain for balanced brightness, focal zone at the target, and the highest frequency that penetrates — resolves most poor images before any equipment change is considered.

questions.q: Before any local-anesthetic injection, best practice for local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) is to:
o: Calculate the dose after the injection
Pre-calculate the maximum dose and have lipid emulsion available
Give a sedative premedication to all patients
questions.x: Safe practice requires a weight-based maximum dose calculated before drawing up the drug, incremental injection with aspiration, verbal contact with the patient, and 20% lipid emulsion immediately available wherever potentially toxic doses are used.

questions.q: Pain produced by a stimulus that does not normally provoke pain is termed:
questions.x: Allodynia is pain from a normally non-painful stimulus (e.g., light touch in postherpetic neuralgia). Hyperalgesia is an exaggerated response to a normally painful stimulus — the distinction is a classic exam discriminator.

questions.q: Central sensitization is best defined as:
o: Increased responsiveness of nociceptive neurons in the peripheral nerve
Increased responsiveness of nociceptive neurons within the CNS to normal or subthreshold input
questions.x: Central sensitization is enhanced synaptic transmission and excitability of central nociceptive neurons (spinal dorsal horn and above), producing pain hypersensitivity, spread of pain beyond the injury site, and pain from low-threshold input. NMDA receptor activation is a key mechanism.

questions.q: The descending inhibitory pain pathway from the brainstem to the dorsal horn uses mainly:
questions.x: The periaqueductal gray and rostroventral medulla project to the dorsal horn, releasing serotonin and norepinephrine to suppress nociceptive transmission. This dual mechanism is why SNRIs and tricyclics are effective in neuropathic and centralized pain states.

questions.q: According to the gate control theory, which fiber closes the 'gate' to nociceptive transmission?
questions.x: Activation of large myelinated A-beta fibers (rubbing, TENS) stimulates inhibitory interneurons in the substantia gelatinosa, reducing transmission from small A-delta and C fibers — the anatomical basis of TENS and rubbing an injured area.

questions.q: The biopsychosocial model of chronic pain emphasizes:
o: Interaction of biological, psychological and social factors
questions.x: Chronic pain is shaped by nociception plus mood, beliefs, catastrophizing, work, family and compensation factors. Assessment and treatment must address all three domains; purely biomedical management of chronic pain repeatedly fails.

questions.q: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for chronic pain primarily targets:
questions.x: CBT identifies and reframes catastrophizing, fear-avoidance beliefs and maladaptive behaviors, replacing them with active coping strategies, pacing and graded activity. It has strong evidence in chronic low back pain and fibromyalgia.

questions.q: First-line management of non-specific chronic low back pain is:
questions.x: Major guidelines place exercise, physical activity and self-management first, with psychological therapy for those with persistent disability; imaging and passive modalities are discouraged early. Opioids and surgery are last resorts for selected patients.

questions.q: A patient with acute non-specific low back pain should be advised to:
o: Take strict bed rest for one week
Stay active and avoid bed rest
questions.x: Advice to remain active, reassurance about the benign natural history, and avoidance of bed rest are the core of acute low back pain care; bed rest prolongs disability. Imaging is reserved for red flags.

questions.q: The cornerstone of treatment for complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) is:
questions.x: CRPS management rests on early, graded functional restoration and desensitization physiotherapy; interventional sympathetic blocks are used as an adjunct to enable therapy, not as stand-alone cures. Immobilization worsens stiffness and trophic change.

questions.q: Diagnosis of fibromyalgia is currently based on:
o: ACR criteria using widespread pain index and symptom severity
questions.x: The 2010/2016 ACR criteria score the widespread pain index and symptom severity scale (fatigue, unrefreshed sleep, cognitive symptoms); the older tender-point examination is no longer required. Fibromyalgia reflects centralized pain processing.

questions.q: Phantom limb pain after amputation arises from:
questions.x: Phantom pain combines peripheral drivers (stump neuroma, ectopic discharges) with central reorganization of the sensory cortex and deafferentation changes. Ultrasound can identify treatable stump neuromas; mirror therapy addresses cortical reorganization.

questions.q: On ultrasound, a post-amputation stump neuroma typically appears as:
o: A fusiform hypoechoic mass in continuity with the nerve
questions.x: A neuroma is a focal, fusiform, hypoechoic enlargement continuous with the proximal nerve, often tender under the probe (sonographic Tinel sign). Identifying it guides injection, ablation or surgical revision.

questions.q: Postherpetic neuralgia is defined as pain persisting for at least:
questions.x: PHN is conventionally defined as pain persisting ≥3 months after herpes zoster rash onset. Risk rises with age and acute pain severity; early antivirals and the recombinant zoster vaccine reduce incidence.

questions.q: Failed back surgery syndrome (FBSS) refers to:
o: Persistent or recurrent pain after one or more spinal surgeries
questions.x: FBSS (persistent spinal pain syndrome type 2) describes chronic axial and/or radicular pain persisting or recurring despite technically adequate surgery. Work-up seeks residual stenosis, epidural fibrosis, adjacent-segment disease and facet or sacroiliac sources.

questions.q: The best indication for spinal cord stimulation among the following is:
o: Neuropathic leg-predominant pain after spinal surgery
questions.x: SCS has its strongest evidence for leg-predominant neuropathic pain of FBSS and for CRPS, after failed conservative care and a successful trial. Pure axial mechanical pain and very short prognoses are poor indications.

questions.q: For a third occipital nerve (TON) block, the patient is positioned:
o: Sitting with the neck fully flexed
Lateral decubitus or prone with the neck neutral
Supine with the head turned away
questions.x: TON blocks are performed with the patient lateral (side-lying, pain side up) or prone, allowing a posterolateral or posterior ultrasound approach to the C2–3 joint line, where the nerve crosses the articulation between the C2 and C3 articular pillars.

questions.q: On a sagittal ultrasound scan of the cervical spine, the facet joint appears as:
o: An anechoic gap between the articular pillars
questions.x: In a parasagittal view the articular pillars appear as a series of hyperechoic humps ('saw-tooth'), and the facet joint is the anechoic gap between adjacent pillars — the landmark for intra-articular injection and medial branch localization.

questions.q: The preferred level for an ultrasound-guided cervical interlaminar epidural injection is:
questions.x: The lower cervical interspaces (C6–7, C7–T1) offer the widest epidural space and the greatest distance from the cord, and the ligamentum flavum is best developed caudally. The C1–2 level has essentially no epidural space and is never used.

questions.q: A sequestered disc fragment is one that:
o: Has separated completely from the parent disc
questions.x: The progression runs bulge → protrusion → extrusion → sequestration. In sequestration the extruded fragment loses continuity with the parent disc and may migrate; paradoxically, sequestered fragments have the highest rate of spontaneous resorption.

questions.q: A high-intensity zone (HIZ) on a T2-weighted lumbar MRI indicates:
o: An annular fissure with granulation tissue
questions.x: HIZ is a bright T2 signal within the posterior annulus representing an annular fissure with vascularized granulation tissue; it correlates with internal disc disruption and discogenic pain in symptomatic patients.

questions.q: Pain that is characteristically worse with sitting and forward flexion suggests a:
questions.x: Sitting and flexion load the disc and increase intradiscal pressure, aggravating discogenic pain; patients often prefer standing. Extension/rotation pain points to facet joints, and the distinction guides the diagnostic block pathway.

questions.q: Lumbar facet-mediated pain is typically aggravated by:
questions.x: Extension and ipsilateral rotation load the facet joints (facet loading test), reproducing facet-mediated pain, usually paramedian without radiation below the knee. Flexion relieves it — the opposite pattern to discogenic pain.

questions.q: Modic type 1 endplate change on MRI represents:
o: Bone marrow edema (low T1, high T2)
questions.x: Modic 1 = edema/inflammation (dark T1, bright T2), associated with active degeneration and back pain; Modic 2 = fatty change (bright T1); Modic 3 = sclerosis (dark on both sequences).

questions.q: Isthmic spondylolisthesis results from a defect in the:
questions.x: A stress fracture or defect of the pars interarticularis (the 'neck of the Scotty dog' on oblique views) permits anterior vertebral slip, most often at L5–S1, and can narrow the foramen and stretch the exiting root.

questions.q: Neurogenic claudication from lumbar spinal stenosis is classically relieved by:
o: Flexion (e.g., leaning on a shopping cart)
questions.x: Flexion opens the canal and foramina ('shopping cart sign'), relieving stenotic leg symptoms; extension and downhill walking worsen them. Vascular claudication, in contrast, is not position-dependent and is relieved simply by stopping.

questions.q: Hypertrophy of the ligamentum flavum contributes primarily to:
questions.x: Buckling and hypertrophy of the ligamentum flavum, together with disc bulging and facet arthropathy, narrows the central canal posterolaterally; it is a major component of degenerative central stenosis in older patients.

questions.q: In adults, the dural sac normally ends at the level of:
questions.x: The dural sac terminates at approximately S2 (the landmark used for caudal epidural depth), while the conus ends at L1–L2. Puncture below the sacral hiatus through the sacrococcygeal ligament therefore stays safely extradural when kept shallow.

questions.q: Tarlov cysts are:
o: Perineural cysts of the sacral nerve root sleeves
questions.x: Tarlov (perineural) cysts are CSF-filled dilations of the sacral nerve root sleeves, usually at S2–S3. Most are incidental, but large cysts can cause sacral radicular pain and may mimic other pathology on imaging.

questions.q: Third occipital nerve radiofrequency neurotomy should be performed only after:
questions.x: Because single blocks carry a high false-positive rate, international practice requires dual comparative or placebo-controlled diagnostic TON blocks with concordant responses before proceeding to radiofrequency neurotomy of the C2–3 joint.

questions.q: Before a C1–2 lateral atlanto-axial joint injection, which conditions must be screened for?
questions.x: Atlanto-axial instability from transverse ligament laxity (Down syndrome) or pannus (rheumatoid arthritis) makes C1–2 instrumentation hazardous; flexion-extension imaging or clinical screening is mandatory before lateral C1–2 joint procedures.

questions.q: A cervical transforaminal epidural steroid injection aims to place injectate in the:
o: Ventral epidural space near the target root
questions.x: The transforaminal route targets the ventral epidural space, bathing the inflamed nerve root directly. It also carries the highest risk of radicular artery injection, which is why particulate steroid, live imaging and digital subtraction precautions apply.

questions.q: Loss of resistance during an interlaminar epidural is performed with:
questions.x: Continuous pressure on a low-resistance syringe of saline (preferred) or air is used; loss of resistance occurs as the needle passes the ligamentum flavum into the epidural space. Ultrasound can measure the skin-to-ligament distance beforehand.

questions.q: Pain relief after lumbar medial branch radiofrequency neurotomy typically lasts:
questions.x: Coagulation of the medial branches denervates the facet joint for roughly 6–12 months until the nerves regenerate, at which point the procedure can be repeated. Comparative-block confirmation beforehand improves success rates.

questions.q: The Gaenslen test stresses the sacroiliac joint by:
o: One hip flexed to the chest, the other extended off the table
questions.x: Gaenslen's test applies torsion across both SIJs by simultaneously flexing one hip and hyperextending the other over the table edge. A positive result reproduces ipsilateral buttock pain and forms part of the SIJ provocative test cluster.

questions.q: The sciatic nerve normally exits the pelvis:
o: Below the piriformis through the greater sciatic foramen
Above the piriformis with the superior gluteal nerve
questions.x: The sciatic nerve passes through the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis in the majority of people; variants in which the nerve (or its peroneal division) pierces or passes above the piriformis are relevant to deep gluteal syndrome.

questions.q: The terminal branches of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus are the:
questions.x: The posterior cord terminates as the radial nerve (via the posterior divisions of all three trunks) and the axillary nerve. Remembering cords by their position around the axillary artery simplifies localization during infraclavicular block.

questions.q: The lateral cord of the brachial plexus gives rise to the:
o: Ulnar nerve and medial root of the median nerve
Musculocutaneous nerve and lateral root of the median nerve
questions.x: The lateral cord splits into the musculocutaneous nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve (the 'M' of the MARMU mnemonic at cord level). This is why a musculocutaneous block must sometimes be added separately to infraclavicular blocks.

questions.q: The median nerve is formed by contributions from:
o: Both the lateral and medial cords
questions.x: The median nerve is formed where the lateral root (lateral cord, C5–C7) and medial root (medial cord, C8–T1) clasp the axillary artery — reflecting its dual motor (forearm flexors) and sensory (hand) territory.

questions.q: During supraclavicular block, the pleural dome is at risk because it lies:
o: Behind the first rib, medial to the subclavian artery
Lateral to the brachial plexus trunks
Anterior to the anterior scalene muscle
questions.x: The pleural dome rises behind the medial first rib close to the plexus corner pocket. Keeping the needle in plane, visualizing the first rib and pleura continuously, and never advancing blindly medial prevents pneumothorax.

questions.q: The dorsal scapular nerve (C5) innervates the:
questions.x: The dorsal scapular nerve arises from the C5 root, pierces the middle scalene and supplies the rhomboid major and minor and the levator scapulae. Its entrapment produces medial scapular border pain.

questions.q: The suprascapular nerve passes through the suprascapular notch:
o: Together with the artery, both under the ligament
Above the superior transverse scapular ligament
Beneath the superior transverse scapular ligament, while the artery passes above it
questions.x: The nerve runs under the superior transverse scapular ligament while the suprascapular artery passes above it ('army over navy'). The nerve is blocked at the notch or floor of the supraspinous fossa for chronic shoulder pain.

questions.q: The axillary nerve travels through the quadrangular space with the:
questions.x: The quadrangular space (teres minor, teres major, long head of triceps, humeral shaft) transmits the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery — the key vascular landmark for the posterior shoulder approach to the nerve.

questions.q: The radial nerve lies in the spiral groove of the humerus between the:
o: Lateral and medial heads of the triceps
questions.x: At the spiral groove the radial nerve hugs the humerus between the lateral and medial triceps heads — a frequent site of compression ('Saturday night palsy') and a convenient ultrasound scanning point for radial neuropathy.

questions.q: The musculocutaneous nerve characteristically pierces the:
questions.x: After leaving the lateral cord, the musculocutaneous nerve pierces the coracobrachialis, then runs between biceps and brachialis before emerging as the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve. Its intramuscular course matters for axillary-block sparing.

questions.q: The deep motor branch of the ulnar nerve in the hand hooks around the:
questions.x: Within Guyon's canal the ulnar nerve divides; the deep motor branch curves around the hook of the hamate to supply the interossei and ulnar two lumbricals. Compression here causes pure motor ulnar hand weakness without sensory loss.

questions.q: The posterior interosseous nerve is most commonly compressed at the:
questions.x: The PIN enters the supinator beneath the arcade of Frohse, the classic compression site causing finger-extension weakness without wrist drop (ECRL is spared) and without sensory loss — the pure motor radial tunnel syndrome.

questions.q: Which structure does NOT pass through the carpal tunnel?
questions.x: The carpal tunnel contains the median nerve and nine flexor tendons; the ulnar nerve and artery cross the wrist through Guyon's canal superficial to the flexor retinaculum — the standard exam discriminator.

questions.q: At the C6 anterior approach, the structure overlying the stellate ganglion and separating the needle path from the carotid is the:
questions.x: The stellate ganglion lies in the prevertebral fascia over the longus colli at C6–C7. Injecting superficial to the muscle's fascia, after displacing the carotid laterally, keeps the needle away from the vertebral artery.

questions.q: For a lumbar sympathetic block, the needle tip target is the:
o: Anterolateral surface of the L2 or L3 vertebral body
questions.x: The lumbar sympathetic chain sits on the anterolateral aspect of the L2–L3 vertebral bodies, anterior to the psoas fascia. Contrast should spread in a thin linear stripe along the vertebral bodies, confirming correct pre-psoas placement.

questions.q: Paraplegia after neurolytic celiac plexus block is thought to result from injury to the:
questions.x: The artery of Adamkiewicz (major radiculomedullary feeder, usually left T9–T12) can be injured or go into spasm during retrocrural neurolysis, causing anterior spinal cord ischemia — the rare but catastrophic complication of the technique.

questions.q: The superior hypogastric plexus is located:
o: Anterior to the L5–S1 junction / sacral promontory
questions.x: The superior hypogastric plexus lies retroperitoneally anterior to the aortic bifurcation, L5 body and sacral promontory. Its block (transdiscal or anterior to L5–S1) treats pelvic visceral pain of bladder, uterus, prostate and rectum.

questions.q: The ilioinguinal and iliohypogastric nerves run between which muscle layers at the ASIS?
questions.x: From the lumbar plexus, both nerves travel in the fascial plane between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis near the ASIS — the target plane for ultrasound-guided injection in post-herniorrhaphy and lower abdominal wall pain.

questions.q: The genitofemoral nerve emerges on the anterior surface of the psoas at approximately the:
questions.x: Formed from L1–L2, the genitofemoral nerve pierces the psoas and runs on its anterior surface, dividing into genital and femoral branches around L3–L4 — the scanning target for genitofemoral neuralgia after groin surgery.

questions.q: Meralgia paresthetica results from entrapment of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve:
o: Under the inguinal ligament near the ASIS
questions.x: The LFCN passes beneath the inguinal ligament about 1 cm medial to the ASIS, where tight belts, obesity and pregnancy compress it, producing anterolateral thigh paresthesia without motor loss. Ultrasound locates its variable course for injection.

questions.q: The saphenous nerve is the terminal cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve and becomes subcutaneous at the:
questions.x: The saphenous nerve travels with the femoral vessels in the adductor canal, then emerges subcutaneously at the medial knee to supply the medial leg — the target for adductor-canal block, which preserves quadriceps strength.

questions.q: The common peroneal (fibular) nerve is most vulnerable as it winds around the:
questions.x: At the fibular neck the nerve lies superficial against bone, making it prone to compression (squatting, casts, crossing legs) with foot drop and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot. Ultrasound shows focal swelling at the entrapment point.

questions.q: In the tarsal tunnel, the tibial nerve lies:
o: Anterior to the posterior tibial artery
Within the flexor retinaculum of the wrist
Posterior to the posterior tibial vessels, behind the medial malleolus
questions.x: Behind the medial malleolus the order from front to back is tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, posterior tibial artery/veins, tibial nerve, flexor hallucis longus ('Tom, Dick And Nervous Harry'). The nerve sits behind the vessels under the flexor retinaculum.

questions.q: The sural nerve is formed by contributions from the:
o: Tibial nerve and common peroneal (communicating branch)
questions.x: The medial sural cutaneous nerve (tibial) usually joins the peroneal communicating branch to form the sural nerve, which runs with the small saphenous vein to supply the lateral heel and foot — a landmark for ultrasound localization.

questions.q: The interscalene groove, where the brachial plexus roots/trunks are blocked, lies between the:
o: Anterior and middle scalene muscles at C6 level
questions.x: At the C6 level the roots/trunks sit in the interscalene groove between the anterior and middle scalene muscles, deep to the sternocleidomastoid and lateral to the carotid — the classic position for shoulder-surgery blockade.

questions.q: At the infraclavicular level, the cords of the brachial plexus are named according to their position relative to the:
questions.x: Deep to the pectoralis minor at the coracoid, the lateral, posterior and medial cords wrap around the second part of the axillary artery. Keeping the injectate posterior to the artery (the 'corner pocket') gives the most reliable spread to all three cords.

questions.q: The rotator interval of the shoulder contains the:
o: Long head of biceps tendon and coracohumeral ligament
questions.x: The rotator interval, between supraspinatus and subscapularis, contains the intra-articular portion of the long head of biceps and the coracohumeral/superior glenohumeral ligaments forming the biceps pulley. It is a route for glenohumeral joint injection.

questions.q: The subscapularis tendon inserts on the:
questions.x: Subscapularis, the anterior rotator cuff muscle, inserts on the lesser tuberosity and is best scanned with the arm externally rotated, which swings the tendon out from behind the coracoid for full-width assessment.

questions.q: The distal biceps tendon is separated from its insertion on the radial tuberosity by the:
questions.x: The bicipitoradial bursa cushions the distal biceps tendon against the radial tuberosity; bursitis here can mimic or accompany distal tendinopathy. The tendon is scanned with the forearm supinated using an anterior oblique approach.

questions.q: A SLAP lesion involves the:
o: Superior labrum at the long head biceps anchor
questions.x: SLAP (superior labrum anterior-posterior) tears involve the superior glenoid labrum where the long head of biceps anchors, causing pain with overhead activity and the O'Brien test. Ultrasound can suggest it via superior joint fluid or cyst formation.

questions.q: For glenohumeral joint injection in osteoarthritis, the posterior approach targets the:
o: Posterior recess at the infraspinatus level
questions.x: The posterior glenohumeral recess is scanned transversely at the infraspinatus level; the needle enters from lateral to medial aiming for the posterior humeral head–glenoid junction. This route avoids the neurovascular structures anteriorly.

questions.q: The gluteus medius and minimus tendons insert on the:
questions.x: Gluteus minimus attaches to the anterior facet and gluteus medius to the lateral and superoposterior facets of the greater trochanter — the 'rotator cuff of the hip.' Tendinopathy or tears here are the commonest cause of greater trochanteric pain syndrome.

questions.q: Ischiofemoral impingement produces edema in the:
questions.x: Narrowing of the ischiofemoral space (lesser trochanter to ischial tuberosity) compresses the quadratus femoris, producing edema and eventually fatty atrophy — a recognized cause of posterior hip and buttock pain.

questions.q: The piriformis muscle inserts on the:
questions.x: The piriformis originates from the anterior sacrum, exits through the greater sciatic foramen and inserts on the superior border of the greater trochanter. On ultrasound it is the key landmark of the deep gluteal space, with the sciatic nerve passing below it.

questions.q: The common hamstring origin on the ischial tuberosity comprises the semimembranosus and the conjoint tendon of the:
o: Semitendinosus and long head of biceps femoris
Short head of biceps and gracilis
questions.x: The semimembranosus has its own footprint on the ischial tuberosity, while the semitendinosus and long head of biceps femoris share a conjoint tendon — the two layers assessed in proximal hamstring tendinopathy and avulsion.

questions.q: Internal snapping hip is produced by the:
o: Gluteus maximus over the greater trochanter
Tensor fascia lata over the ASIS
Iliopsoas tendon snapping over the iliopectineal eminence
questions.x: In internal (intra-articular-type) snapping hip, the iliopsoas tendon catches on the iliopectineal eminence or the anterior hip capsule during flexion-to-extension. Dynamic ultrasound directly visualizes the sudden tendon flip.

questions.q: Ultrasound diagnosis of medial meniscus pathology includes body extrusion beyond the tibial margin of more than:
questions.x: Meniscal extrusion >3 mm beyond the tibial plateau margin is abnormal and correlates with meniscal tears, root tears and progressive osteoarthritis. Ultrasound assesses the body of the medial and lateral menisci in the coronal plane.

questions.q: The pes anserine tendon group inserting on the proximal medial tibia comprises sartorius, gracilis and:
questions.x: The pes anserine ('goose foot') is the conjoint insertion of sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus on the anteromedial proximal tibia; the overlying bursa is a common source of medial knee pain amenable to injection.

questions.q: A Baker's (popliteal) cyst is located between the tendons of the:
o: Semimembranosus and medial head of gastrocnemius
questions.x: A Baker's cyst forms in the semimembranosus–medial gastrocnemius bursa, communicating with the knee joint through a slit-like neck. Rupture produces calf pain mimicking DVT — an important ultrasound exclusion before any calf injection.

questions.q: Patellar tendinopathy (jumper's knee) most commonly affects the:
o: Proximal tendon at the inferior pole of the patella
questions.x: Jumper's knee involves the deep proximal fibers of the patellar tendon at the inferior patellar pole, seen as focal hypoechoic thickening with possible neovascularity on Doppler — distinguishing it from quadriceps tendinopathy at the superior pole.

questions.q: The lateral collateral ligament and biceps femoris share a conjoint insertion on the:
questions.x: The LCL and biceps femoris form a conjoint insertion on the fibular head, best scanned from the lateral femoral epicondyle to the fibular head. Injury here often accompanies posterolateral corner damage.

questions.q: In posterior tibial tendon dysfunction, the first structure to fail along with the tendon is the:
questions.x: The spring ligament supports the talar head; its failure with posterior tibial tendinopathy allows the arch to collapse into acquired adult flatfoot. Ultrasound assesses tendon thickening, tears and tenosynovial fluid at the medial malleolus.

questions.q: Unlike other tendons, the Achilles tendon lacks a synovial sheath and is instead surrounded by a:
questions.x: The Achilles is enveloped by a paratenon rather than a true synovial sheath, so Achilles 'tendinitis' is often paratenonitis or midportion tendinosis. It inserts on the middle third of the posterior calcaneus.

questions.q: Plantar fasciosis is suggested when the fascia at the medial calcaneal tubercle exceeds:
questions.x: Plantar fascia thicker than ~4 mm with hypoechoic change at its calcaneal origin indicates fasciosis. Ultrasound also guides injection (avoiding intrafascial steroid where possible) and excludes tears.

questions.q: A Morton neuroma most commonly occurs in which intermetatarsal space?
questions.x: Morton neuroma is perineural fibrosis of the interdigital nerve, most often in the third intermetatarsal space, plantar to the intermetatarsal ligament. Squeezing the forefoot during scanning elicits the sonographic Mulder click.

questions.q: The triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) stabilizes the:
questions.x: The TFCC, on the ulnar side of the wrist between the ulna and the carpus, is the primary stabilizer of the distal radioulnar joint; tears cause ulnar-sided wrist pain and clicking, especially in pronation-supination.

questions.q: De Quervain tenosynovitis involves the first dorsal compartment containing:
o: Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis
questions.x: The first extensor compartment (APL and EPB) is thickened over the radial styloid, with retinacular thickening and possible septation between the two tendons — an important variant to identify before injection, which must treat both subcompartments.

questions.q: Trigger finger results from stenosis at which pulley?
o: A1 pulley at the volar MCP
questions.x: Trigger finger is caused by thickening of the A1 pulley over the metacarpal head, impeding gliding of the flexor tendons. Ultrasound shows pulley thickening and can guide release or steroid injection.

questions.q: Dupuytren contracture arises from fibrosis of the:
questions.x: Dupuytren disease is fibromatosis of the palmar fascia forming pretendinous cords that flex the ring and little fingers. Ultrasound delineates the hypoechoic cords, their relation to the flexor tendons, and guides fasciotomy or collagenase injection.

questions.q: Golfer's elbow involves the common flexor origin at the:
questions.x: Medial epicondylitis is tendinosis of the common flexor origin (pronator teres and flexor carpi radialis) at the medial epicondyle — the medial counterpart of the common extensor tendinosis of tennis elbow, seen as hypoechoic thickening.

questions.q: The supraspinatus fossa, used as a landmark for suprascapular nerve block, lies:
questions.x: The supraspinatus muscle occupies the supraspinous fossa above the scapular spine, while infraspinatus fills the fossa below it. The scapular spine is the dividing landmark when scanning for the suprascapular notch and nerve.

questions.q: Switching from a 5 MHz to a 12 MHz transducer will produce:
questions.x: Resolution improves and penetration falls as frequency rises, because attenuation increases with frequency. Choose the highest frequency that still reaches the target — high frequency for superficial nerves, lower for deep structures like the sciatic nerve.

questions.q: Acoustic impedance of a tissue is the product of:
questions.x: Z = density x propagation speed. The reflection at an interface is proportional to the impedance mismatch between the two tissues; soft tissue-bone and soft tissue-air mismatches reflect nearly everything, creating shadowing.

questions.q: Bending of the ultrasound beam as it crosses an oblique interface between tissues with different propagation speeds is described by:
questions.x: Refraction follows Snell's law, relating the angles of incidence and transmission to the propagation speeds. Refraction at oblique interfaces causes edge shadowing (e.g., at the curved margins of vessels or tendons).

questions.q: Tissue harmonic imaging forms the image from returning echoes at:
questions.x: Tissue generates harmonic frequencies (mainly the second harmonic, 2f0) as the pulse propagates. Receiving only these harmonics reduces near-field artifact and improves contrast resolution, especially in difficult-to-scan patients.

questions.q: Decreasing the dynamic range (compression) on the machine will:
o: Increase the number of gray shades
Increase image contrast with fewer gray shades
questions.x: Dynamic range sets how many decibels of echo amplitude are mapped to the gray scale. A narrow range produces a high-contrast, 'black-and-white' image with fewer gray shades; a wide range shows subtle texture differences in soft tissue.

questions.q: Time-gain compensation (TGC) is used to:
o: Equalize brightness at different depths by compensating for attenuation
questions.x: Echoes from deeper structures are weaker because of attenuation. TGC sliders apply increasing electronic amplification with depth so that similar reflectors appear equally bright throughout the image.

questions.q: Reverberation artifact appears as:
o: A single bright line behind bone
Equally spaced repeating lines between two strong reflectors
questions.x: When the beam bounces repeatedly between two strong reflectors (e.g., the needle and the transducer face), the machine displays the delayed echoes as equally spaced, repeating bright lines at multiples of the true distance.

questions.q: A comet-tail artifact is produced by:
o: Small highly reflective objects such as metal clips or tiny gas bubbles
questions.x: Comet-tail is a short, tapering bright trail behind a small, highly reflective object — a form of reverberation. It is clinically useful for confirming a needle tip or metal foreign body.

questions.q: Mirror-image artifact typically occurs at the:
o: Diaphragm, duplicating liver or spleen tissue above it
questions.x: A strong specular reflector like the diaphragm acts as a mirror: echoes from tissue beyond it return by a longer path and are mapped deeper, duplicating the structure on the far side of the reflector.

questions.q: Posterior acoustic enhancement (increased through-transmission) is characteristically seen:
o: Deep to fluid-filled structures such as cysts and vessels
questions.x: Fluid attenuates the beam far less than surrounding tissue, so echoes returning from behind a cyst or vessel are relatively stronger and the region appears brighter — a helpful clue that a structure is fluid-filled.

questions.q: The term 'anechoic' describes a structure that:
o: Contains no internal echoes, appearing black (e.g., simple fluid)
questions.x: Anechoic = echo-free, black on the image, typical of simple fluid (vessels, cysts, bladder). Hypoechoic means darker than reference tissue but not echo-free; hyperechoic means brighter.

questions.q: With an in-plane needle approach, the operator should see:
o: Only the needle tip as a dot
Nothing until the target is reached
The entire shaft and tip of the needle as a bright line
questions.x: In-plane (long-axis) guidance displays the whole needle — shaft and tip — crossing the image plane, which is the safest approach for blocks near vessels and pleura. Steep angles reduce needle brightness; beam steering or heel-toe pressure helps.

questions.q: The main limitation of the out-of-plane (short-axis) needle approach is that:
o: The needle cannot be seen at all
The tip appears only as a bright dot and can be mistaken for the shaft
It cannot be used for deep blocks
questions.x: Out-of-plane shows the needle as a bright dot; without confirming the dot is the tip (by walking the probe or watching tissue movement/hydrodissection), the operator may advance beyond the intended depth, risking structures behind the target.

questions.q: For accurate velocity measurement with spectral Doppler, the angle of insonation should be kept at or below:
questions.x: Doppler shift depends on cos(theta); above 60 degrees small angle errors cause large velocity errors, and at 90 degrees no shift is detected. Vessels are therefore scanned with beam-vessel angles of 60 degrees or less.

questions.q: Compared with color Doppler, power Doppler:
o: Is more sensitive to low-velocity flow but shows no direction
Is less sensitive to slow flow
questions.x: Power Doppler displays the amplitude (energy) of the Doppler signal, giving roughly three-fold better sensitivity to slow, small-vessel flow (e.g., tendon neovascularity, synovitis), but provides no direction or velocity information and is more motion-sensitive.

questions.q: Gabapentin dosing in chronic kidney disease requires:
o: Dose reduction according to renal function
questions.x: Gabapentin is renally eliminated unchanged; dose and interval must be reduced as GFR falls, and supplemental doses given after hemodialysis. Failure to adjust causes sedation, myoclonus and toxicity.

questions.q: Amitriptyline's main cautions in pain practice relate to its:
questions.x: Amitriptyline, a tricyclic first-line agent for neuropathic pain, blocks muscarinic receptors (dry mouth, urinary retention, confusion in the elderly) and can prolong QT; screen for glaucoma, prostatism and cardiac disease before starting.

questions.q: Duloxetine is licensed for which combination of pain conditions?
o: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy, fibromyalgia and chronic musculoskeletal pain
questions.x: Duloxetine, an SNRI, has approvals for painful diabetic neuropathy, fibromyalgia, and chronic musculoskeletal pain (including chronic low back pain and osteoarthritis), exploiting the noradrenergic-serotonergic descending inhibition pathway.

questions.q: The 5% lidocaine patch is a first-line option for:
o: Localized neuropathic pain such as postherpetic neuralgia
questions.x: The lidocaine 5% patch acts peripherally on sodium channels with minimal systemic absorption, making it ideal for localized neuropathic pain, particularly PHN, with an excellent safety profile in elderly patients.

questions.q: Transdermal fentanyl patches should be initiated only in patients who are:
questions.x: Because of the depot effect and potency, fentanyl patches are indicated only for opioid-tolerant patients (typically on at least 60 mg oral morphine equivalents daily); use in opioid-naive patients has caused fatal respiratory depression.

questions.q: When rotating from one opioid to another, the equianalgesic dose of the new opioid should be reduced by:
questions.x: Incomplete cross-tolerance means the calculated equianalgesic dose overestimates what the patient tolerates; reduce the new opioid by 25-50% (more for methadone and fentanyl) and titrate to effect.

questions.q: The active morphine metabolite that accumulates in renal failure and contributes to sedation and respiratory depression is:
questions.x: M6G is an analgesically active, renally cleared metabolite; in renal impairment it accumulates causing delayed sedation and respiratory depression. Morphine should be used cautiously or avoided in significant renal failure.

questions.q: Tapentadol's analgesic mechanism combines:
o: Mu-opioid agonism with norepinephrine reuptake inhibition
Sodium channel blockade with GABA agonism
questions.x: Tapentadol is a centrally acting analgesic with moderate mu-receptor agonism plus norepinephrine reuptake inhibition, giving efficacy in nociceptive and neuropathic pain with somewhat less gastrointestinal burden than classical opioids.

questions.q: For cervical transforaminal epidural injection, the steroid of choice is:
questions.x: Dexamethasone sodium phosphate is non-particulate and does not form aggregates; particulate steroids can occlude radicular or vertebral arteries if accidentally injected intra-arterially, causing spinal cord or brainstem infarction.

questions.q: Particulate corticosteroids such as triamcinolone and methylprednisolone acetate are hazardous in transforaminal injections because they:
o: Can form aggregates that embolize end-arteries
questions.x: Particulate preparations aggregate to sizes comparable to red cells and can occlude the radiculomedullary or vertebral arteries after inadvertent intra-arterial injection, producing cord or brain infarction - the rationale for non-particulate dexamethasone near critical vessels.

questions.q: The generally quoted maximum dose of plain bupivacaine is approximately:
questions.x: Plain bupivacaine maximum is about 2 mg/kg (up to 2.5 mg/kg with caution, absolute ~175 mg; with epinephrine slightly more). Bupivacaine cardiotoxicity (resistant arrhythmias) dictates strict dose discipline and incremental injection.

questions.q: Compared with bupivacaine, ropivacaine is preferred in many blocks because it:
o: Has less cardiotoxicity at equivalent doses
questions.x: Ropivacaine is the S-enantiomer with lower affinity for cardiac sodium channels, giving a wider safety margin and slightly more differential sensory block; potency and duration are somewhat less than bupivacaine.

questions.q: Clonidine is added to local anesthetics in peripheral blocks mainly to:
o: Prolong block duration via alpha-2 agonism
questions.x: Clonidine (alpha-2 agonist) prolongs sensory block of peripheral nerve blocks by local vasoconstriction and direct action on hyperpolarization-activated channels; side effects include sedation, hypotension and bradycardia at higher doses.

questions.q: Hyaluronidase is added to injectate in interventional pain procedures to:
o: Improve spread through adhesions and fascial planes
questions.x: Hyaluronidase temporarily depolymerizes hyaluronic acid in connective tissue, enhancing spread of local anesthetic and steroid through scarred or adherent planes (e.g., epidural adhesiolysis, perineural scarring).

questions.q: For localized osteoarthritis of the hand or knee, guidelines recommend which pharmacological option first?
questions.x: Topical NSAIDs give comparable relief to oral NSAIDs for hand and knee OA with far lower systemic exposure and gastrointestinal/cardiovascular risk, so they are recommended first, particularly in older patients.

questions.q: A positive provocative lumbar discogram requires:
o: Concordant pain at the target disc with a negative adjacent control disc
questions.x: Discography is positive when pressurizing the suspect disc reproduces the patient's familiar (concordant) pain at the preset intensity threshold, while a neighboring control disc is painless or non-concordant - otherwise false positives are common.

questions.q: The lumbar medial branches (L1-L4) cross the junction of the:
o: Transverse process and superior articular process
questions.x: Each medial branch runs in a groove where the transverse process meets the superior articular process, held by the mamillo-accessory ligament. Ultrasound localizes this junction for medial branch blocks and radiofrequency.

questions.q: The L5 dorsal ramus is blocked at the:
o: Sacral ala at the base of the S1 superior articular process
questions.x: The L5 level has no true medial branch groove; the L5 dorsal ramus itself crosses the sacral ala in the groove between the ala and the S1 superior articular process - the target for the lowest 'medial branch' block.

questions.q: Radiofrequency denervation of the sacroiliac joint targets the:
o: S1-S3 lateral branches (plus L5 dorsal ramus)
questions.x: The posterior SIJ is innervated by the L5 dorsal ramus and S1-S3 lateral branches. Cooled or conventional RF lesions placed around the sacral foramina denervate the joint after positive controlled lateral-branch blocks.

questions.q: The sacral hiatus results from failure of midline fusion of the laminae of:
questions.x: Non-fusion of the S5 laminae (variably S4) leaves the sacral hiatus, covered by the sacrococcygeal ligament - the gateway to the caudal epidural space, flanked by the palpable sacral cornua.

questions.q: Kambin's triangle in the lumbar foramen is bounded by the traversing root, the exiting root and the:
o: Superior endplate of the caudal vertebra
questions.x: Kambin's (safe) triangle is bordered medially by the traversing root/dura, superiorly by the exiting root, and inferiorly by the superior endplate of the vertebra below. It is the working zone for transforaminal access and endoscopic discectomy.

questions.q: In the lumbar spine, the exiting nerve root:
o: Leaves below the pedicle of the same-numbered vertebra
Always exits at the disc level below
Is never affected by disc herniation
questions.x: The L4 root, for example, exits beneath the L4 pedicle through the L4-5 foramen. A posterolateral L4-5 disc usually hits the traversing (L5) root, whereas foraminal/far-lateral herniations catch the exiting (L4) root.

questions.q: A far-lateral (extraforaminal) disc herniation typically compresses the:
questions.x: Herniations lateral to the foramen compress the exiting root after it has left the canal (e.g., L4 root at L4-5). They cause severe radicular pain but are easily missed on axial MRI cuts centered on the canal.

questions.q: A Schmorl's node is:
o: Herniation of disc material through the vertebral endplate into the vertebral body
questions.x: Schmorl's nodes are vertical herniations of nucleus pulposus through the endplate into the cancellous bone of the vertebral body. Usually incidental, they may be painful when acute with surrounding marrow edema.

questions.q: Baastrup disease ('kissing spines') involves:
o: Contact of adjacent spinous processes with interspinous bursitis
questions.x: Close apposition and degeneration of adjacent lumbar spinous processes (often L4-5) creates a painful interspinous bursa. Ultrasound shows the interspinous fluid collection, which can be injected under guidance.

questions.q: Bertolotti syndrome refers to low back pain associated with:
questions.x: A lumbosacral transitional vertebra (sacralized L5 or lumbarized S1) with an enlarged transverse process articulating with the sacrum can generate pain at the pseudoarticulation; diagnostic injection of the articulation confirms it.

questions.q: Spinal epidural lipomatosis is characterized by:
o: Pathological excess of epidural fat causing canal stenosis, associated with exogenous steroids and obesity
questions.x: Overgrowth of unencapsulated epidural fat (thoracic and lumbosacral) compresses the thecal sac. It is strongly linked to chronic exogenous corticosteroid use and obesity - an ironic consideration in patients receiving repeated epidural steroids.

questions.q: Adhesive arachnoiditis on MRI classically shows:
o: Clumped nerve roots and an 'empty sac' appearance
questions.x: Inflamed, adherent cauda equina roots clump centrally or stick to the dural periphery, leaving an 'empty sac' sign. It follows meningitis, bleeding, surgery or oil-based contrast, and causes intractable radicular and axial pain.

questions.q: An important safety point for midline cervical interlaminar epidurals is that the ligamentum flavum:
o: Is always fused in the midline
May have midline gaps or fail to fuse at cervical levels
questions.x: Midline fusion defects of the ligamentum flavum are frequent in the cervical region, so loss of resistance can be absent or misleading. Pre-procedural ultrasound and careful depth control are essential to avoid dural puncture or cord injury.

questions.q: The epidural venous plexus of Batson is clinically important because it:
o: Is valveless, allowing spread of infection and tumor to the spine
questions.x: Batson's valveless internal vertebral venous plexus communicates with pelvic and abdominal veins; raised intra-abdominal pressure can shunt blood (and metastases or septic emboli) to the spine - and explains epidural vein engorgement in pregnancy.

questions.q: Anterior spinal artery syndrome produces:
o: Motor loss with loss of pain and temperature, sparing dorsal column sensation
questions.x: The anterior two-thirds of the cord (corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts) is infarcted while the posterior columns remain intact. It is the feared outcome of radicular artery injury during transforaminal or sympathetic procedures.

questions.q: The filum terminale:
o: Anchors the distal cord to the coccyx; thickening can tether the cord
Is a ligament of the atlas
questions.x: The filum terminale extends from the conus to the coccyx, stabilizing the cord. A thickened, fatty filum causes tethered cord syndrome with progressive neurological and bladder dysfunction.

questions.q: During a midline lumbar interlaminar epidural, the needle passes through the interspinous ligament located between:
questions.x: The midline trajectory crosses skin, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament (between the spinous processes), ligamentum flavum, then epidural space. Knowing the layers explains the changing resistance felt during advancement.

questions.q: The denticulate ligaments:
o: Anchor the lateral spinal cord to the dura between the nerve roots
questions.x: Denticulate ligaments are lateral extensions of pia anchoring the cord to the dura between ventral and dorsal roots. They can occasionally be encountered as resistance during intrathecal procedures and define surgical planes.

questions.q: For ultrasound-guided intra-articular sacroiliac joint injection, the accessible target is the:
questions.x: Only the posterior-inferior portion of the SIJ is a true synovial joint accessible to a needle; ultrasound guides the needle into the inferior recess between the sacrum and ilium, just below the posterior superior iliac spine level.

questions.q: During an axillary brachial plexus block, which nerve most often requires separate blockade because it has already left the neurovascular sheath?
questions.x: The musculocutaneous nerve departs the lateral cord high in the axilla and lies within or between the coracobrachialis and biceps, outside the axillary sheath. It must be blocked separately to anesthetize the lateral forearm.

questions.q: At the elbow, the radial nerve divides into the superficial sensory branch and the posterior interosseous nerve at the level of the:
questions.x: In the lateral elbow between brachioradialis and brachialis, the radial nerve splits at about the radiocapitellar joint into the superficial (sensory) branch and the deep motor (posterior interosseous) branch entering the supinator.

questions.q: Pronator teres syndrome differs from carpal tunnel syndrome in that:
o: Night paresthesia is less prominent and palm sensation may be lost
It affects only the little finger
questions.x: In pronator syndrome the median nerve is compressed in the proximal forearm, above the takeoff of the palmar cutaneous branch, so palm sensation may be lost - unlike carpal tunnel syndrome, where the palmar cutaneous branch (arising before the tunnel) spares the palm and night paresthesia dominates. Provocative resisted pronation or resisted middle-finger PIP flexion reproduces the symptoms.

questions.q: Anterior interosseous nerve syndrome causes weakness of the:
o: Flexor pollicis longus, flexor digitorum profundus to the index, and pronator quadratus
questions.x: The AIN is purely motor to FPL, the index FDP and pronator quadratus; patients cannot make an 'OK' pinch sign and have no sensory loss - distinguishing it from more proximal median lesions.

questions.q: In Guyon's canal, a lesion in zone 1 (proximal, before the bifurcation) produces:
o: Combined motor and sensory ulnar deficits in the hand
questions.x: Zone 1 contains the undivided ulnar nerve, so compression affects both the deep motor and superficial sensory branches. Distal zone 2 (motor) or zone 3 (sensory) lesions give selective deficits that localize the ganglion or compression site.

questions.q: Genicular nerve radiofrequency for knee osteoarthritis targets the superolateral, superomedial and:
questions.x: The anteromedial knee capsule is innervated by the superolateral, superomedial and inferomedial genicular nerves running at the bone junctions. RF or cooled RF of these three nerves relieves OA knee pain after positive diagnostic blocks.

questions.q: The iPACK block anesthetizes the posterior knee by injecting local anesthetic:
o: Between the popliteal artery and the posterior femur
Around the common peroneal nerve at the fibular head
questions.x: iPACK (interspace between popliteal artery and capsule of the knee) bathes the genicular branches and posterior capsule articular nerves while sparing the tibial and peroneal nerves, preserving motor function after knee surgery.

questions.q: The greater occipital nerve is blocked along the superior nuchal line:
questions.x: The GON (dorsal ramus of C2) crosses the superior nuchal line roughly 2 cm lateral to the external occipital protuberance, just medial to the palpable/Doppler-identified occipital artery - the standard ultrasound landmark.

questions.q: The lesser occipital nerve arises from:
o: The ventral rami of C2-C3 via the cervical plexus
The dorsal root ganglion of C1
questions.x: The lesser occipital nerve (C2-C3 ventral rami, superficial cervical plexus) emerges at the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid and supplies the scalp behind and above the ear - blocked for occipital neuralgia variants.

questions.q: The auriculotemporal nerve, a branch of V3, classically splits around the:
questions.x: The auriculotemporal nerve arises from the mandibular division by two roots that encircle the middle meningeal artery, then ascends over the zygomatic arch with the superficial temporal vessels to supply the temple and anterior ear.

questions.q: The supraorbital nerve exits the orbit through the:
questions.x: The supraorbital nerve (V1) exits via the supraorbital notch/foramen on the superior orbital rim, supplying the forehead and scalp to the vertex - the target for supraorbital neuralgia and post-traumatic headache.

questions.q: The infraorbital nerve reaches the face through the infraorbital foramen located:
o: Below the infraorbital rim in line with the pupil
questions.x: The infraorbital nerve (V2) exits the infraorbital foramen about 1 cm below the orbital rim on the mid-pupillary line, supplying the lower lid, cheek, side of the nose and upper lip.

questions.q: The mental nerve, supplying the chin and lower lip, exits the:
o: Mental foramen near the second premolar
questions.x: The mental nerve (terminal branch of the inferior alveolar nerve, V3) exits the mental foramen below the second premolar. Ultrasound-guided mental nerve block treats mental neuralgia and painful scars in its territory.

questions.q: In the costal groove, the intercostal nerve runs:
o: Above the vein and artery (nerve-artery-vein from above)
Below the intercostal vein and artery, in the subcostal groove
Anterior to the internal intercostal muscle only
questions.x: From top to bottom the groove contains vein, artery, nerve (VAN), the nerve lying most inferiorly under the rib's inferior border - which is why intercostal blocks target the inferior border and why pleural puncture is the main risk.

questions.q: The thoracic paravertebral space, target of the paravertebral block, contains the:
o: Spinal nerve root, intercostal nerve and sympathetic chain
questions.x: The wedge-shaped thoracic paravertebral space (bounded by pleura anteriorly and superior costotransverse ligament posteriorly) contains the spinal nerve dividing into rami plus the sympathetic chain, and communicates with the epidural space.

questions.q: The serratus anterior plane block at the 5th rib in the midaxillary line deposits local anesthetic:
o: Superficial or deep to the serratus anterior muscle
questions.x: Injecting in the fascial plane above or below serratus anterior over the 4th-5th ribs blocks the lateral cutaneous branches of the intercostal nerves, providing lateral thoracic analgesia for rib fractures and thoracotomy.

questions.q: The pudendal nerve is most commonly blocked where it passes between the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments or within the:
questions.x: The pudendal nerve (S2-S4) exits via the greater sciatic foramen, crosses the sacrospinous ligament at the ischial spine, and travels in Alcock's canal on the obturator internus fascia - the targets for blockade in pudendal neuralgia.

questions.q: At the ankle, the deep peroneal nerve runs with the dorsalis pedis artery between the tendons of the:
o: Tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus
questions.x: On the dorsum of the ankle the deep peroneal nerve lies between the tibialis anterior (medially) and extensor hallucis longus (laterally) tendons beside the dorsalis pedis artery - the landmark for ankle block and neuroma assessment.

questions.q: In the thoracic outlet, the brachial plexus and subclavian artery pass between the anterior and middle scalene muscles, while the subclavian vein runs:
o: With them in the scalene triangle
Anterior to the anterior scalene muscle
questions.x: The neurovascular bundle (plexus + artery) traverses the interscalene triangle; the subclavian vein crosses anterior to the anterior scalene behind the clavicle - explaining why vascular TOS more often involves the vein at the costoclavicular space.

questions.q: A Martin-Gruber anastomosis refers to:
o: Median-to-ulnar motor fiber crossover in the forearm
questions.x: In Martin-Gruber anastomosis, motor fibers destined for ulnar-innervated hand muscles travel initially in the median nerve and cross to the ulnar nerve in the forearm - an important anomaly when interpreting conduction studies and incomplete blocks.

questions.q: Successful stellate ganglion block is confirmed by Horner syndrome plus:
o: Ipsilateral facial and arm warming with increased skin temperature
questions.x: Sympathetic blockade produces Horner triad (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) plus vasodilation: ipsilateral facial flushing, nasal stuffiness and a measurable temperature rise in the face and upper limb - the objective endpoint of the block.

questions.q: Hoarseness immediately after a stellate ganglion block indicates spread to the:
questions.x: Local anesthetic tracking medially anesthetizes the recurrent laryngeal nerve, causing hoarseness and a weak cough; patients should not eat or drink until it resolves. It signals medial spread and prompts monitoring for airway symptoms.

questions.q: The strongest indication for neurolytic celiac plexus block is:
o: Pain from pancreatic and upper abdominal malignancy
questions.x: Neurolytic celiac plexus block has its best evidence for pain of pancreatic cancer and other upper abdominal malignancies, reducing opioid requirements; benign disease (chronic pancreatitis) gives less durable responses and neurolysis is used cautiously.

questions.q: At the femoral triangle, the femoral nerve lies:
o: Posterior to the femoral artery within the sheath
Lateral to the femoral artery beneath the fascia iliaca
questions.x: The femoral nerve sits outside the femoral sheath, lateral to the artery, in the groove between psoas and iliacus under the fascia iliaca - the plane filled during femoral or fascia-iliaca blocks.

questions.q: The superficial cervical plexus emerges at the midpoint of the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid, known as:
o: Erb's point (nerve point of the neck)
questions.x: At Erb's point the four cutaneous branches (lesser occipital, great auricular, transverse cervical, supraclavicular) fan out around the posterior SCM border - the landmark for superficial cervical plexus block.

questions.q: The most common ultrasound finding in acromioclavicular joint arthrosis is:
o: Capsular hypertrophy with osteophytes and joint space irregularity
questions.x: Degenerative AC joints show capsular hypertrophy, marginal osteophytes and cortical irregularity, often with a downward-projecting spur contributing to impingement. The small joint accepts only a tiny injectate volume under ultrasound guidance.

questions.q: Ultrasound findings of adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) include thickening of the:
o: Coracohumeral ligament and rotator interval tissue
questions.x: Frozen shoulder shows thickening of the coracohumeral ligament and rotator interval capsule, sometimes with increased vascularity, plus restricted gliding on dynamic scanning. Glenohumeral joint injection and hydrodilatation target this contracted capsule.

questions.q: Subluxation of the long head of biceps out of the bicipital groove is usually associated with a tear of the:
questions.x: The biceps pulley (SGHL/coracohumeral ligament) and the adjacent subscapularis insertion restrain the tendon in the groove. Their failure allows medial subluxation or dislocation of the long head of biceps, best assessed dynamically.

questions.q: To best visualize the infraspinatus tendon, the patient's hand is placed:
o: Behind the back in internal rotation
On the contralateral shoulder, keeping the elbow at the side
In full extension behind the chair
questions.x: With the palm on the opposite shoulder (a modified Crass position), the infraspinatus tendon is stretched and accessible over the posterior humeral head without excessive internal rotation that would hide it behind the coracoid.

questions.q: On the greater tuberosity, the teres minor inserts on the:
questions.x: The greater tuberosity has three facets: supraspinatus on the superior, infraspinatus on the middle, and teres minor on the inferior facet. Knowing the facet map localizes cuff tears on longitudinal scanning.

questions.q: The annular ligament of the elbow stabilizes the:
o: Radial head within the proximal radioulnar joint
questions.x: The annular ligament encircles the radial head, holding it against the radial notch of the ulna. Subluxation ('nursemaid's elbow') in children and tears with RCL injuries in adults involve this structure.

questions.q: The triceps tendon inserts on the:
questions.x: The triceps converges onto the olecranon; a superficial olecranon bursa overlies the insertion. Distal triceps tears are assessed with the elbow flexed, and enthesophytes or partial tears are seen at the footprint.

questions.q: Subluxation of the extensor carpi ulnaris tendon at the wrist results from injury to its:
o: Subsheath within the sixth dorsal compartment
questions.x: The ECU is held in the ulnar groove by its own fibro-osseous subsheath (independent of the extensor retinaculum). Subsheath tears permit painful ECU subluxation in supination, visible on dynamic ultrasound.

questions.q: The most common carpal instability pattern follows rupture of the:
questions.x: Scapholunate ligament rupture widens the scapholunate gap and leads to DISI deformity and SLAC wrist. Ultrasound assesses the dorsal segment of the ligament and measures the gap dynamically.

questions.q: The flexor carpi radialis tendon at the wrist runs:
o: In its own fibro-osseous tunnel adjacent to the scaphotrapezial joint
questions.x: FCR occupies a separate fibro-osseous tunnel at the wrist crease, outside the carpal tunnel, adjacent to the scaphotrapezial joint - a frequent site of tendinopathy and a landmark for the wrist's volar anatomy.

questions.q: The most common site of symptomatic hand osteoarthritis requiring injection is the:
questions.x: The first carpometacarpal joint is the commonest hand OA target. Ultrasound guides precise intra-articular injection of the small saddle joint between trapezium and first metacarpal base, avoiding the radial artery nearby.

questions.q: A 'boxer's knuckle' with painful snapping of the extensor tendon at the MCP joint is caused by rupture of the:
o: Sagittal band of the extensor hood
questions.x: The sagittal bands centralize the extensor tendon over the MCP joint. Radial sagittal band rupture (typically middle finger) lets the tendon sublux ulnarly during flexion - best demonstrated with dynamic scanning in flexion.

questions.q: Hip labral tears most frequently involve the:
questions.x: The anterosuperior acetabular labrum is the commonest tear location, associated with femoroacetabular impingement. Ultrasound has limited sensitivity but can detect the secondary paralabral cyst and guide diagnostic intra-articular injection.

questions.q: The reflected (indirect) head of the rectus femoris originates from the:
o: Superior acetabular ridge and hip capsule
questions.x: Rectus femoris has two origins: the direct head from the AIIS and the reflected head from the superior acetabular ridge/capsule. Tears of the reflected head mimic hip joint pathology near the anterosuperior acetabulum.

questions.q: The posterior cruciate ligament can be assessed sonographically:
o: Through the posterior approach with the knee extended or slightly flexed
questions.x: With the probe transverse in the popliteal fossa angled superiorly, the PCL can be visualized in most patients; swelling or discontinuity suggests injury. The ACL, in contrast, is essentially inaccessible to ultrasound.

questions.q: The medial collateral ligament complex of the knee includes a bursa located:
o: Between its superficial and deep layers
questions.x: The MCL has superficial and deep (meniscofemoral/meniscotibial) layers, with an intervening bursa; bursitis mimics MCL tears. Long-axis scanning from the medial femoral epicondyle to the proximal tibia shows all three layers.

questions.q: The deltoid ligament of the medial ankle includes which components?
questions.x: The deltoid ligament has superficial bands (tibionavicular, tibiocalcaneal, tibiospring) and deep anterior/posterior tibiotalar bands, providing medial ankle stability; ultrasound evaluates each band from the medial malleolus fanning distally.

questions.q: In the retromalleolar groove, the peroneus brevis tendon lies:
o: Anteromedial to the peroneus longus, against the fibula
On the dorsum of the foot
questions.x: Behind the lateral malleolus the peroneus brevis sits anteromedial (closer to the fibula) and peroneus longus posterolateral. This arrangement explains brevis splits against the sharp fibular ridge and helps identify each tendon on short-axis scans.

questions.q: Recurrent subluxation of the peroneal tendons over the lateral malleolus follows injury to the:
questions.x: The superior peroneal retinaculum restrains the tendons in the retromalleolar groove; its avulsion (often from the fibula, sometimes with a fleck of bone) permits painful snapping subluxation, confirmed by dynamic eversion scanning.

questions.q: Anterior ankle impingement on ultrasound shows:
o: Tibial and talar osteophytes with anterior recess synovitis
questions.x: Anterior impingement ('footballer's ankle') combines dorsal tibiotalar spurs and capsular synovitis in the anterior recess, causing painful limited dorsiflexion. Ultrasound grades the effusion/synovitis and guides anterior recess injection.

questions.q: Plantar plate rupture most commonly affects which joint?
questions.x: The plantar plate of the second MTP fails under repetitive hyperextension (second ray overload, hallux valgus), producing metatarsalgia and toe deviation. Ultrasound shows plate thinning/defect and the flexor tendon approximation to the joint.

questions.q: The flexor hallucis longus tendon at the posterior ankle passes:
o: Between the medial and lateral tubercles of the posterior talus
questions.x: FHL runs in the fibro-osseous tunnel between the medial and lateral posterior talar tubercles, adjacent to the os trigonum - the site of posterior ankle impingement and 'dancer's tendinitis' in plantarflexion athletes.

questions.q: Posterior ankle impingement in ballet dancers often involves an:
o: Os trigonum posterior to the talus
questions.x: The os trigonum (unfused lateral tubercle) is compressed between the tibia and calcaneus in forced plantarflexion, causing posterior impingement; FHL tenosynovitis frequently coexists. Ultrasound-guided injection of the region confirms the diagnosis.

questions.q: The tibialis anterior tendon inserts on the:
o: Medial cuneiform and base of the first metatarsal
questions.x: Tibialis anterior crosses the anterior ankle under the extensor retinaculum to insert on the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal base; distal tendinopathy and rupture cause foot-drop gait and a palpable gap at the dorsomedial midfoot.

questions.q: The gluteus maximus inserts mainly into the:
o: Iliotibial tract and gluteal tuberosity of the femur
questions.x: Gluteus maximus fibers insert into the iliotibial tract (deep to which lies the trochanteric bursa region) and the gluteal tuberosity. Its superficial position makes it the landmark for deep gluteal injections near the sciatic nerve.

questions.q: Axial (depth) resolution in ultrasound equals approximately:
questions.x: Axial resolution = spatial pulse length / 2; shorter pulses (higher frequency, more damping) separate closer reflectors along the beam axis. It is always better than lateral resolution, which depends on beam width.

questions.q: Lateral resolution is best (narrowest beam) at the:
questions.x: The beam converges to its narrowest width at the focal zone, where lateral resolution is maximal. Positioning the focus at the target level is the single most effective way to sharpen lateral detail.

questions.q: Frame rate can be increased by all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.x: Each extra focal zone requires a separate transmit pulse per line, multiplying the time to build each frame and slowing the frame rate. Narrowing the sector, reducing depth and using one focus all speed it up.

questions.q: Speckle in an ultrasound image arises from:
o: Interference of echoes from sub-resolution scatterers
questions.x: Speckle is the granular texture produced by constructive and destructive interference of echoes from scatterers smaller than the resolution cell. Compound imaging and persistence reduce speckle to smooth the image.

questions.q: The heel-toe (rocking) maneuver with the transducer is used to:
o: Steepen or shallow the beam-to-needle angle to improve needle visibility
questions.x: Rocking the probe heel-toe changes the insonation angle so the beam meets the needle closer to perpendicular, dramatically improving needle brightness during steep in-plane approaches.

questions.q: For imaging very superficial structures (within 5 mm of the skin), image quality is improved by:
o: Pressing firmly to displace the skin
Using a thick gel layer or standoff pad
