questions.x: Structures in the first few millimeters lie in the noisy near field; a generous gel layer or standoff pad moves the target into the beam's usable zone and prevents the near-field artifact from obscuring it.

questions.q: Spatial compound imaging improves the image by:
o: Averaging frames steered from several angles, reducing speckle and artifact
questions.x: Compound imaging acquires the same frame from multiple beam angles and averages them, suppressing speckle and angle-dependent artifact and smoothing borders - at the cost of reduced shadowing cues and lower temporal resolution.

questions.q: The ALARA principle in diagnostic ultrasound means:
o: Use color Doppler for every exam
Keep acoustic exposure As Low As Reasonably Achievable
questions.x: ALARA requires using the lowest output power and shortest scan time that still yields diagnostic information, monitored via the displayed mechanical and thermal indices - especially for prolonged interventional scanning.

questions.q: The mechanical index (MI) displayed on the machine estimates the likelihood of:
questions.x: MI relates peak negative pressure to frequency and predicts non-thermal (cavitation) bioeffects; values are kept low (typically below 1.9, and far lower for contrast studies). The thermal index estimates heating instead.

questions.q: When scanning near bone or in obstetric-type calculations, the appropriate thermal index variant is:
o: Bone thermal index (TIB) because bone absorbs strongly and heats adjacent tissue
There is no thermal concern with bone
questions.x: Bone absorbs ultrasound far more than soft tissue and heats rapidly; the TIB estimates worst-case temperature rise at or near bone - relevant during prolonged scanning over periosteum and near joints.

questions.q: Probes used for injections with a sterile field (semi-critical procedures) require:
o: No disinfection if gel is sterile
High-level disinfection plus a sterile cover
questions.x: Guidance-classified semi-critical use (contact with non-intact skin or sterile fields) requires high-level disinfection and a sterile transducer cover with sterile gel; low-level wipes suffice only for intact-skin scanning.

questions.q: Before any ultrasound-guided injection, best practice includes:
o: Aspiration before and intermittent during injection
Skipping skin antisepsis for small needles
questions.x: Aspiration before injection and intermittently during it, with incremental dosing and constant verbal contact, detects intravascular placement before toxic volumes accumulate. Combined with ultrasound visualization of the needle tip, it is the core safety ritual of every block.

questions.q: Full barrier precautions (sterile gloves, sterile probe cover, sterile gel) are required for:
questions.x: Every injection performed through skin antisepsis with ultrasound guidance requires sterile gel, a sterile probe cover and sterile gloves, with skin preparation (e.g., chlorhexidine-alcohol) allowed to dry fully before needle insertion - the same aseptic standard regardless of block size.

questions.q: A 'time-out' immediately before the procedure should confirm:
o: Patient identity, procedure, site/side and consent
questions.x: The WHO-style time-out verifies correct patient, correct procedure, correct site and side, valid consent, allergies and anticoagulation status before any needle is placed - a mandatory step that prevents wrong-site interventions.

questions.q: To minimize infection risk when drawing up injectates, guidelines recommend:
o: Single-dose vials with a new sterile needle and syringe for each entry
questions.x: Single-dose vials, fresh sterile needle and syringe for every vial entry, and avoidance of hand-recapping eliminate the main causes of injection-transmitted infection; multidose vials entered repeatedly have caused outbreaks of joint sepsis and meningitis.

questions.q: Patients at high gastrointestinal risk who need an oral NSAID should receive:
o: A non-selective NSAID plus a proton pump inhibitor (or a COX-2 selective agent)
questions.x: GI risk factors (age >65, prior ulcer, anticoagulation, steroid use) mandate gastroprotection: add a PPI to a non-selective NSAID or use a COX-2 selective agent (plus PPI if very high risk). Combining NSAIDs or adding aspirin multiplies ulcer risk.

questions.q: Among oral NSAIDs, which has the most favorable cardiovascular safety profile?
questions.x: Naproxen carries the lowest observed cardiovascular risk among traditional NSAIDs; diclofenac and high-dose ibuprofen carry higher thrombotic risk. All NSAIDs raise blood pressure and can precipitate heart failure - use the lowest dose, shortest course.

questions.q: The maximum recommended daily dose of acetaminophen (paracetamol) for a healthy adult is:
o: 4 g (often limited to 3 g in at-risk patients)
questions.x: Above 4 g/day the hepatotoxic metabolite NAPQI accumulates; malnourished, alcoholic or enzyme-induced patients are capped at 2-3 g. Counsel patients about hidden acetaminophen in combination products.

questions.q: Parenteral ketorolac should not be continued for more than:
questions.x: Ketorolac carries a 5-day maximum (any route) because gastrointestinal bleeding and renal failure risk rise sharply with duration. It is a short-term analgesic for acute moderate-to-severe pain, not a chronic therapy.

questions.q: Which corticosteroid has the longest biological (HPA-suppressing) half-life?
questions.x: Dexamethasone is a long-acting steroid (biological half-life 36-72 h), versus hydrocortisone (short, 8-12 h), prednisone (intermediate) and methylprednisolone (intermediate). Long-acting agents cause more HPA suppression per dose.

questions.q: A characteristic local complication of subcutaneous corticosteroid injection is:
questions.x: Superficial steroid injection can cause local hypopigmentation and lipoatrophy, especially with particulate preparations and dark skin; deep placement and non-particulate steroid reduce the risk. Tendon rupture follows intratendinous injection instead.

questions.q: A diabetic patient should be warned that an epidural steroid injection may cause:
o: Transient elevation of blood glucose for days
questions.x: Systemic absorption of epidural steroid transiently raises blood glucose, typically for several days; diabetic patients should monitor more frequently after injection. This does not contraindicate the procedure but should be planned for.

questions.q: True local anesthetic allergy is most likely with:
o: Esters such as procaine, which form PABA metabolites
questions.x: Ester local anesthetics hydrolyze to para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA), the classic allergen; amide allergy is rare and often due to methylparaben preservative. A careful history usually reveals vasovagal or epinephrine reactions instead of true allergy.

questions.q: Methemoglobinemia after local anesthesia is classically associated with:
questions.x: Benzocaine (topical) and prilocaine oxidize hemoglobin to methemoglobin; patients present cyanotic with a normal PaO2 and chocolate-brown blood. Treatment is IV methylene blue. The risk limits topical dosing in mucosal procedures.

questions.q: First-line treatment of local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) with cardiac toxicity is:
questions.x: LAST management: stop injection, call for help, airway/oxygenation, benzodiazepine for seizures, and 20% lipid emulsion (1.5 mL/kg bolus then infusion, repeat per protocol). Epinephrine is used in small doses only; vasopressin is avoided.

questions.q: In LAST, central nervous system symptoms typically appear:
questions.x: The classic sequence is perioral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus and agitation progressing to seizures, followed by cardiovascular depression and arrhythmia - CNS signs precede cardiovascular toxicity, giving a warning window if verbal contact is maintained.

questions.q: The most effective prophylaxis for opioid-induced constipation is:
o: A stimulant laxative (e.g., senna) started with the opioid
questions.x: Opioids slow peristalsis without tolerance developing to this effect; a stimulant laxative (often with a softener) should be co-prescribed from day one, with PEG as an effective alternative. Bulk fiber alone may worsen symptoms.

questions.q: First-line pharmacological treatment of trigeminal neuralgia is:
questions.x: Carbamazepine (or oxcarbazepine) is first-line for classical trigeminal neuralgia, with strong evidence; monitor sodium, blood counts and interactions. Refractory cases proceed to glycerol/radiofrequency rhizotomy, balloon compression or microvascular decompression.

questions.q: OnabotulinumtoxinA for chronic migraine is injected according to the:
o: PREEMPT fixed-site protocol across the head and neck
questions.x: Chronic migraine (15+ headache days/month) is treated with onabotulinumtoxinA 155- 195 units at 31-39 fixed PREEMPT sites across the forehead, temporalis, occipitalis, cervical and trapezius muscles, repeated every 12 weeks.

questions.q: Serotonin syndrome, a risk when serotonergic analgesics are combined with SSRIs or MAOIs, presents with the triad of:
o: Autonomic hyperactivity, neuromuscular hyperexcitability and altered mental status
questions.x: Agitation/confusion, autonomic instability (hyperthermia, tachycardia, sweating) and neuromuscular signs (clonus, hyperreflexia - typically greater in the lower limbs) define serotonin syndrome. Stop the serotonergic agents, give supportive care and cyproheptadine in severe cases.

questions.q: On a sagittal scan of the cervical articular pillars, the medial branches (C3-C6) are found at the:
o: Deepest point (waist) of the articular pillar between two facet joint gaps
questions.x: Cervical medial branches wrap around the waist of each articular pillar, seen on sagittal scan as the deepest point of the 'hump' midway between adjacent joint gaps - the ultrasound target for medial branch blocks and radiofrequency.

questions.q: The C7 medial branch is located differently from C3-C6 because it lies:
o: Higher, over the apex of the C7 superior articular process
questions.x: The C7 medial branch crosses more superiorly, near the apex of the C7 superior articular process rather than the pillar waist - an important variant to avoid false-negative C7 medial branch blocks.

questions.q: Each zygapophysial (facet) joint is innervated by medial branches from:
o: Two levels - the same level and the level above
questions.x: Every facet joint receives dual innervation from the medial branch at its own level and the level above (e.g., L4-5 facet from L3 and L4 medial branches). Denervation therefore requires lesioning two levels per joint.

questions.q: Cervical facet joint pain from C2-3 characteristically refers to the:
o: Occiput and suboccipital region, often with headache
questions.x: Upper cervical facets refer pain to the occiput and head (C2-3 to the occiput/eye region, C3-4 to the suboccipital neck); lower cervical facets refer to the shoulder girdle and scapular region - the referral maps guide block selection.

questions.q: The atlanto-occipital (C0-1) joint is injected for suspected:
o: Upper cervical headache aggravated by head flexion-extension
questions.x: The C0-1 joint can generate suboccipital pain and headache, typically provoked by flexion-extension with restricted motion. Ultrasound-guided injection of its posterolateral recess is a diagnostic-therapeutic option after imaging review.

questions.q: The most common type of odontoid (dens) fracture in the elderly is:
o: Type II, at the base of the dens
Type III, into the C2 body
questions.x: Anderson-D'Alonzo type II fractures through the base of the dens are the commonest and most unstable, especially in osteoporotic elderly patients; they carry the highest nonunion rate and often require surgical fixation.

questions.q: A hangman's fracture involves bilateral fractures of the:
o: C2 pars interarticularis (traumatic spondylolisthesis of the axis)
questions.x: Hangman's fracture is bilateral C2 pars interarticularis fracture with anterior displacement of C2 on C3, classically from hyperextension-distraction. Despite the dramatic appearance, the canal is often decompressed and neurological injury may be absent.

questions.q: A posterolateral C5-6 disc herniation typically compresses which root?
questions.x: Cervical roots exit above their same-numbered pedicle, so at C5-6 the exiting C6 root is compressed by the posterolateral herniation - unlike the lumbar spine, where the traversing root (one below) is usually affected.

questions.q: Clinical signs suggesting cervical myelopathy include:
o: Hoffmann sign, hyperreflexia and gait disturbance
questions.x: Cord compression produces upper motor neuron signs below the level: Hoffmann sign, Babinski, hyperreflexia, clumsy hands and gait imbalance - red flags that mandate MRI before any cervical epidural or manipulation.

questions.q: A lumbar facet synovial cyst arises from the facet joint and can cause:
o: Radiculopathy by compressing the traversing root in the lateral recess
questions.x: Degenerative facet joints can form synovial cysts projecting into the lateral recess or canal, compressing the traversing root and mimicking a disc herniation (usually L4-5). Ultrasound-guided cyst rupture/aspiration is a described treatment.

questions.q: On T2-weighted MRI, a 'dark disc' indicates:
o: Loss of water content from disc desiccation/degeneration
questions.x: Healthy nucleus is bright on T2 from its high water content; progressive loss of signal ('dark disc') reflects proteoglycan and water loss of degeneration. Signal loss alone, however, correlates poorly with pain.

questions.q: Which annular fissure type is most associated with discogenic pain?
o: Radial fissures reaching the innervated outer annulus
questions.x: Radial fissures extend from the nucleus to the outer third of the annulus, where nociceptive nerve endings (sinuvertebral branches) and ingrowing vessels carry pain signals - the substrate of internal disc disruption.

questions.q: The vacuum phenomenon on spinal imaging refers to:
o: Gas (nitrogen) within a degenerated disc or facet joint
questions.x: Gas (mainly nitrogen) collects in clefts of degenerated discs or facet joints, seen as black on radiographs and CT; it is a sign of degeneration and instability rather than infection, though gas-forming discitis must be excluded clinically.

questions.q: A limbus vertebra results from:
o: Intraosseous disc herniation separating a corner fragment of the vertebral body
questions.x: Herniation of nucleus material through the ring apophysis before fusion separates a small triangular corner fragment - a limbus vertebra. It is usually an incidental finding at the anterosuperior corner, distinct from an acute fracture.

questions.q: Clay-shoveler's fracture is an avulsion fracture of the:
o: Lower cervical/upper thoracic spinous process (classically C7)
questions.x: Sudden forceful flexion or direct pull of the supraspinous ligament avulses a lower cervical or upper thoracic spinous process (classically C7). It is stable, treated symptomatically, and often visible on lateral cervical imaging.

questions.q: A Chance fracture is best described as:
o: A compression fracture of the anterior column
A flexion-distraction injury through all three columns, often at the thoracolumbar junction
questions.x: Chance fractures are horizontal flexion-distraction injuries (classically seat-belt injuries) passing through bone or disc across all three columns at the thoracolumbar junction; they are unstable and associated with abdominal injuries.

questions.q: The most important risk factor for osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture is:
o: Low bone mineral density with age (postmenopausal osteoporosis)
questions.x: Compression fractures occur when axial loading exceeds the strength of osteoporotic bone, typically at the thoracolumbar junction; risk rises with low BMD, age, steroids and prior fragility fracture. Vertebral augmentation is considered for refractory pain.

questions.q: A typical vertebral hemangioma on imaging shows:
o: Corduroy/striated vertical trabecular thickening - usually benign and incidental
Spinal cord compression in most cases
questions.x: Hemangiomas show thickened vertical trabeculae ('corduroy' on radiographs, 'polka-dot' on axial CT) from fatty replacement and vessel channels. The vast majority are incidental; only the rare aggressive subtype (T1-hypointense) causes symptoms.

questions.q: The basivertebral nerve, target of radiofrequency ablation for vertebrogenic pain, innervates the:
questions.x: The basivertebral nerve enters through the basivertebral foramen and supplies the vertebral endplates; its ablation (Intracept-type procedure) treats chronic low back pain of endplate (Modic change) origin after facet and disc causes are excluded.

questions.q: The sinuvertebral (recurrent meningeal) nerve innervates the posterior longitudinal ligament, outer annulus and:
o: The anterior dura and epidural vessels
questions.x: The sinuvertebral nerve re-enters the canal to supply the PLL, outer annulus fibrosus, anterior dura and epidural vessels - the pathway by which disc pathology and epidural procedures generate axial pain.

questions.q: The intercostobrachial nerve, a cause of upper medial arm and axillary pain, is the lateral cutaneous branch of the:
questions.x: The intercostobrachial nerve is the lateral cutaneous branch of T2, crossing the axilla to supply the upper posteromedial arm. It is injured in axillary surgery and mastectomy, producing neuropathic pain amenable to ultrasound-guided block.

questions.q: Sensory innervation over the 'shoulder cape' and acromioclavicular region is supplied by the:
questions.x: The supraclavicular nerves (superficial cervical plexus, C3-C4) fan over the clavicle to supply the shoulder cape and AC region; their block supplements interscalene anesthesia for clavicle and shoulder surgery and treats post-surgical neuropathic pain.

questions.q: Suprascapular nerve entrapment at the spinoglenoid notch causes isolated weakness of the:
questions.x: At the spinoglenoid notch (under the inferior transverse scapular ligament) the supraspinatus branch has already departed, so compression weakens only the infraspinatus (external rotation) with posterior shoulder pain; ganglion cysts from labral tears are the commonest cause.

questions.q: The lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve, the sensory terminal of the musculocutaneous nerve, emerges at the elbow:
o: Lateral to the biceps tendon, deep then superficial to the fascia
questions.x: The MCN continues between biceps and brachialis, then emerges lateral to the biceps tendon at the elbow crease as the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve, supplying the lateral forearm - a target for injection and a site of entrapment by the biceps aponeurosis.

questions.q: In the mid-forearm, the ulnar nerve runs with the ulnar artery beneath the:
questions.x: From the elbow to the wrist the ulnar nerve travels under the flexor carpi ulnaris, joined by the ulnar artery on its radial side in the distal two-thirds - the scanning landmark for tracing the nerve and for hydrodissection of forearm entrapment.

questions.q: A wrist-to-forearm cross-sectional area ratio of the median nerve greater than approximately 1.4 suggests:
questions.x: Median nerve CSA at the tunnel inlet >10 mm2, or a wrist-to-forearm ratio >1.4 (both measured inside the epineurium), supports carpal tunnel syndrome with high accuracy - a key quantitative ultrasound criterion.

questions.q: A bifid median nerve in the carpal tunnel is often accompanied by a:
questions.x: A persistent median artery frequently runs within or between the two bundles of a bifid median nerve; recognizing it on Doppler prevents mistaking the artery for a tendon or injuring it during injection or release.

questions.q: On short-axis ultrasound, a normal peripheral nerve shows:
o: Hypoechoic fascicles in a hyperechoic epineurium ('honeycomb')
questions.x: Nerves display a fascicular honeycomb: dark fascicles (nerve bundles) within bright interfascicular and outer epineurium. Loss of fascicular architecture with enlargement and hypoechogenicity indicates neuropathy proximal to an entrapment.

questions.q: When measuring nerve cross-sectional area, the caliper trace is placed:
o: Around the perineurium of the limb
Just inside the hyperechoic epineurial border
questions.x: CSA is measured with a continuous trace just inside the hyperechoic epineurial rim, at a site away from joints and without probe pressure (which deforms the nerve). Standardized technique is essential because CSA defines entrapment thresholds.

questions.q: At the gluteal fold, the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve lies:
o: Medial and deep to the sciatic nerve under the gluteus maximus
questions.x: The posterior femoral cutaneous nerve (S1-S3) descends under the gluteus maximus, medial to the sciatic nerve at the ischial level, supplying the posterior thigh - a cause of posterior thigh pain distinct from sciatica.

questions.q: The inferior cluneal nerves, a source of lower buttock pain, arise from the:
questions.x: Inferior cluneal branches of the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve curve around the inferior buttock to supply the lower gluteal skin; entrapment mimics sacroiliac or ischial pain and responds to ultrasound-guided injection.

questions.q: The sciatic nerve typically divides into the tibial and common peroneal nerves:
o: About 5-7 cm above the popliteal crease (popliteal apex)
questions.x: Division occurs variably but usually near the apex of the popliteal fossa, 5-7 cm proximal to the crease. Ultrasound localizes the division ('paraneural sheath' sign) so popliteal block is placed before the split for complete anesthesia.

questions.q: In the popliteal fossa, the tibial nerve lies:
o: Superficial and lateral to the popliteal vessels
questions.x: At the popliteal crease the arrangement from deep to superficial is artery, vein, tibial nerve, with the nerve lateral to the vessels - it is scanned first (the most superficial structure) and traced to the sciatic division.

questions.q: In the popliteal fossa, the common peroneal nerve is found along the:
o: Medial border of the biceps femoris tendon
Posterior aspect of the popliteal artery
questions.x: After the sciatic division, the common peroneal nerve tracks laterally along the medial edge of the biceps femoris toward the fibular head. Scanning from the fibular neck backward is the easiest way to locate it.

questions.q: Anterior knee pain after total knee arthroplasty or saphenous surgery often involves the:
o: Infrapatellar branch of the saphenous nerve
questions.x: The infrapatellar saphenous branch crosses the anteromedial knee to the patellar region and is injured by knee incisions, causing neuroma pain below the patella. Ultrasound identifies the neuroma for injection or ablation.

questions.q: The stellate (cervicothoracic) ganglion is formed by fusion of the inferior cervical and first thoracic ganglia in approximately:
questions.x: In about 80% of individuals the inferior cervical and T1 sympathetic ganglia fuse into the stellate ('star-shaped') ganglion anterior to the C7 transverse process/first rib; when unfused, the T1 ganglion serves the same role.

questions.q: Established indications for stellate ganglion block include:
o: CRPS of the upper limb, Raynaud phenomenon and upper limb vascular insufficiency
questions.x: SGB is indicated for sympathetically maintained pain of the face and upper limb (CRPS I/II), Raynaud and vasospastic or ischemic conditions, refractory angina, and hot flashes - not for lower limb or musculoskeletal joint pain.

questions.q: Stellate ganglion block is hazardous or contraindicated in a patient with:
o: Contralateral phrenic nerve palsy or pneumonectomy
questions.x: SGB can transiently block the ipsilateral phrenic and recurrent laryngeal nerves; in a patient whose contralateral diaphragm or lung is already lost, this risks respiratory failure. Recent myocardial infarction and complete heart block are further cautions.

questions.q: Lumbar sympathetic block is most appropriately used for:
o: Sympathetically maintained pain/CRPS of the lower limb and ischemic rest pain
questions.x: The lumbar sympathetic chain mediates sympathetic outflow to the leg; blockade treats CRPS of the lower limb, sympathetically maintained pain, ischemic rest pain and some neuropathic pains, with temperature rise confirming success.

questions.q: The transdiscal approach to the superior hypogastric plexus passes the needle through the:
questions.x: When the iliac crest blocks a paramedian path to the anterior L5-S1 junction, the transdiscal route passes the needle straight through the L5-S1 disc to the prevertebral plexus - accepted despite the theoretical discitis risk.

questions.q: Neurolytic ganglion impar (ganglion of Walther) block is indicated for:
o: Perineal and coccygeal pain, particularly of malignant origin
questions.x: The ganglion impar, the fused terminal sympathetic ganglion anterior to the sacrococcygeal joint, conveys sympathetic fibers from the perineum. Neurolysis relieves perineal, coccygeal and rectal pain, especially in pelvic cancer.

questions.q: Double crush syndrome proposes that:
o: A proximal nerve lesion predisposes the nerve to symptomatic distal entrapment
questions.x: Axoplasmic flow compromised by a proximal compression (e.g., cervical radiculopathy) renders the nerve more vulnerable to distal entrapment (e.g., carpal tunnel); treating only the distal site may fail - a key principle in evaluating overlapping neuropathies.

questions.q: In the antecrural approach to the celiac plexus, the needle tip is placed:
o: Anterior to the diaphragmatic crura and the aorta at T12-L1
questions.x: The antecrural (transcrural) technique advances the needle through the crus to lie anterolateral to the aorta at the T12-L1 level, directly at the celiac plexus around the celiac trunk and superior mesenteric artery origins.

questions.q: The suprascapular nerve provides sensory innervation to approximately what proportion of the shoulder joint?
questions.x: The suprascapular nerve carries about 70% of the shoulder joint's sensory supply (with the axillary nerve covering most of the rest) - the rationale for its block and pulsed radiofrequency in chronic shoulder pain.

questions.q: The thoracodorsal nerve, a branch of the posterior cord, supplies the:
questions.x: The thoracodorsal nerve (C6-C8) arises from the posterior cord and descends with the thoracodorsal vessels to the latissimus dorsi; it is relevant to axillary surgery and breast reconstruction where its injury weakens extension and adduction.

questions.q: A full-thickness supraspinatus tear on ultrasound appears as:
o: A focal anechoic/hypoechoic defect with loss of tendon substance, sometimes exposing the cartilage
questions.x: Full-thickness tears show a focal hypoechoic or anechoic gap replacing the tendon fibers, often with the cartilage interface sign and non-visualization of the retracted tendon. Dynamic scanning confirms loss of tendon gliding.

questions.q: A rim-rent tear of the supraspinatus is:
o: A bursal-side tear at the musculotendinous junction
An articular-side partial tear at the footprint of the greater tuberosity
questions.x: Rim-rent tears involve the deep articular-side fibers where they insert on the footprint - the classic location for partial cuff tears from overuse. They may be occult on external inspection and are best seen with the arm extended and internally rotated.

questions.q: Barbotage of a calcific supraspinatus deposit involves:
o: Needle fenestration and lavage/aspiration of the calcium under ultrasound guidance
Steroid injection into the AC joint
questions.x: Barbotage fragments and irrigates the calcific deposit with saline through one or two needles, aspirating the calcium paste; subacromial bursa steroid follows. It is the standard interventional treatment for the formative/resting phases of calcific tendinitis.

questions.q: Dynamic ultrasound assessment of subacromial impingement demonstrates:
o: The supraspinatus and bursa bunching under the acromion/coracoacromial arch during abduction
questions.x: During abduction, impingement is seen as painful pooling of bursal fluid and bunching of the supraspinatus as it fails to glide freely beneath the coracoacromial arch - a functional sign unavailable to static imaging.

questions.q: Fluid distending the bicipital groove around the long head of biceps usually indicates:
o: Tenosynovitis, or communication with a glenohumeral joint effusion
questions.x: The bicipital sheath communicates with the glenohumeral joint, so groove fluid may reflect either biceps tenosynovitis or joint effusion tracking down the sheath; the distinction guides whether to inject the sheath or the joint.

questions.q: Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) on ultrasound shows tendinosis of the:
o: Common extensor origin (principally ECRB) at the lateral epicondyle
questions.x: Tennis elbow is tendinosis (not primarily inflammation) of the common extensor origin, mainly the ECRB, with hypoechoic thickening, possible tears and neovascularity. Ultrasound guides needling, steroid or PRP injection.

questions.q: A positive posterior 'sail sign' on an elbow radiograph indicates:
o: Displacement of the fat pads by joint effusion, suggesting occult fracture (e.g., radial head)
questions.x: Effusion lifts the anterior and posterior elbow fat pads out of the fossae ('sail sign'); in adults after trauma it strongly suggests an occult radial head fracture. Ultrasound can directly show the lipohemarthrosis and cortical step-off.

questions.q: Before injecting an olecranon bursa, the essential step is to:
o: Aspirate and send fluid to exclude septic bursitis or gout
questions.x: Olecranon bursitis is commonly septic (Staphylococcus) or crystalline; fluid must be aspirated for Gram stain, culture and crystals before any corticosteroid is injected, since steroid into an infected bursa is disastrous.

questions.q: The most common origin of a dorsal wrist ganglion cyst is the:
questions.x: Dorsal wrist ganglia typically arise from the scapholunate interval through a tortuous stalk; ultrasound shows the anechoic multiloculated sac and its neck, guiding aspiration or distinguishing it from solid tumors.

questions.q: A Stener lesion of the thumb describes:
o: The torn ulnar collateral ligament displaced superficial to the adductor aponeurosis
questions.x: In complete tears of the thumb's ulnar collateral ligament (gamekeeper/skier's thumb), the retracted stump can flip superficial to the adductor aponeurosis (Stener lesion), preventing healing and mandating surgery - the key ultrasound finding.

questions.q: Rock climbers who injure the A2 pulley of a finger demonstrate on ultrasound:
o: Bowstringing of the flexor tendon away from the phalanx
questions.x: A2 (and A4) pulley rupture lets the flexor tendon lift off the bone ('bowstringing'), measurable as increased tendon-phalanx distance, especially during resisted flexion - the hallmark of pulley injury in climbers.

questions.q: Jersey finger is an avulsion of the:
o: Flexor digitorum profundus from the distal phalanx
questions.x: Jersey finger (rugby jersey) is FDP avulsion from its distal phalanx insertion when the grasped finger is forcibly extended. Ultrasound localizes the retracted stump, which determines the Leddy-Packer surgical classification.

questions.q: A mallet finger results from injury to the:
o: Terminal extensor tendon at the distal interphalangeal joint
questions.x: Mallet finger is disruption of the terminal extensor tendon at or near its distal phalanx insertion (with or without a bony avulsion), causing a flexion droop of the DIP joint that the patient cannot actively extend.

questions.q: A glomus tumor of the finger typically presents as:
o: A small, exquisitely painful, hypervascular subungual nodule
questions.x: Glomus tumors are benign perivascular hamartomas, classically subungual, causing the triad of point tenderness, cold hypersensitivity and paroxysmal pain. Ultrasound shows a small hypoechoic, markedly hypervascular nodule with possible bone erosion.

questions.q: Athletic pubalgia ('sports hernia') most often involves injury at the:
o: Rectus abdominis/adductor longus aponeurotic plate at the pubic symphysis
questions.x: Athletic pubalgia centers on the conjoint rectus abdominis-adductor longus aponeurosis at the pubis; ultrasound (with dynamic maneuvers) assesses the aponeurotic plate, and guided injection can be both diagnostic and therapeutic.

questions.q: Prepatellar bursitis ('housemaid's knee') involves the bursa:
o: Superficial to the patella, between skin and bone
questions.x: The prepatellar bursa lies between the skin and the anterior patella; repetitive kneeling inflames it with a compressible fluid collection. Aspiration precedes steroid to exclude sepsis, as with the olecranon bursa.

questions.q: The popliteus tendon passes through the popliteal hiatus and is a stabilizer of the:
questions.x: The popliteus tendon courses from the lateral femoral condyle through the popliteal hiatus to the posterior tibia, forming part of the posterolateral corner complex; tenosynovitis or injury contributes to posterolateral knee pain.

questions.q: Medial plica syndrome produces:
o: An inflamed synovial fold on the medial side of the patellofemoral joint causing snapping pain
questions.x: The medial patellar plica is a synovial fold that, when thickened and inflamed (often after direct trauma or overuse), snaps over the medial femoral condyle, causing anteromedial knee pain - visible on dynamic ultrasound with flexion.

questions.q: Quadriceps tendon rupture is best suspected in an elderly patient who:
o: Cannot actively extend the knee, with a suprapatellar gap after a fall
questions.x: Quadriceps tendon rupture (typically at the osteotendinous junction above the patella in patients over 40) abolishes active knee extension with a palpable suprapatellar gap. Ultrasound shows fiber discontinuity and hematoma; complete tears need surgical repair.

questions.q: The most commonly sprained ligament of the ankle is the:
questions.x: The ATFL is the weakest and most frequently injured lateral ligament in inversion sprains, followed by the CFL. Ultrasound assesses ligament continuity, laxity on stress views and associated peroneal or osteochondral injury.

questions.q: Baxter neuropathy, a treatable cause of chronic heel pain, involves the:
o: Inferior calcaneal nerve (first branch of the lateral plantar nerve)
questions.x: The inferior calcaneal (Baxter) nerve is compressed between the quadratus plantae fascia and the medial calcaneus, causing medial heel pain that mimics plantar fasciitis, often with abductor digiti minimi denervation.

questions.q: An early metatarsal stress fracture on ultrasound shows:
o: Cortical irregularity with periosteal reaction and surrounding hyperemia
A normal cortex in all cases
questions.x: Before radiographs turn positive, ultrasound can show a cortical break or step-off, periosteal elevation/callus and hyperemic soft tissue over the symptomatic metatarsal - useful for early diagnosis in runners.

questions.q: A Jones fracture is located at the:
o: Metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction of the fifth metatarsal
questions.x: The Jones fracture crosses the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction of the fifth metatarsal - a vascular watershed with high nonunion risk, unlike the more distal avulsion ('pseudo-Jones') fracture of the tuberosity that heals well.

questions.q: The Lisfranc ligament connects the medial cuneiform to the:
questions.x: The Lisfranc ligament anchors the medial cuneiform to the second metatarsal base, stabilizing the tarsometatarsal complex; its rupture with second-metatarsal 'fleck sign' indicates a Lisfranc injury requiring orthopedic referral.

questions.q: A full-thickness Achilles tendon rupture on ultrasound demonstrates:
o: Complete fiber discontinuity with a retracted, echogenic stump and intervening hematoma
questions.x: Complete Achilles tears show total fiber disruption 2-6 cm above the insertion (the watershed zone) with a hematoma-filled gap and dynamic retraction of the proximal stump on plantarflexion - distinguishing complete from partial tears for management.

questions.q: The piezoelectric effect, fundamental to ultrasound transducers, describes:
o: Heating of tissue by sound waves
Generation of an electric voltage when certain crystals are deformed (and vice versa)
questions.x: Piezoelectric crystals (PZT) deform when voltage is applied, emitting sound, and generate voltage when returning echoes deform them - the same element both transmits and receives. The resonant thickness sets the operating frequency.

questions.q: The backing (damping) material behind the piezoelectric element:
o: Shortens the pulse, improving axial resolution but reducing sensitivity
questions.x: Backing material absorbs the backward wave and damps crystal ringing, shortening the spatial pulse length for better axial resolution at the cost of sensitivity. The matching layer in front improves energy transfer into tissue.

questions.q: Side lobe artifacts are caused by:
o: Off-axis low-energy beams that create false echoes from strong reflectors
questions.x: Side lobes are low-energy beams emitted at angles to the main beam; strong reflectors encountered by these lobes are mapped onto the main beam line, creating spurious echoes (e.g., false debris in a bladder). Grating lobes are the array equivalent.

questions.q: Continuous-wave (CW) Doppler, compared with pulsed-wave Doppler:
o: Has no maximum measurable velocity but no depth resolution
questions.x: CW Doppler transmits and receives continuously, so it measures very high velocities without aliasing but cannot tell where along the beam the signal originated. PW Doppler gives depth localization at the cost of a Nyquist limit.

questions.q: B-flow imaging displays blood flow by:
o: Directly displaying moving echo amplitude (speckle) from blood, without Doppler
questions.x: B-flow uses coded B-mode excitation to display the moving speckle pattern of blood itself, offering high frame rate and spatial resolution without angle dependence or color bleeding beyond the vessel wall.

questions.q: Strain elastography assesses tissue stiffness by:
o: Measuring compression-induced displacement under probe pressure
questions.x: Strain elastography displays relative tissue deformation under gentle probe compression: stiff lesions deform less and appear harder on the color overlay. Shear-wave elastography instead quantifies the speed of an acoustic push-pulse wave in kPa or m/s.

questions.q: Contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) uses:
o: Intravenously injected gas-filled microbubbles that resonate at low MI
questions.x: CEUS microbubbles (perfluorocarbon gas in a lipid shell) resonate nonlinearly at low mechanical index, outlining microvascularity and perfusion in real time. The agent is intravascular, exhaled via the lungs, and safe in renal impairment.

questions.q: Panoramic (extended field-of-view) imaging is produced by:
o: Freehand sweeping of the probe with real-time image registration
questions.x: As the probe slides along the skin, the machine registers successive frames and stitches them into one long image - ideal for documenting the full length of a torn tendon, a large lipoma or the sciatic nerve course.

questions.q: A duplex ultrasound examination combines:
o: B-mode imaging with Doppler flow assessment
questions.x: Duplex = simultaneous B-mode imaging plus Doppler (usually spectral); adding color Doppler makes it triplex. Duplex scanning is the standard for vascular access assessment before fistula creation or line placement.

questions.q: Doppler frequency shifts used in vascular ultrasound fall within the:
o: Audible range, allowing speaker output of the flow signal
questions.x: The difference between transmitted and received frequencies (the Doppler shift) for physiologic flow velocities is only a few kHz - within human hearing - which is why the flow signal can be played through the machine's speakers.

questions.q: Steering (angling) the color Doppler box on a linear transducer:
o: Has no effect on the image
Aligns the beam closer to the vessel axis for optimal Doppler angle
questions.x: Linear arrays need the color box steered to create an acute beam-vessel angle; without steering, flow perpendicular to the beam shows little or no color (cosine 90 = 0). Box steering is essential for vessels parallel to the skin.

questions.q: Attachable needle guides (infusion brackets) on the transducer:
o: Constrain the needle to the scan plane, aiding out-of-plane-angle control but limiting freehand adjustment
questions.x: Needle guides hold the needle in the image plane at a fixed angle, improving accuracy for deep targets and beginners, but they restrict the fine angular adjustments that freehand technique allows - both approaches are acceptable with training.

questions.q: A vasovagal reaction during a procedure should be managed initially by:
o: Stopping the procedure, laying the patient supine with legs raised, and monitoring
questions.x: Vasovagal reactions (pallor, sweating, bradycardia, hypotension) are managed by stopping, lying the patient flat with legs elevated, reassurance and monitoring; atropine is reserved for persistent symptomatic bradycardia. Most resolve within minutes.

questions.q: After an accidental needle-stick injury, the first step is to:
o: Wash the site and report immediately for risk assessment and possible post-exposure prophylaxis
Squeeze the wound until it bleeds freely then forget it
questions.x: Needle-stick protocol: let the site bleed gently, wash with soap and water (no scrubbing or bleach), and report at once for source-patient testing and time-critical HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (within 72 hours, ideally within hours).

questions.q: The matching layer on the front face of the transducer:
o: Has intermediate impedance to maximize energy transmission from the crystal into tissue
questions.x: A quarter-wavelength matching layer with impedance between that of PZT and skin maximizes sound energy transfer into the patient (and echo return), analogous to an anti-reflection coating; without it most energy would reflect at the crystal-tissue boundary.

questions.q: For an elderly patient with neuropathic pain who cannot tolerate amitriptyline, the preferred tricyclic is:
o: Nortriptyline, which has fewer anticholinergic effects
questions.x: Nortriptyline, the active metabolite of amitriptyline, causes less sedation, orthostasis and anticholinergic burden - the preferred TCA in older adults. Therapeutic drug monitoring is available, and doses are started low.

questions.q: Venlafaxine for neuropathic pain is most effective at:
o: Higher doses (150-225 mg/day) where noradrenergic activity adds to serotonergic effects
questions.x: Venlafaxine is serotonergic at low doses; clinically useful noradrenergic reuptake inhibition (needed for analgesia) emerges at 150-225 mg/day. Blood pressure should be monitored at higher doses.

questions.q: The 8% capsaicin patch is applied:
o: Daily at home by the patient
For 30-60 minutes in clinic, after local anesthetic preparation of the skin
questions.x: The high-concentration capsaicin patch (Qutenza) is applied for 30-60 minutes by trained staff after pretreating the area with topical anesthetic; defunctionalization of TRPV1 fibers gives months of relief in peripheral neuropathic pain (PHN, painful DPN).

questions.q: Before initiating chronic opioid therapy, recommended risk-stratification includes:
o: A validated tool such as the Opioid Risk Tool (ORT) plus review of the prescription drug monitoring program
questions.x: Guidelines recommend assessing misuse risk with a validated tool (ORT, SOAPP, DIRE) and checking the PDMP before starting opioids, then periodically during therapy. High-risk patients need tighter structure or non-opioid alternatives.

questions.q: Urine drug monitoring in chronic opioid therapy primarily aims to:
o: Confirm adherence, and detect undisclosed substances or diversion
questions.x: UDT (presumptive immunoassay plus confirmatory testing) verifies that the prescribed opioid is present and that non-prescribed or illicit substances are absent. Unexpected results should prompt discussion, not automatic dismissal.

questions.q: A written opioid treatment agreement typically documents:
o: Goals, risks, single-prescriber sourcing, monitoring and conditions for discontinuation
questions.x: The opioid agreement sets out treatment goals, informed consent on risks, one prescriber/one pharmacy, no early refills, urine monitoring and the circumstances that lead to tapering - a communication and safety tool, not a legal waiver.

questions.q: Current opioid-prescribing guidance flags daily doses approaching which morphine milligram equivalents (MME) for heightened caution?
o: 50 MME, with strong justification needed beyond 90 MME/day
questions.x: Overdose risk rises progressively with dose; guidelines urge careful reassessment as doses approach 50 MME/day and to avoid or justify exceeding 90 MME/day, using the lowest effective dose with non-opioid and non-drug measures.

questions.q: When opioid tapering is indicated, a commonly recommended rate is:
o: About 10% per month (or slower for long-term users), individualized
questions.x: Gradual tapers of roughly 10% per month - slower after years of use - minimize withdrawal and pain flare. Abrupt cessation risks severe withdrawal, uncontrolled pain and crisis; shared decision-making guides the pace.

questions.q: Naloxone should be co-prescribed to patients on opioids who:
o: Have risk factors such as higher doses (e.g., 50 MME or more), benzodiazepine co-use, or prior overdose
questions.x: Guidelines recommend offering naloxone with risk factors: doses at or above roughly 50 MME/day, concurrent benzodiazepines, respiratory disease, or history of overdose/substance-use disorder - plus education of household members.

questions.q: Intravenous lidocaine infusion in pain medicine is used mainly for:
o: Neuropathic pain states and fibromyalgia in selected patients
questions.x: Systemic lidocaine (sodium-channel blockade) can relieve central and peripheral neuropathic pain and fibromyalgia in selected patients under monitored infusion protocols; a positive response may predict response to oral mexiletine.

questions.q: Tizanidine, used for spasticity and myofascial pain, acts as:
questions.x: Tizanidine is a centrally acting alpha-2 agonist reducing motor neuron excitation; it is used short-term for muscle spasm and spasticity. Watch for hypotension, sedation and transaminase elevation, and interactions with ciprofloxacin.

questions.q: Baclofen relieves spasticity by agonism of:
o: GABA-B receptors in the spinal cord
questions.x: Baclofen is a GABA-B agonist acting at spinal interneurons for spasticity of spinal origin. Abrupt withdrawal (oral or intrathecal) is dangerous, causing rebound spasticity, hallucinations, seizures and hyperthermia.

questions.q: Cyclobenzaprine, a centrally acting muscle relaxant, is structurally related to:
questions.x: Cyclobenzaprine is a TCA-like compound acting on the brainstem; it shares anticholinergic and serotonergic cautions (avoid with MAOIs, caution with SSRIs) and is indicated for short-term use in acute musculoskeletal spasm.

questions.q: For any single joint, repeat corticosteroid injections are generally limited to:
o: About 3-4 injections per year, with an interval of at least 3 months
questions.x: Frequent intra-articular steroid risks cartilage damage, tendon weakening and systemic effects; most guidelines suggest no more than 3-4 injections per joint per year at intervals of 3 months or more, individualizing by response.

questions.q: The risk of septic arthritis after an aseptic intra-articular steroid injection is approximately:
questions.x: With proper aseptic technique, iatrogenic joint sepsis is rare - quoted at roughly 1/15,000-1/50,000 injections. Increasing pain, swelling and fever days after injection demand urgent aspiration and culture.

questions.q: The paramedian approach to the lumbar interlaminar epidural space is particularly useful when:
o: Midline access is difficult (severe stenosis, fused spine, interspinous ligament calcification)
questions.x: The paramedian route bypasses calcified supraspinous/interspinous ligaments and narrowed interspaces, angling from lateral to medial to reach the flavum - valuable in ankylosed, fused or severely stenotic spines.

questions.q: Transforaminal epidural injection at L5-S1 is technically challenging because of the:
o: High iliac crest overlying the L5-S1 foramen
questions.x: The iliac crest frequently overlies the L5-S1 foramen, forcing a steep caudocranial needle angle or the use of the S1 sacral foramen instead. Ultrasound helps plan the trajectory before fluoroscopy.

questions.q: An S1 transforaminal epidural injection passes through the:
questions.x: The S1 root is reached through the posterior S1 sacral foramen, with the needle passing the posterior sacral foramina into the ventral epidural region - useful when the L5-S1 foramen is inaccessible or after surgery.

questions.q: A caudal epidural steroid injection typically uses a total injectate volume of:
questions.x: Caudal injections use larger volumes (10-20 mL total) to spread cephalad through the epidural space and bathe the lower lumbar roots; the dural sac ends at S2, well above the injection site at the sacral hiatus.

questions.q: Epidural adhesiolysis (Racz procedure) aims to:
o: Break down epidural adhesions to improve injectate spread and relieve nerve entrapment
questions.x: The Racz technique threads a steerable catheter to the affected level and uses repeated injection (saline, hyaluronidase, steroid) to lyse epidural adhesions - most evidence in post-surgical epidural fibrosis with radicular pain.

questions.q: The characteristic late complication of an intrathecal drug-delivery catheter tip is:
o: Catheter-tip granuloma, an inflammatory mass that can compress the cord
questions.x: High-concentration opioids (especially morphine) can provoke an inflammatory granuloma at the catheter tip, presenting with rising pain and new neurological deficits - MRI confirms the mass, and drug concentration/flow are modified or surgery considered.

questions.q: Abrupt interruption of intrathecal baclofen delivery causes:
o: A life-threatening withdrawal syndrome with rebound spasticity, fever, seizures and rhabdomyolysis
questions.x: Intrathecal baclofen withdrawal (pump failure, empty reservoir, catheter disruption) is a medical emergency: pruritus, rebound spasticity, hyperthermia, seizures, rhabdomyolysis and multi-organ failure. Oral baclofen, benzodiazepines and urgent pump interrogation are required.

questions.q: For conventional spinal cord stimulation for low back and leg pain, lead placement is typically at the:
questions.x: Leads for low back/leg coverage are positioned in the posterior epidural space around T8- T9 (lower thoracic), where stimulation of the dorsal columns covers the target dermatomes; fine position is confirmed by intraoperative testing or mapping.

questions.q: A spinal cord stimulation trial is considered successful when the patient reports at least:
questions.x: A trial of several days with an externalized lead must achieve about 50% or greater pain reduction, improved function/activity and stable or reduced medication before permanent implantation is offered.

questions.q: High-frequency (10 kHz) spinal cord stimulation differs from conventional SCS in that it:
questions.x: 10 kHz (HF10) stimulation relieves back and leg pain without producing paresthesia, so patients feel no tingling and leads are placed anatomically. Evidence shows superior back-pain outcomes versus traditional low-frequency SCS.

questions.q: Dorsal root ganglion (DRG) stimulation is especially suited for:
o: Focal neuropathic pain such as CRPS of the knee, foot or groin
questions.x: DRG stimulation places leads beside the ganglion in the foramen, giving precise coverage of focal territories (knee, foot, groin) that are hard to cover with dorsal-column SCS - with evidence in CRPS and causalgia of the lower limb.

questions.q: The Fortin finger test for sacroiliac joint pain is positive when the patient:
o: Points to the lumbar spinous processes
Points with one finger to the area within 1 cm of the PSIS as the site of pain
questions.x: Consistently localizing pain with one finger just inferomedial to the PSIS (Fortin finger) suggests SIJ origin and increases the predictive value of the provocative test cluster.

questions.q: A clinical SIJ diagnosis is supported when how many of the five provocative tests reproduce the familiar pain?
questions.x: The SIJ provocation cluster (distraction, compression, thigh thrust, Gaenslen, sacral thrust) has useful diagnostic accuracy when at least 3 of 5 tests reproduce the patient's pain - and the whole cluster is negative, SIJ pain is unlikely.

questions.q: The FABER (Patrick) test stresses the hip and sacroiliac joint by placing the leg in:
questions.x: FABER positions the ankle on the opposite knee and presses the flexed knee downward; groin pain suggests hip pathology, while posterior buttock pain suggests SIJ involvement - a combined screening test in the SIJ cluster.

questions.q: The thigh thrust (posterior shear) SIJ test is performed by:
o: Applying a posteriorly directed force through the femur with the hip flexed to 90 degrees
questions.x: With the hip flexed to about 90 degrees and slightly adducted, a posterior shearing force along the femoral shaft loads the SIJ; reproduction of the familiar buttock pain is positive. It is among the most sensitive tests of the cluster.

questions.q: Degenerative (non-isthmic) spondylolisthesis most commonly occurs at:
questions.x: Degenerative spondylolisthesis results from facet arthrosis and disc degeneration permitting forward slip, typically at L4-5 in women over 50, often with associated spinal stenosis - unlike isthmic slips from pars defects at L5-S1.

questions.q: Retrolisthesis (posterior vertebral displacement) is typically accentuated by:
questions.x: Posterior slippage increases in extension; dynamic flexion-extension radiographs (or standing vs. recumbent films) reveal instability that static supine MRI can miss - relevant when planning stabilization advice and procedures.

questions.q: On ultrasound of the lumbar spine, the ligamentum flavum is identified to:
o: Measure skin-to-flavum depth before epidural needle insertion
questions.x: Paramedian sagittal oblique sonography shows the flavum-posterior dura complex; measuring skin-to-ligament depth estimates epidural depth, correlating with actual loss-of-resistance depth and reducing insertion attempts - especially useful in obesity and pregnancy.

questions.q: The estimated depth to the lumbar epidural space correlates most strongly with:
questions.x: Skin-to-epidural depth increases with BMI and weight; published formulas (e.g., based on weight/height) predict depth within about a centimeter for most patients, guiding needle length selection before insertion.

questions.q: A diagnostic lumbar puncture is safely performed at L3-L4 or L4-L5 because:
o: The epidural space is widest there
The ligamentum flavum is thickest there
The spinal cord (conus) has already ended, and only the mobile cauda equina roots remain
questions.x: Below the conus (which ends at L1-L2), the subarachnoid space contains only the cauda equina roots floating in CSF, which move away from the needle; puncture at L3-4 or L4-5 therefore avoids cord injury.

questions.q: The principal vascular risk of a deep cervical plexus block is injection into the:
questions.x: Deep cervical plexus block places the needle near the transverse foramina; the vertebral artery lies just deep/anterior, so aspiration, small test doses and ultrasound visualization are mandatory. Superficial plexus block avoids this depth.

questions.q: For shoulder analgesia, the lateral pectoral nerve is relevant because it:
o: Carries sensory fibers from the anterior shoulder joint
Is part of the lumbar plexus
questions.x: The lateral pectoral nerve contributes articular branches to the anterior glenohumeral joint; together with the suprascapular and axillary nerves it forms the target trio for shoulder denervation strategies in refractory shoulder pain.

questions.q: The PENG (pericapsular nerve group) block anesthetizes articular branches of the:
o: Femoral, obturator and accessory obturator nerves to the anterior hip capsule
questions.x: PENG targets the anterior hip capsule innervation - articular branches of the femoral and accessory obturator nerves (with obturator contribution) - in the plane between the psoas tendon and the pubic ramus, preserving motor strength for hip surgery analgesia.

questions.q: The anterior hip joint receives sensory innervation mainly from the femoral and obturator nerves, while the posterior capsule is supplied by the:
questions.x: Hip innervation follows Hilton's law: anteriorly femoral/obturator (plus accessory obturator), posteriorly the sciatic contribution via the nerve to quadratus femoris and superior gluteal branches - the map used for hip denervation.

questions.q: An accessory obturator nerve is present in approximately what proportion of people?
questions.x: The accessory obturator nerve (L3-L4), present in roughly 10-30%, descends medial to the psoas to contribute to hip innervation - one reason obturator-only blocks sometimes give incomplete anterior hip analgesia.

questions.q: For wrist denervation, the terminal sensory branch of the posterior interosseous nerve is targeted at the:
o: Distal forearm, just proximal to Lister's tubercle on the radius
questions.x: The PIN becomes purely sensory on the posterior distal radius near Lister's tubercle, innervating the dorsal wrist capsule; its block (often with the AIN branch) is used for wrist denervation in arthritis and post-traumatic pain.

questions.q: The anterior interosseous nerve's terminal sensory branch innervates the:
questions.x: After its motor branches, the AIN continues with the anterior interosseous artery to supply the volar wrist capsule - blocked alongside the PIN sensory branch for comprehensive wrist joint denervation.

questions.q: The dorsal sensory branch of the ulnar nerve arises approximately:
o: 5 cm proximal to the wrist, passing dorsally under the flexor carpi ulnaris
questions.x: The dorsal ulnar sensory branch leaves the main nerve about 5 cm above the wrist and crosses dorsally beneath the FCU to supply the dorsoulnar hand - its entrapment causes pain that is missed by standard Guyon-focused assessment.

questions.q: Thoracic sympathetic block at T2-T3 is used for:
o: Upper limb sympathetically maintained pain, facial blushing or hyperhidrosis
questions.x: The upper thoracic sympathetic chain (T2-T3 ganglia) carries sympathetic outflow to the head, neck and upper limb; its block treats upper limb CRPS, ischemic pain, palmar hyperhidrosis and facial blushing when stellate block is unsuitable.

questions.q: The nerve of Kuntz refers to:
o: A collateral sympathetic pathway from T2 bypassing the stellate ganglion to the brachial plexus
questions.x: Intra- and inter-thoracic rami (nerve of Kuntz) connect T2 directly to the lower brachial plexus, bypassing the stellate ganglion - explaining incomplete sympathetic blockade of the hand after stellate ganglion block.

questions.q: White rami communicantes carry:
o: Myelinated preganglionic sympathetic fibers from the spinal cord to the chain
questions.x: White rami (present only T1-L2) carry myelinated preganglionic sympathetic axons from the intermediolateral cell column to the sympathetic chain; gray rami return unmyelinated postganglionic fibers to every spinal nerve.

questions.q: The Budapest criteria for CRPS require continuing disproportionate pain plus signs and symptoms in which categories?
o: Sensory, vasomotor, sudomotor/edema, and motor/trophic categories
questions.x: Budapest clinical criteria need: ongoing pain disproportionate to the inciting event, at least one symptom in 3 of 4 categories (sensory, vasomotor, sudomotor/edema, motor/trophic), at least one sign in 2 of 4, and no better explanation.

questions.q: Erythromelalgia is characterized by:
o: Paroxysmal burning pain, redness and warmth of the feet/hands, relieved by cooling
questions.x: Erythromelalgia causes episodic intense burning with erythema and heat of the extremities, triggered by warmth and relieved by cooling. It may be primary (SCN9A sodium-channel mutation) or secondary to myeloproliferative disease.

questions.q: Endoscopic thoracic sympathicolysis for palmar hyperhidrosis targets the T2-T3 chain; its main troublesome side effect is:
questions.x: Ablating T2-T3 relieves palmar sweating effectively, but compensatory hyperhidrosis of the trunk and thighs is the commonest and most regretted complication, alongside Horner risk if T1 is injured.

questions.q: Cryoneurolysis relieves pain for months because it produces:
o: Permanent nerve death in all cases
Wallerian degeneration of the axons with preservation of the epineurium, allowing regrowth
questions.x: Freezing (about -70 degrees C) disrupts axons and myelin (Wallerian degeneration) while the connective-tissue scaffold survives, so the nerve regenerates over weeks to months - pain relief without the neuroma risk of nerve transection.

questions.q: Conventional (thermal) radiofrequency neurotomy heats the tissue to approximately:
questions.x: Conventional RF coagulates nerve tissue at 80-90 degrees C for 60-90 seconds; this temperature achieves reliable protein denaturation and Wallerian disruption of the target nerve - higher than pulsed RF, which stays at or below 42 degrees C.

questions.q: Before lesioning, radiofrequency impedance measurement confirms:
o: Electrical continuity and tissue contact at the electrode tip (typically a few hundred ohms)
questions.x: Impedance (usually 200-500 ohms in tissue) verifies circuit integrity and that the electrode is embedded in tissue rather than air or against bone; an open circuit or very high impedance indicates a problem to correct before lesioning.

questions.q: The size of a radiofrequency lesion increases with all of the following EXCEPT:
o: Shorter lesion time at target temperature
questions.x: Lesion volume grows with tip diameter and length, higher temperature and longer lesion time (up to a plateau near 60-90 seconds); shortening the time reduces the lesion. Cooled RF enlarges the effective lesion by preventing charring at the tip.

questions.q: Pulsed radiofrequency is believed to act mainly through:
o: An electric-field (neuromodulatory) effect without significant thermal damage, at tip temperatures of 42 degrees C or less
questions.x: Pulsed RF delivers brief high-voltage pulses with pauses that keep tip temperature at or below 42 degrees C, avoiding coagulation; its analgesia is attributed to electric-field neuromodulation (altered c-fos expression and synaptic transmission), making it safe near motor nerves.

questions.q: Neurolysis with ethyl alcohol works by:
o: Dehydrating and extracting proteins/lipids from the nerve (50-100% concentrations)
questions.x: Alcohol (50-100%) extracts cholesterol, phospholipids and lipoproteins and precipitates proteins, producing Wallerian degeneration; it spreads beyond the target and is painful on injection, so it is reserved for sympathetic plexus neurolysis (celiac) with imaging control.

questions.q: Phenol for neurolysis is typically used at concentrations of:
questions.x: Phenol (3-10%) denatures proteins and has an intrinsic local anesthetic effect, so injection is initially painless; higher concentrations risk vascular and neural damage. It is used for motor-point, sympathetic and intrathecal neurolysis in selected cases.

questions.q: During ultrasound-guided perineural injection, resistance to injection with the patient reporting severe pain suggests:
questions.x: High injection pressure with severe pain indicates intraneural placement, which can cause fascicular damage and persistent neuropathy; withdraw slightly, reassess tip position and confirm spread outside the epineurium before injecting.

questions.q: Hydrodissection for nerve entrapment uses injectate to:
o: Separate the nerve from surrounding adhesions and fascia
questions.x: Hydrodissection injects fluid (often 5% dextrose or saline) under ultrasound to mechanically free an entrapped nerve from scar and fascial adhesions - used in carpal tunnel, cubital tunnel and superficial radial entrapment, avoiding steroid when 5% dextrose is chosen.

questions.q: On ultrasound, a schwannoma differs from a neurofibroma in that it is typically:
o: Eccentric to the nerve, displacing fascicles, often with a capsule
questions.x: Schwannomas grow eccentrically from the nerve sheath with a capsule, allowing surgical shelling-out, whereas neurofibromas expand centrally within the nerve involving the fascicles. Both appear as fusiform hypoechoic masses in continuity with the nerve.

questions.q: Peripheral nerve stimulation (PNS) places the electrode:
o: Adjacent to the target peripheral nerve to modulate its signals
questions.x: Peripheral nerve stimulation places a small lead in the soft tissue alongside the target nerve (e.g., femoral, suprascapular, sciatic branches) to deliver modulating current without entering the nerve itself - an option for focal neuropathic pain refractory to blocks.

questions.q: In a chronic massive rotator cuff tear, ultrasound of the supraspinatus fossa may show:
o: Fatty infiltration and muscle atrophy of the supraspinatus (Goutallier change)
questions.x: Chronic retracted tears lead to fatty degeneration and atrophy of the cuff muscle belly (graded by Goutallier on MRI, assessable on ultrasound as a shrunken hyperechoic muscle), which predicts poor repair outcomes.

questions.q: The 'critical zone' of the supraspinatus tendon, where most degenerative tears begin, is:
o: A hypovascular area about 1 cm from the greater tuberosity insertion
questions.x: The watershed of poor blood supply roughly 1 cm proximal to the footprint predisposes to degenerative tendinopathy and tears. This region should be scanned carefully in both planes for fiber disruption.

questions.q: A painful arc between 60 and 120 degrees of abduction suggests:
o: Subacromial impingement of the supraspinatus/bursa under the coracoacromial arch
questions.x: Pain in the mid-arc occurs as the greater tuberosity and cuff pass beneath the acromion and coracoacromial ligament; pain at end-range suggests the AC joint instead. Dynamic ultrasound can correlate the bunching with symptoms.

questions.q: Lateral elbow snapping with pain in a young athlete may be caused by:
o: A lateral synovial plica/fringe in the radiocapitellar joint
questions.x: A thickened posterolateral synovial plica snapping over the radial head mimics lateral epicondylitis and intra-articular loose bodies. Dynamic ultrasound with forearm rotation can demonstrate the snapping plica.

questions.q: Osteochondritis dissecans of the elbow in adolescent throwers typically affects the:
questions.x: Repetitive valgus and axial loading injures the tenuous blood supply of the capitellum, producing osteochondritis dissecans with lateral elbow pain and locking. Ultrasound can show the capitellar irregularity and loose bodies.

questions.q: Kienbock disease is avascular necrosis of the:
questions.x: Kienbock disease is AVN of the lunate, associated with negative ulnar variance and repetitive loading, presenting with dorsal wrist pain and stiffness; imaging shows lunate sclerosis, fragmentation and collapse.

questions.q: The most common dorsal wrist fracture visible on ultrasound is an avulsion chip from the:
questions.x: Dorsal triquetral chip fractures result from avulsion of the dorsal radiotriquetral ligament in wrist hyperflexion; ultrasound shows the small cortical fragment dorsally, while radiographs show the classic 'pooping duck' flake on lateral view.

questions.q: A hyperextension injury of the PIP joint most commonly damages the:
questions.x: The volar plate resists hyperextension; forced hyperextension tears it (often at its distal attachment, sometimes with a bony flake), causing PIP swelling and pain - ultrasound visualizes the plate and any avulsion fragment.

questions.q: A boutonniere deformity results from injury to the:
o: Central slip of the extensor tendon at the PIP joint
questions.x: Disruption of the central slip lets the PIP flex and the lateral bands slip volarly, hyperextending the DIP - the boutonniere (buttonhole) deformity. Ultrasound shows the absent or thinned central slip insertion at the middle phalanx base.

questions.q: A digital mucous cyst at the DIP joint is associated with:
o: Osteoarthritis with Heberden nodes and a dorsal osteophyte stalk
questions.x: Mucous cysts are ganglion-like lesions of the DIP joint, connected by a stalk to the joint and associated with osteoarthritis and Heberden nodes; pressure on the germinal matrix can groove the nail.

questions.q: External snapping hip is produced by:
o: The iliotibial band or anterior gluteus maximus snapping over the greater trochanter
questions.x: In external snapping hip the posterior ITB or anterior gluteus maximus fibers catch on the greater trochanter during flexion-extension; dynamic ultrasound in lateral decubitus directly demonstrates the snap.

questions.q: Ischial (ischiogluteal) bursitis, or 'weaver's bottom', causes pain:
o: Over the ischial tuberosity, worse with prolonged sitting
questions.x: The ischiogluteal bursa between the ischial tuberosity and gluteus maximus becomes inflamed by prolonged sitting on hard surfaces; ultrasound shows the fluid collection deep to the gluteus over the tuberosity and guides injection.

questions.q: The obturator internus and gemelli muscles, part of the deep gluteal space, act as:
o: External rotators of the hip near the sciatic nerve
questions.x: The short external rotators (piriformis, obturator internus/gemelli, quadratus femoris) lie deep in the buttock adjacent to the sciatic nerve; their pathology contributes to deep gluteal syndrome.

questions.q: Ultrasound of hip osteoarthritis typically shows:
o: A normal capsule in all cases
Anterior capsular distension with effusion and osteophyte formation at the head-neck junction
A torn labrum in every case
questions.x: Hip OA shows anterior recess distension by effusion/synovitis, osteophytes at the femoral head-neck junction and capsular thickening; the anterior longitudinal scan also guides joint injection along the femoral neck.

questions.q: A parameniscal cyst arises from:
o: A horizontal meniscal tear extruding joint fluid through the capsule
questions.x: Horizontal meniscal cleavage tears pump synovial fluid through the capsule, forming a loculated parameniscal cyst adjacent to the joint line - treated by addressing the meniscal tear and aspirating/injecting the cyst under guidance.

questions.q: A discoid meniscus, prone to snapping and tears in children, most often involves the:
questions.x: A discoid (disc-shaped rather than crescentic) meniscus is usually lateral; the Wrisberg type lacks posterior attachment and causes the classic 'snapping knee' of childhood. Ultrasound shows the abnormally wide meniscal body.

questions.q: Hoffa's disease refers to impingement of the:
o: Infrapatellar fat pad between the patellar tendon and the femoral condyle
questions.x: The infrapatellar (Hoffa) fat pad becomes impinged and inflamed after hyperextension trauma or surgery, causing anterior knee pain; ultrasound shows hypoechoic swelling and hyperemia of the fat pad.

questions.q: A bipartite patella most commonly occurs at the:
questions.x: Bipartite patella is an unfused accessory ossification center, most often at the superolateral pole. Usually incidental, it can become painful after stress or trauma - the smooth, rounded corticated margins distinguish it from fracture.

questions.q: Sinding-Larsen-Johansson syndrome is traction apophysitis at the:
o: Inferior pole of the patella at the patellar tendon origin
questions.x: SLJ is the proximal counterpart of Osgood-Schlatter: traction overload at the patellar tendon origin on the inferior patellar pole in adolescents, with tenderness and possible fragmentation on imaging.

questions.q: In a severe inversion ankle sprain, the ligament most often torn together with the ATFL is the:
questions.x: Lateral sprains follow a sequence: ATFL first, then the CFL as severity increases; the PTFL is rarely injured. Combined ATFL-CFL tears define a grade III sprain and may need longer protection or repair.

questions.q: Turf toe is a sprain of the:
o: Plantar plate and capsuloligamentous complex of the first MTP joint
questions.x: Turf toe is hyperextension injury of the first MTP plantar plate complex (sesamoid-capsule apparatus), common on artificial turf; ultrasound assesses the plantar plate, sesamoids and any retraction to grade the injury.

questions.q: Hallux rigidus on ultrasound and radiographs shows:
o: Dorsal osteophytes and joint space narrowing of the first MTP joint
questions.x: Hallux rigidus is first MTP osteoarthritis with dorsal osteophytes, joint space loss and restricted dorsiflexion, causing push-off pain; ultrasound confirms the dorsal spur and guides joint injection.

questions.q: A symptomatic accessory navicular is commonly associated with:
o: Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction and medial arch pain
questions.x: The accessory navicular (type II synchondrosis) alters posterior tibial tendon mechanics; tension at the synchondrosis causes medial midfoot pain and may coexist with flatfoot and PTT tendinopathy.

questions.q: Kager's fat pad is located:
o: Anterior to the Achilles tendon, between the flexor hallucis longus and the deep fascia
questions.x: Kager's fat pad fills the pre-Achilles space; its obliteration by fluid suggests Achilles rupture or infection, and its anterior displacement occurs in retrocalcaneal bursitis - a useful landmark on both ultrasound and radiographs.

questions.q: Painful os peroneum syndrome (POPS) involves the sesamoid within the:
o: Peroneus longus tendon at the cuboid
questions.x: The os peroneum sits in the peroneus longus tendon near the cuboid tunnel; fracture, diastasis or degenerative change causes lateral foot pain, and its proximal migration signals peroneus longus rupture.

questions.q: Dynamic receive focusing in modern transducers works by:
o: Continuously updating electronic delays so echoes are focused at their exact depth of origin
questions.x: On receive, the beamformer applies time-varying delays across the array so every echo depth is optimally focused ('track the returning wavefront'). Transmit focusing is fixed at one depth per pulse - hence multiple transmit focal zones slow the frame rate.

questions.q: Increasing the transducer aperture (active element count) at the focal zone:
o: Narrows the beam and improves lateral resolution
Has no effect on the beam
questions.x: Lateral resolution = focal depth x wavelength / aperture; a larger aperture produces a narrower focused beam and better lateral resolution, which is why synthetic-aperture and large-array probes give sharper images.

questions.q: Apodization in array transducers is used to:
o: Reduce side and grating lobes by varying element excitation amplitude
questions.x: Apodization tapers the voltage applied across the array elements (stronger centrally, weaker at the edges), suppressing side and grating lobes that otherwise generate artifactual echoes - at a slight cost to main-lobe width.

questions.q: A curvilinear (convex) array is preferred for deep abdominal and pelvic scanning because it:
o: Is smaller than a linear probe
Provides a wide far field with good penetration at lower frequency
questions.x: Curvilinear arrays (typically 2-6 MHz) spread diverging beams from a curved face, giving a wide far field and good penetration for deep structures such as the piriformis, hip or abdomen - at the cost of lateral resolution with depth.

questions.q: A phased (sector) array transducer is especially useful for:
o: Imaging between ribs (e.g., cardiac) with a small footprint
questions.x: Phased arrays steer and focus electronically from a tiny footprint, producing a sector image from a narrow acoustic window - ideal between ribs (cardiac, thoracic) but less suited to high-resolution superficial MSK work.

questions.q: When color Doppler shows no flow in a vessel known to be patent, the first control to adjust is the:
o: Pulse repetition frequency (scale) - lower it to detect slower flow
questions.x: The PRF/scale sets the detectable velocity range: too high a scale misses slow flow (e.g., small perineural vessels), too low causes aliasing. Also check color gain, box angle and wall filter before concluding absence of flow.

questions.q: The wall filter in Doppler imaging:
o: Eliminates low-frequency signals from vessel-wall motion, but can also erase slow flow
questions.x: The high-pass wall filter removes low-frequency clutter from pulsating walls and moving tissue; set too high it also deletes genuine slow flow near the vessel wall - balance it against the PRF for perineural and tendon flow.

questions.q: Excessive color Doppler gain produces:
o: Color bleeding beyond the vessel wall with noise
questions.x: Too much color gain fills the box with random color noise that 'bleeds' outside vessel walls, obscuring anatomy and mimicking flow. Increase gain until speckle appears, then back off slightly - the standard optimization step.

questions.q: Spectral broadening on a Doppler waveform indicates:
o: Filling of the spectral window with a range of velocities, as in turbulent or disturbed flow
questions.x: In laminar flow most cells move at similar velocities, leaving a clear 'window' under the systolic peak; stenosis or turbulence spreads velocities and fills the window (spectral broadening) - a sign of disturbed flow.

questions.q: Shifting the spectral Doppler baseline downward is done to:
o: Display higher velocities in one direction without aliasing
questions.x: Moving the baseline reallocates the available velocity range to one flow direction, preventing aliasing wrap-around of the systolic peak without changing the PRF - a standard spectral optimization step.

questions.q: All sharps from an interventional procedure must be disposed of:
o: Recapped and thrown in general waste
Immediately into a puncture-resistant sharps container at the point of use
In the procedure tray for later sorting
questions.x: Needles go directly from use into a sharps container at the bedside without recapping, bending or passing hand-to-hand - the core measure preventing needle-stick injuries and blood-borne virus transmission.

questions.q: Every syringe on the sterile field must be:
o: Labeled with drug name and concentration
questions.x: Unlabeled syringes are a leading cause of medication error (wrong drug, wrong dose, wrong route). All syringes drawn up are labeled immediately with drug and concentration, and injectates are prepared fresh for each patient.

questions.q: Valid consent for an interventional pain procedure must include discussion of:
o: The procedure, expected benefit, material risks, alternatives and the option of no treatment
