questions.x: Informed consent requires explaining what the procedure involves, its intended benefit, common and serious risks (infection, bleeding, nerve injury, failure), alternatives including doing nothing, and answering questions - documented before the day of the procedure where possible.

questions.q: After a neuraxial or sympathetic block, post-procedure monitoring should specifically observe for:
o: Hypotension, neurological deficit, and signs of bleeding or intravascular injection before discharge
questions.x: Monitoring after neuraxial/sympathetic procedures watches blood pressure, motor/sensory recovery, and delayed signs of hematoma or intravascular injection; discharge criteria and written advice (including emergency contact) are part of safe practice.

questions.q: A compact 'hockey-stick' (small-footprint linear) transducer is most advantageous for:
o: Superficial structures in tight areas such as the ankle, wrist and digits
questions.x: Hockey-stick probes combine a small footprint with high frequency, giving excellent superficial resolution where a standard linear probe cannot maintain contact - around the ankle malleoli, wrist, fingers and for vascular access in small patients.

questions.q: Subanesthetic intravenous ketamine infusion for refractory chronic pain typically uses:
o: Low-dose infusions (roughly 0.1-0.5 mg/kg/h) over hours to days with monitoring
questions.x: Ketamine infusions for refractory neuropathic pain, CRPS and central pain use subanesthetic dosing with cardiac and blood-pressure monitoring; psychotomimetic effects (dysphoria, hallucinations) are managed with benzodiazepines or clonidine.

questions.q: Dexmedetomidine as a perineural adjuvant:
o: Prolongs sensory block via alpha-2 agonism with less hypotension than clonidine
questions.x: Perineural dexmedetomidine (highly selective alpha-2 agonist) prolongs peripheral block duration and improves quality, with bradycardia and hypotension as dose-related cautions - a modern alternative to clonidine.

questions.q: Systemic fungal infection and administration of live vaccines are:
o: Contraindications or strong cautions to corticosteroid administration
questions.x: Corticosteroids are contraindicated in uncontrolled systemic fungal infection, and live vaccines are avoided in immunosuppressive-dose steroid courses; unstable diabetes, glaucoma and active infection at the injection site are further cautions.

questions.q: The most important skeletal complication of long-term systemic corticosteroids is:
o: Osteomalacia from vitamin D deficiency only
questions.x: Chronic steroids suppress osteoblasts and increase resorption, causing rapid trabecular bone loss and vertebral/hip fragility fractures; calcium/vitamin D and antiresorptive therapy are recommended for long courses.

questions.q: Bisphosphonates (e.g., IV pamidronate, neridronate) have evidence in which pain condition?
questions.x: Bisphosphonates, targeting the exaggerated osteoclast activity and bone turnover of early CRPS, have trial evidence for pain and function improvement in early-stage disease - one of the few disease-modifying options.

questions.q: Vitamin C (500 mg/day for ~50 days) is recommended as prophylaxis against CRPS after:
questions.x: Randomized trials showed that vitamin C 500 mg daily after wrist fracture reduces CRPS incidence, presumably by antioxidant effects; it is a cheap, safe prophylactic measure after distal radius fractures.

questions.q: Calcitonin in pain medicine has been used for:
questions.x: Calcitonin (intranasal or subcutaneous) has analgesic effects in CRPS, phantom pain and acute osteoporotic vertebral fracture pain, probably via central serotonergic and beta-endorphin mechanisms, though evidence is moderate.

questions.q: Antiviral therapy for herpes zoster is most effective when started within:
o: It is ineffective at any time
questions.x: Acyclovir/valacyclovir started within 72 hours of rash onset (or later if new lesions appear) shortens viral shedding and acute pain and modestly reduces postherpetic neuralgia risk, especially in older patients.

questions.q: The recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) is recommended for:
o: Adults 50 years and older (including the immunocompromised) to prevent herpes zoster and PHN
questions.x: The adjuvanted recombinant zoster vaccine is over 90% effective at preventing zoster and postherpetic neuralgia and is recommended for immunocompetent adults 50+, and for immunocompromised adults, in two doses.

questions.q: Codeine should be used cautiously in known CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolizers because they:
o: Convert codeine to morphine rapidly, risking opioid toxicity
questions.x: Codeine is a prodrug activated by CYP2D6 to morphine; ultra-rapid metabolizers generate dangerous morphine levels (fatal cases in children and breastfeeding infants), while poor metabolizers get no analgesia at all.

questions.q: Oxycodone metabolism can be significantly altered by inhibitors of:
questions.x: Oxycodone is metabolized by CYP3A4 (to noroxycodone) and CYP2D6 (to oxymorphone); strong inhibitors of either pathway (e.g., azole antifungals, macrolides) raise oxycodone levels and sedation risk.

questions.q: Perineural injection therapy with 5% dextrose (D5W) is used to:
o: Hydrodissect and calm neuropathic pain without steroid or local anesthetic
questions.x: Ultrasound-guided perineural D5W (without steroid) hydrodissects the nerve and may downregulate neurogenic inflammation via TRPV1 effects; it is used for entrapment neuropathies (carpal tunnel, ulnar) where steroid is undesirable.

questions.q: Evidence for cannabinoids in chronic non-cancer pain is best summarized as:
o: Small average benefit for neuropathic pain with frequent side effects - not first-line
questions.x: Meta-analyses show small effect sizes of cannabinoids in neuropathic pain, with high rates of dizziness, sedation and psychoactive effects; most guidelines place them behind established agents and caution about psychiatric and dependence risks.

questions.q: Low-dose naltrexone (LDN) is an emerging, off-label option investigated for:
o: Fibromyalgia and centralized pain via glial modulation
questions.x: Low-dose naltrexone (1-5 mg) is hypothesized to modulate glial activation and neuroinflammation; small trials in fibromyalgia and CRPS show promise, but it remains off-label with limited evidence and is incompatible with concurrent opioids.

questions.q: Intravenous magnesium sulfate has analgesic potential because magnesium:
questions.x: Magnesium physiologically blocks the NMDA receptor channel; IV magnesium has been studied as adjunct for neuropathic pain, postoperative analgesia and CRPS, with modest evidence and a safety profile limited by flushing and hypotension.

questions.q: Vertebroplasty for an osteoporotic compression fracture involves injection of:
o: Polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) bone cement into the vertebral body
questions.x: Vertebroplasty injects PMMA cement through a transpedicular needle into the fractured vertebral body to stabilize microfractures and relieve pain; it does not restore height - that is the goal of kyphoplasty's balloon.

questions.q: Kyphoplasty differs from vertebroplasty in that it first uses:
o: A balloon tamp to create a cavity and partially restore vertebral height
questions.x: Kyphoplasty inflates a balloon within the vertebral body before cement injection, creating a low-pressure cavity that may restore some height and reduce cement leakage compared with vertebroplasty.

questions.q: The most feared immediate complication of vertebral cement augmentation is:
o: Cement leakage into the canal or venous system (cord compression, pulmonary embolism)
questions.x: PMMA can leak into the epidural space (cord/root compression) or the basivertebral venous plexus (cement pulmonary embolism); careful fluoroscopic monitoring, paste viscosity and stopping on any posterior-wall breach are essential safeguards.

questions.q: Vertebroplasty is contraindicated in the presence of:
o: Local or systemic infection and significant posterior wall disruption with retropulsion
questions.x: Active infection (discitis/osteomyelitis or sepsis), uncorrected coagulopathy, and retropulsed fragments or posterior cortical disruption risking cement displacement into the canal are key contraindications to cement augmentation.

questions.q: CT myelography is the preferred study for detailed intrathecal anatomy when:
o: The patient has a pacemaker or other MRI contraindication
Only soft tissue is of interest
questions.x: When MRI is contraindicated (non-conditional pacemaker, some implants) or degraded by metal artifact, CT myelography with intrathecal iodinated contrast provides excellent cord/root and bony canal detail.

questions.q: After lumbar surgery, gadolinium-enhanced MRI best distinguishes recurrent disc herniation from epidural scar because:
o: Epidural fibrosis enhances early, while disc material does not enhance early
questions.x: Epidural scar tissue is vascular and enhances early after gadolinium, whereas avascular recurrent disc material enhances only peripherally and late - the classic discriminator in failed back surgery syndrome.

questions.q: Needle EMG evidence of acute radiculopathy typically becomes detectable after:
o: 2-3 weeks of axonal injury (fibrillations, positive sharp waves)
questions.x: Denervation potentials (fibrillations and positive sharp waves) appear in the paraspinal and limb muscles 2-3 weeks after axonal injury; earlier studies may be normal despite clear radiculopathy, so timing matters.

questions.q: Somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEPs) in spinal assessment monitor:
o: Dorsal column sensory pathway conduction from periphery to cortex
questions.x: SSEPs record responses along the dorsal column-lemniscal pathway after peripheral nerve stimulation, localizing conduction delays in the cord or roots; they complement (not replace) EMG and imaging in myelopathy evaluation.

questions.q: Upright or flexion-extension imaging is most valuable for diagnosing:
o: Dynamic instability and positional stenosis missed on supine MRI
questions.x: Some spondylolisthesis and stenosis appear only under load; standing, weight-bearing or flexion-extension radiographs/MRI reveal dynamic slip and positional canal narrowing that recumbent imaging underestimates.

questions.q: Intrathecal drug-delivery trials before pump implantation may be performed by:
o: Single bolus, continuous epidural/intrathecal infusion trial, or both
questions.x: Trialing methods include single-shot intrathecal bolus, multiple boluses, or continuous intrathecal/epidural infusion over days; practice varies, and a successful trial (50%+ relief with tolerable side effects) precedes implantation.

questions.q: Routine refill intervals for an intrathecal drug pump are typically every:
o: 1-6 months, depending on flow rate and reservoir size
questions.x: Refills are scheduled by calculated reservoir volume divided by daily flow, typically every 1-6 months, with an alarm buffer before the 'low reservoir' date; missed refills risk withdrawal (especially with baclofen).

questions.q: Before MRI in a patient with an intrathecal pump or spinal cord stimulator, one must verify:
o: Device MRI-conditional status, and follow device-specific instructions (e.g., pump motor stop, stimulator off)
questions.x: SCS systems and pumps have model-specific MRI conditions (lead configuration, field strength, scan region); MRI can stop pump rotors temporarily (recovering after) and can heat or damage stimulators - always confirm the conditions with the device ID card/manufacturer.

questions.q: Minimally invasive sacroiliac joint fusion is indicated for:
o: Confirmed SIJ pain (positive provocative tests plus high-grade response to diagnostic blocks) refractory to conservative care
questions.x: SIJ fusion (lateral triangular titanium implants or transfixing screws) is reserved for patients with concordant provocative testing and substantial relief from controlled diagnostic SIJ blocks who fail conservative management.

questions.q: Sacroiliac joint pain is common in pregnancy because:
o: Relaxin-mediated ligamentous laxity plus increased load and lordosis
questions.x: Relaxin and progesterone loosen the SIJ and pubic ligaments while weight gain and lumbar lordosis increase shear through the joint; peripartum SIJ and pelvic girdle pain usually improve postpartum but can persist.

questions.q: In the Quebec Task Force classification, whiplash-associated disorder (WAD) grade II includes:
o: Neck complaint with musculoskeletal signs (decreased range, point tenderness) but no neurological signs
questions.x: WAD grades: 0 no complaint; I neck pain only; II pain plus musculoskeletal signs; III pain plus neurological signs; IV fracture or dislocation. Most ultrasound/injection candidates with facet-mediated pain fall in grades I-II.

questions.q: Diagnostic criteria for cervicogenic headache require that the headache:
o: Is referred from a cervical source and is abolished or markedly reduced by diagnostic blockade of that structure
questions.x: Cervicogenic headache is referred pain from cervical structures (C1-3 joints and their nerves), typically unilateral without side shift, with restricted neck motion; complete or substantial relief after controlled diagnostic blocks of the suspect joint/nerve confirms the source.

questions.q: Klippel-Feil syndrome, relevant to cervical interventions, is characterized by:
o: Congenital fusion of cervical vertebrae with atlanto-axial instability risk
questions.x: Congenital fusion of two or more cervical segments (low hairline, short neck, restricted rotation) concentrates stress at adjacent segments and is associated with atlanto-axial instability and renal/cardiac anomalies - screen before upper cervical procedures.

questions.q: Rupture of the transverse ligament of the atlas is suggested on open-mouth odontoid views by:
o: Combined lateral mass overhang of C1 on C2 (rule of Spence) beyond ~7 mm
questions.x: Combined lateral displacement of the C1 lateral masses over C2 exceeding about 7 mm (rule of Spence) implies transverse ligament disruption and atlanto-axial instability - an absolute stop for any C1-2 procedure.

questions.q: The arcuate foramen (ponticulus posterior) of the atlas is important because it:
o: Is the site of cervical disc herniation
Creates a bony bridge over the vertebral artery, a variant that matters for C1 lateral mass procedures
questions.x: A bony arc over the sulcus of the vertebral artery on the C1 posterior arch (present in a minority) can mislead lateral mass screw or needle placement and is associated with VA injury risk - review imaging before C1 instrumentation.

questions.q: Os odontoideum refers to:
o: A small ossicle separate from the C2 body at the dens level, with potential atlanto-axial instability
questions.x: Os odontoideum is a smooth, corticated ossicle separate from the axis body (congenital or post-traumatic), which can render the C1-2 segment unstable; dynamic imaging assessment is mandatory before upper cervical interventions.

questions.q: An ultrasound-guided maxillary nerve (V2) block is performed via the:
o: Infrazygomatic approach into the pterygopalatine fossa
questions.x: The maxillary nerve is reached through the mandibular notch below the zygoma, advancing between the lateral pterygoid plate and the maxilla into the pterygopalatine fossa - for V2 trigeminal neuralgia and facial procedures.

questions.q: The mandibular nerve (V3) is blocked as it exits the skull through the:
o: Foramen ovale, approached below the zygomatic arch at the coronoid notch
questions.x: V3 exits via the foramen ovale; extraoral block uses the sigmoid (coronoid) notch between the condylar and coronoid processes to reach the nerve lateral to the lateral pterygoid plate - for V3 neuralgia and mandibular surgery.

questions.q: Radiofrequency lesioning of the gasserian ganglion for trigeminal neuralgia is reserved for:
o: Patients refractory to or intolerant of pharmacological therapy
questions.x: Trigeminal RF rhizotomy (or balloon compression/glycerol) is an option for classical trigeminal neuralgia failing carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine, accepting facial sensory loss as the trade-off; microvascular decompression is the main alternative.

questions.q: Glossopharyngeal nerve block for glossopharyngeal neuralgia targets the nerve:
o: Near the styloid process as it exits the jugular foramen
questions.x: The glossopharyngeal nerve is blocked where it passes between the internal carotid artery and internal jugular vein just below the skull base near the styloid process; severe bradycardia and hypotension (vagal effects) must be anticipated.

questions.q: The supratrochlear nerve, blocked for forehead procedures, supplies the:
o: Medial forehead and frontal scalp near the midline
questions.x: The supratrochlear nerve (V1) exits at the supraorbital rim medial to the supraorbital nerve, supplying the medial forehead, frontal scalp and upper nose - blocked together with the supraorbital for forehead analgesia.

questions.q: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is blocked at the level of the:
o: Greater horn of the hyoid bone
questions.x: The internal superior laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane near the greater cornu of the hyoid; its block provides mucosal anesthesia of the larynx above the vocal cords (for awake intubation) and treats superior laryngeal neuralgia.

questions.q: A complete wrist block for hand surgery requires anesthetizing the median, ulnar and:
questions.x: Wrist block combines subfascial injection around the median nerve (between PL and FCR), the ulnar nerve (lateral to FCU), and the superficial radial branch in the anatomical snuffbox/subcutaneous lateral wrist for full hand coverage.

questions.q: A digital (ring) block anesthetizes a finger by injecting around the:
o: Volar and dorsal digital nerves at the base of the finger
questions.x: Ring block places local anesthetic (without epinephrine per traditional teaching) around the base of the digit to reach the two volar and two dorsal digital nerves, anesthetizing the whole finger distal to the injection.

questions.q: The dorsal nerve of the penis, blocked for penile procedures, is a terminal branch of the:
questions.x: Dorsal penile block infiltrates lateral to the midline beneath Buck's fascia at the penile base, targeting the paired dorsal nerves (terminal pudendal branches) for circumcision and distal penile surgery analgesia.

questions.q: The pecto-intercostal fascial block (PIFB) provides analgesia over the:
o: Anterior chest wall and sternum (e.g. sternotomy)
questions.x: PIFB injects local anesthetic between pectoralis major and the external intercostal muscles beside the sternum, blocking the anterior cutaneous branches of the intercostal nerves - used for sternotomy, cardiac device and breast surgery analgesia.

questions.q: Parasternal intercostal blocks target the intercostal nerves near the:
o: Sternal border, blocking anterior cutaneous branches
questions.x: Parasternal blocks anesthetize the anterior cutaneous branches of T2-T6 as they emerge beside the sternum; pleural puncture and pneumothorax are the key risks, minimized by in-plane ultrasound guidance.

questions.q: The subcostal TAP block extends TAP analgesia to the upper abdomen by injecting in the plane:
o: Between internal oblique and transversus abdominis along the costal margin
questions.x: The subcostal TAP approach follows the costal margin obliquely in the TAP plane, covering T6-T9 for upper abdominal incisions that the classic (posterior) TAP block misses; combining both covers most of the abdominal wall.

questions.q: The retrolaminar block deposits local anesthetic:
o: Between the lamina and the overlying erector spinae muscle
questions.x: Retrolaminar block spreads injectate over the posterior lamina under the erector spinae, achieving multilevel thoracic analgesia through paravertebral spread with a simpler, shallower target than the paravertebral space itself.

questions.q: The rhomboid intercostal subserratus (RISS) block targets the plane:
o: Between rhomboids/serratus anterior and the intercostal muscles for upper thoracic analgesia
questions.x: RISS places injectate deep to the rhomboids (upper) or serratus anterior (lower) on the intercostal muscles, covering the lateral and posterior hemithorax (T3-T9) - an alternative to erector spinae and paravertebral blocks.

questions.q: For benign chronic abdominal pain (e.g., chronic pancreatitis), the preferred target is often the:
o: Splanchnic nerves rather than the celiac plexus
questions.x: Splanchnic nerve block (T11-T12, retrocrural) targets the afferents above the diaphragm and is favored for benign upper abdominal pain because it spares the celiac plexus for possible later neurolysis and may carry fewer risks.

questions.q: A therapeutic epidural blood patch for post-dural puncture headache typically injects:
o: 15-20 mL of autologous blood into the epidural space
questions.x: Autologous blood (15-20 mL, or until back pressure/discomfort) injected at or near the puncture level forms a clot sealing the dural tear and raises CSF pressure; it is the definitive treatment when conservative measures fail, with high success.

questions.q: Optimal timing of an epidural blood patch after dural puncture is:
o: After conservative measures fail, usually after 24-48 hours
questions.x: Conservative care (hydration, caffeine, analgesia, abdominal binder) is tried first; a blood patch is offered for severe or persistent PDPH, commonly after 24-48 hours, though early patch is reasonable in severe cases.

questions.q: For analgesia after shoulder surgery, the gold-standard regional technique is:
questions.x: Interscalene block covers C5-C7, anesthetizing the shoulder (suprascapular, axillary, lateral pectoral contributions); combined with multimodal analgesia it is the reference technique for arthroscopic and open shoulder surgery.

questions.q: Continuous perineural catheters offer the advantage of:
o: Prolonged, titratable analgesia for days after surgery
questions.x: Perineural catheters with infusion pumps extend single-shot blocks for 2-4 days, allowing titration, patient-controlled boluses and earlier discharge with ambulatory pumps - with attention to infection, dislodgement and local anesthetic dosing.

questions.q: Ambulatory perineural infusions commonly use:
o: Ropivacaine 0.2% via an elastomeric or electronic pump
questions.x: Home infusion typically delivers dilute ropivacaine (0.2%) at basal rates of 4-8 mL/h through portable elastomeric or electronic pumps, balancing analgesia with motor-sparing and safety outside hospital.

questions.q: Tunneling a perineural catheter under the skin is performed to:
o: Secure the catheter and reduce dislodgement and infection during longer infusions
questions.x: Subcutaneous tunneling away from the insertion site anchors the catheter, reduces accidental pull-out and migration of skin organisms along the track, and is standard when catheters remain for several days.

questions.q: A continuous adductor canal catheter after knee arthroplasty is preferred over a femoral catheter because it:
o: Provides analgesia with quadriceps-sparing effect, enabling early mobilization
questions.x: Adductor canal (saphenous) infusion gives predominantly sensory analgesia to the knee while largely preserving quadriceps strength - supporting early ambulation and reduced fall risk compared with femoral nerve catheters.

questions.q: Continuous popliteal sciatic catheters are typically used for:
questions.x: Popliteal sciatic catheters cover the tibial and common peroneal territories below the knee (except the saphenous strip), providing excellent analgesia for foot and ankle surgery with hamstring-sparing placement above the fossa.

questions.q: Continuous TAP or rectus sheath catheters are used mainly for:
o: Postoperative analgesia of the anterior abdominal wall
questions.x: TAP and rectus sheath catheters infuse local anesthetic along the abdominal wall planes for midline and transverse abdominal incisions, reducing opioid requirements as part of enhanced-recovery protocols.

questions.q: At the ankle, the saphenous nerve is blocked where it runs with the great saphenous vein:
questions.x: The saphenous nerve's terminal branches accompany the great saphenous vein anterior to the medial malleolus, supplying the medial foot - the final component of the five-nerve ankle block and a target for medial foot neuralgia.

questions.q: In the Bigliani classification, which acromial morphology is most associated with supraspinatus impingement and tears?
questions.x: Bigliani type I is flat, II curved, III hooked; the hooked type III acromion narrows the subacromial outlet and is strongly associated with impingement and cuff tears. Ultrasound and radiographs (supraspinatus outlet view) classify the shape.

questions.q: An os acromiale represents:
o: An unfused acromial apophysis that may contribute to impingement
A normal finding in all adults
questions.x: Os acromiale is failure of fusion of an acromial ossification center (meso/meta/m pre-acromion); the mobile segment can be pulled down by the deltoid, narrowing the outlet, and can be tender itself.

questions.q: Posterior sternoclavicular joint dislocation is dangerous because of potential injury to the:
o: Retrosternal great vessels trachea and esophagus
questions.x: Posterior SC dislocation drives the medial clavicle toward the brachiocephalic vessels, trachea and esophagus - a true emergency requiring prompt reduction. Ultrasound can confirm the direction of displacement at the joint.

questions.q: The coracoid process serves as the anterior shoulder landmark for the conjoint tendon of the:
o: Short head of biceps and coracobrachialis (plus pectoralis minor)
questions.x: The conjoint tendon (coracobrachialis and short head of biceps) and the pectoralis minor attach to the coracoid; it anchors the coracoacromial ligament roof of the outlet and guides infraclavicular block orientation.

questions.q: A Monteggia injury consists of:
o: Ulnar shaft fracture with radial head dislocation
questions.x: Monteggia is a proximal ulnar fracture with dislocation of the proximal radioulnar/radiocapitellar joint; missing the radial head dislocation leads to chronic instability. Ultrasound can assess the annular ligament and joint alignment in children.

questions.q: Snapping of the medial triceps over the medial epicondyle during elbow flexion is often accompanied by:
o: Coexisting dislocation of the ulnar nerve out of the cubital tunnel
questions.x: Snapping triceps syndrome occurs when an anomalous medial triceps slips over the medial epicondyle, frequently with concurrent ulnar nerve dislocation - a dynamic ultrasound diagnosis in the flexed elbow.

questions.q: An anconeus epitrochlearis muscle is a cause of:
o: Cubital tunnel syndrome (ulnar nerve compression at the elbow)
questions.x: The anomalous anconeus epitrochlearis spans the cubital tunnel roof from medial epicondyle to olecranon, compressing the ulnar nerve; ultrasound shows the muscle replacing the normal retinaculum with nerve swelling proximal to it.

questions.q: Rupture of the extensor pollicis longus tendon is a recognized late complication of:
o: Distal radius fracture (attrition over Lister's tubercle)
questions.x: EPL passes around Lister's tubercle in the third dorsal compartment; after distal radius fractures (even nondisplaced) it can undergo attrition rupture weeks later, presenting as inability to lift the thumb off a table.

questions.q: From radial to ulnar, the six dorsal wrist compartments contain, respectively, APL/EPB, ECRL/ECRB, EPL, EDC/EI, EDM and:
questions.x: The compartments run: 1 APL+EPB, 2 ECRL+ECRB, 3 EPL, 4 EDC+EI, 5 EDM, 6 ECU. Memorizing the sequence localizes tenosynovitis and guides compartment-specific injections.

questions.q: A carpal boss (carpometacarpal boss) is a bony prominence at the:
o: Base of the second/third metacarpals at the CMC joints
questions.x: Carpal boss is an osteophytic bony bump at the second/third carpometacarpal joints, sometimes with a small ganglion; it is tender with grip and can mimic a dorsal wrist mass.

questions.q: A swan-neck deformity of a finger consists of:
questions.x: Swan-neck deformity (PIP hyperextension, DIP flexion) results from volar plate laxity and lateral band dorsal migration - seen in rheumatoid arthritis and after mallet injuries; the opposite pattern to boutonniere.

questions.q: Pincer-type femoroacetabular impingement results from:
o: Acetabular overcoverage (deep socket, protrusio or retroversion) contacting the femoral neck
questions.x: Pincer FAI is overcoverage of the acetabular rim (coxa profunda, protrusio or retroversion) crushing the labrum against the femoral neck in flexion; cam deformity is the femoral-sided counterpart.

questions.q: The coronary (meniscotibial) ligaments attach the meniscus to the:
questions.x: Coronary ligaments anchor the meniscal body to the tibial rim; their injury produces meniscal hypermobility and extrusion, and they form part of the deep MCL complex on the medial side.

questions.q: Chondromalacia patellae refers to:
o: Softening and degeneration of the patellar articular cartilage
questions.x: Chondromalacia patellae is cartilage softening/fibrillation of the patellar facet causing retropatellar pain on stairs and prolonged sitting; ultrasound assesses overlying soft tissues while MRI grades the cartilage.

questions.q: The ultrasound 'double contour sign' in gout is produced by:
o: Monosodium urate crystals deposited on the surface of the articular cartilage
questions.x: Urate crystals coating the hyaline cartilage surface create a hyperechoic line parallel to the subchondral bone - the double contour sign, highly specific for gout and distinct from the intracartilage deposition of CPPD.

questions.q: A gouty tophus on ultrasound typically appears as a:
o: Heterogeneous hyperechoic mass with a hypoechoic rim, sometimes with shadowing foci
questions.x: Tophi are heterogeneous hyperechoic aggregates of urate with an anechoic/hypoechoic inflammatory rim, often periarticular or within tendons, and may erode adjacent bone with characteristic 'punched-out' lesions.

questions.q: In rheumatoid arthritis, power Doppler signal within synovial hypertrophy indicates:
questions.x: Power Doppler detects hyperemia within pannus, grading synovitis activity and monitoring treatment response; PD-positive synovitis predicts progression to erosions better than grayscale thickening alone.

questions.q: Compared with radiography, ultrasound detects rheumatoid erosions:
o: Earlier and with greater sensitivity especially at the MCP/MTP joints
questions.x: Ultrasound identifies cortical breaks in two perpendicular planes with an adjacent synovitis, detecting small erosions at the ulnar styloid, MCP and MTP joints earlier than plain films - influencing early DMARD decisions.

questions.q: Dactylitis ('sausage digit') in psoriatic arthritis reflects:
o: Diffuse tenosynovitis plus synovitis and soft-tissue/entheseal inflammation of the whole digit
questions.x: Dactylitis combines flexor tenosynovitis, joint synovitis, enthesitis and soft-tissue edema of an entire digit; ultrasound dissects the components, showing the characteristic 'flexor tendon with surrounding fluid' and entheseal hyperemia.

questions.q: Freiberg infraction is osteochondrosis of the:
questions.x: Freiberg infraction is avascular necrosis of the metatarsal head (classically the second) in adolescents and young women, causing forefoot pain with flattening and sclerosis of the head on imaging.

questions.q: A bunion in hallux valgus is pain and swelling over the:
o: Medial eminence of the first metatarsal head with an inflamed adventitious bursa
questions.x: Hallux valgus deviates the great toe laterally, exposing the medial eminence; pressure forms a painful adventitious bursa ('bunion') that ultrasound can aspirate or inject, distinct from joint synovitis.

questions.q: The classic first presentation of gout is podagra, involving the:
questions.x: Podagra - sudden, exquisitely painful red swelling of the first MTP joint - is the classic gout debut; ultrasound may show the double contour sign, tophaceous aggregates and erosions even at first presentation.

questions.q: Bilateral Achilles tendon xanthomas in a young patient suggest:
questions.x: Achilles xanthomas are cholesterol deposits within the tendon (fusiform hypoechoic thickening with preserved fiber pattern) strongly associated with familial hypercholesterolemia - an important cardiovascular risk flag found on tendon scanning.

questions.q: The most common tarsal coalition causing a rigid painful flatfoot in adolescents is:
questions.x: Tarsal coalitions (calcaneonavicular, then talocalcaneal) restrict subtalar motion, causing rigid flatfoot and peroneal spasm in adolescents; the calcaneonavicular bar is visible on oblique radiographs and ultrasound.

questions.q: Plantar fibromatosis (Ledderhose disease) presents as:
o: Firm hypoechoic nodules within the plantar fascia, typically non-weight-bearing midfoot
questions.x: Ledderhose disease is fibroblastic proliferation within the plantar fascia (non-insertional, mid-arch), forming firm hypoechoic nodules continuous with the fascia - the foot counterpart of Dupuytren disease.

questions.q: The speed of sound in air (about 330 m/s) compared with soft tissue explains:
o: Why gas causes 'dirty' shadowing and obscures deeper structures
questions.x: Gas has extremely low impedance and speed; nearly all energy reflects at a tissue-gas interface, and the reverberating echoes create a hazy 'dirty' shadow - why lung air limits scanning and why bowel gas must be displaced by probe pressure.

questions.q: The propagation time for the ultrasound pulse-echo round trip in soft tissue is approximately:
questions.x: The machine assumes 1540 m/s; the round trip to a reflector takes about 13 microseconds per centimeter of depth. The time-of-flight of each returning echo is converted directly into its displayed depth.

questions.q: A ring-down artifact differs from a comet tail in that it is produced by:
o: Resonant vibration of fluid trapped between gas bubbles or crystals
questions.x: Ring-down is a continuous bright streak from resonant oscillation of fluid between tetrahedra of gas bubbles (or cholesterol crystals in adenomyomatosis), whereas the comet tail is a tapering series of discrete reverberations behind small metal objects.

questions.q: Partial-volume (slice-thickness) artifact results from:
o: Beam width in the elevational plane averaging structures into the image
questions.x: The beam has thickness in the out-of-image (elevational) direction, so echoes from structures above and below the intended slice are averaged in - for example, false 'sludge' in a cyst. Thin-section focusing and harmonic imaging reduce it.

questions.q: The average attenuation of soft tissue is approximately:
questions.x: Soft tissue attenuates about 0.5 dB per cm per MHz (one-way); a 10 MHz beam loses roughly 5 dB per cm of depth - the quantitative basis for the frequency-penetration trade-off and for TGC design.

questions.q: An isoechoic structure is one that:
o: Has the same echogenicity as the surrounding reference tissue
questions.x: Isoechoic = same brightness as the reference (e.g., liver parenchyma); such lesions are hard to detect - a small isoechoic tendon tear or metastasis may show only by contour or vascular changes.

questions.q: Cortical bone appears on ultrasound as:
o: A smooth bright (hyperechoic) line with strong posterior acoustic shadowing
questions.x: The soft tissue-bone interface reflects almost all energy, displaying a bright continuous cortical line with a clean anechoic shadow beyond it. Cortical breaks, step-offs and callus are assessed against this line.

questions.q: The decibel scale used in ultrasound is:
o: Logarithmic, allowing compression of a huge intensity range into displayable numbers
questions.x: Decibels express ratios logarithmically (10 log10 of intensity ratio); a 3 dB change doubles/halves intensity. The log scale compresses the enormous range between transmitted pulse and faintest echo into manageable dynamic range settings.

questions.q: Spatial peak temporal average intensity (ISPTA) is the intensity metric most relevant to:
o: Thermal bioeffects and the displayed thermal index
questions.x: ISPTA - the highest spatial intensity averaged over time - correlates with tissue heating and underlies the thermal index displayed for ALARA monitoring during prolonged interventional scanning.

questions.q: Edge (refractile) shadowing appears as:
o: A broad clean shadow behind bone
Narrow shadows projecting from the curved margins of rounded structures
questions.x: Where the beam grazes a curved boundary (vessel wall, tendon edge, cyst margin), refraction deflects it, leaving narrow anechoic 'edge' shadows distal to the margin - a clue to curved anatomy, not pathology.

questions.q: Anisotropy in tendon imaging is corrected by:
o: Angling the probe so the beam is perpendicular to the tendon fibers
questions.x: Tendon is strongly anisotropic: oblique insonation makes normal tendon appear hypoechoic and mimics tendinosis. Rocking the transducer to restore a 90-degree beam-fiber angle immediately re-brightens the normal fibrillar pattern.

questions.q: Quality assurance of an ultrasound machine includes periodic testing with:
o: A tissue-mimicking phantom to verify resolution, depth accuracy and sensitivity
questions.x: QA programs use tissue-mimicking phantoms with embedded targets to check axial/lateral resolution, depth and distance accuracy, dead zone and sensitivity over time, ensuring measurements (e.g., nerve CSA) remain reliable.

questions.q: Ultrasound transducers should never be decontaminated by:
o: Heat-based methods such as autoclaving, which damage the crystals and housing
Rinsing gel off with damp cloth
questions.x: Standard probes are heat-sensitive: autoclaving, boiling or dry-heat ovens crack housings, delaminate the lens and depolarize the piezoelectric elements. Only manufacturer-approved chemical methods are used (some specialized probes are rated for sterilization).

questions.q: Warming ultrasound gel before scanning is done to:
o: Improve patient comfort, especially in sensitive areas
questions.x: Gel temperature has no acoustic significance; warming is purely for patient comfort. Beyond comfort, the gel's role is to displace air between probe and skin for acoustic coupling.

questions.q: Which artifact helps confirm that a structure is solid rather than a simple cyst?
o: Posterior acoustic enhancement - its absence argues against simple fluid
questions.x: Simple cysts show posterior enhancement because fluid barely attenuates; a round structure without through-transmission is more likely solid. Combined with internal echoes and Doppler flow, this distinguishes solid lesions from cysts.

questions.q: Milnacipran is approved in some countries specifically for:
questions.x: Milnacipran is a noradrenaline-predominant SNRI approved for fibromyalgia in the US and elsewhere; like duloxetine it boosts descending inhibition, with nausea and blood-pressure elevation as common issues.

questions.q: Topiramate in pain practice is used mainly for:
o: Migraine prophylaxis (and as a migraine-preventive with weight-loss effect)
questions.x: Topiramate 50-100 mg/day is an established migraine preventive; cognitive slowing ('Dopamax'), paresthesias, weight loss and nephrolithiasis limit tolerability. It is not an acute analgesic.

questions.q: A key caution with sodium valproate for migraine prophylaxis in women of childbearing potential is:
o: High teratogenicity (neural tube defects) requiring reliable contraception
questions.x: Valproate is an effective migraine preventive but strongly teratogenic (neural tube defects, neurodevelopmental effects); it should be avoided in pregnancy and used with effective contraception and clear counseling.

questions.q: Propranolol prevents migraine by blocking:
questions.x: Propranolol (and other beta-blockers such as metoprolol, timolol) is first-line for migraine prophylaxis; avoid in asthma, bradycardia and decompensated heart failure.

questions.q: Triptans are contraindicated in patients with:
o: Coronary artery disease or uncontrolled hypertension
questions.x: Triptans (5-HT1B/1D agonists) constrict cranial and coronary vessels; they are contraindicated in coronary artery disease, prior stroke, uncontrolled hypertension and hemiplegic/basilar migraine. Chest tightness is a common benign side effect.

questions.q: Monoclonal antibodies against CGRP or its receptor (e.g., erenumab) are used for:
o: Migraine prevention, injected monthly or quarterly
questions.x: Anti-CGRP (ligand) or anti-CGRP-receptor monoclonal antibodies are the first mechanism-specific migraine preventives, given subcutaneously monthly/quarterly, with constipation and injection-site reactions as the main side effects.

questions.q: Verapamil is the first-line prophylactic for:
questions.x: High-dose verapamil is the prophylactic of choice for cluster headache during a bout (with ECG monitoring for heart block), while high-flow oxygen and subcutaneous sumatriptan treat acute attacks.

questions.q: Carisoprodol should be used cautiously or avoided because it:
o: Metabolizes to meprobamate with abuse and dependence potential
questions.x: Carisoprodol converts to meprobamate, a barbiturate-like sedative with dependence and withdrawal risk; it is combined with aspirin/codeine in some products and is recommended only for short courses, if at all.

questions.q: Chloroprocaine is favored for short epidural blocks and labor analgesia top-ups because of its:
o: Rapid ester hydrolysis giving fast onset and very low systemic toxicity
questions.x: Chloroprocaine, an ester, is hydrolyzed by plasma cholinesterase within seconds, giving quick onset, short duration and minimal systemic accumulation - ideal for short procedures and rapid epidural top-ups.

questions.q: The maximum dose of lidocaine with epinephrine is approximately:
questions.x: Plain lidocaine is limited to about 4.5 mg/kg (300 mg); epinephrine's vasoconstriction slows absorption, allowing up to roughly 7 mg/kg (500 mg). Doses are always minimized in the elderly, hepatic impairment and pregnancy.

questions.q: An intravascular test dose for epidural injection classically contains:
o: Epinephrine 15 micrograms in local anesthetic, watching for tachycardia/hypertension
questions.x: Epinephrine 15 micrograms injected intravascularly produces a transient heart-rate rise (>10 bpm) and blood-pressure increase within about a minute - a sensitive marker of intravascular needle or catheter placement.

questions.q: Adding sodium bicarbonate to a local anesthetic solution:
o: Alkalinizes the solution, increasing the non-ionized fraction and speeding onset
questions.x: Alkalinization raises the proportion of lipid-soluble non-ionized base that crosses the nerve membrane, speeding onset and reducing injection pain; it must be freshly prepared to avoid precipitation (especially with bupivacaine).

questions.q: Epinephrine 1:200,000 added to local anesthetic primarily:
o: Reduces vascular absorption, prolonging the block and lowering peak plasma levels
questions.x: Epinephrine 5 micrograms/mL (1:200,000) causes local vasoconstriction, slowing anesthetic uptake, prolonging duration and reducing systemic peak concentrations - while also serving as an intravascular marker.

questions.q: Neuraxial morphine differs from neuraxial fentanyl in that morphine is:
o: Hydrophilic with long duration and risk of delayed respiratory depression
questions.x: Hydrophilic morphine spreads rostrally in CSF, giving prolonged analgesia but risking delayed respiratory depression up to 24 hours; lipophilic fentanyl acts segmentally, briefly, with lower late respiratory risk.

questions.q: Typical epidural steroid doses per injection are:
questions.x: Common practice uses dexamethasone 10 mg (non-particulate, foramina) or particulate triamcinolone 40-80 mg / methylprednisolone 40-80 mg for interlaminar injections; higher doses add systemic side effects without proven extra benefit.

questions.q: The vertebral artery segment that runs within the transverse foramina of C6 to C1 is the:
questions.x: V1 runs from the subclavian origin to the C6 foramen; V2 is the foraminal segment C6-C1; V3 curves from the atlas to the foramen magnum; V4 is intracranial. Doppler screening for V2 flow is prudent before cervical procedures.

questions.q: The carotid tubercle (Chassaignac's tubercle) is the prominent anterior tubercle of the:
questions.x: The C6 anterior tubercle (carotid tubercle of Chassaignac) is palpable and serves as the landmark for the C6 level in stellate ganglion and interscalene approaches; the carotid can be compressed against it.

questions.q: At the interscalene groove, the cervical nerve roots lie between the anterior and posterior tubercles of the:
o: Transverse processes, appearing as a 'two-humped camel' sign
questions.x: On transverse scan at C5-C7, each transverse process shows anterior and posterior tubercles with the nerve root in the groove between - the 'two-humped camel' - where the interscalene block places injectate.

questions.q: The costovertebral joint, where a medial branch-type pain can arise, connects the rib head to the:
o: Vertebral body (and disc) of the same and the level above
questions.x: Each rib head articulates with the demifacets of its own and the superior vertebral bodies plus the intervening disc; costovertebral joint arthropathy causes paraspinal thoracic pain and can be injected under imaging.

questions.q: The costotransverse joint links the rib tubercle to the:
o: Transverse process of the corresponding vertebra
questions.x: The rib tubercle articulates with the transverse process at the costotransverse joint, stabilized by the superior costotransverse ligament - the posterior boundary of the paravertebral space and an occasional pain generator.

questions.q: Thoracic facet (zygapophysial) joints are oriented mainly in the:
questions.x: Thoracic facets lie close to the coronal (frontal) plane, permitting rotation but limiting flexion-extension; this orientation differs from lumbar sagittal facets and cervical oblique facets and guides needle angles.

questions.q: Thoracic disc herniations are clinically important because they:
o: Can compress the spinal cord, producing myelopathy rather than radiculopathy alone
questions.x: Thoracic herniations are uncommon (most at T8-L1) but the narrow thoracic canal means even small herniations can cause cord compression with myelopathy - a surgical consideration rather than a routine injection target.

questions.q: Scoliosis severity on standing radiographs is quantified by the:
questions.x: The Cobb angle, measured between the most tilted endplates of the curve, grades scoliosis (mild 10-25 degrees, moderate 25-40, severe >40-50) and drives observation/bracing/surgery decisions.

questions.q: Scheuermann disease causes:
o: Adolescent thoracic kyphosis with wedged vertebrae and endplate irregularity
questions.x: Scheuermann kyphosis is osteochondrosis of the vertebral ring apophyses in adolescents, producing wedged vertebrae, endplate irregularity, Schmorl's nodes and a rigid thoracic kyphosis (>40-45 degrees).

questions.q: The iliolumbar ligament, a stabilizer and occasional pain source, connects the:
o: L4-L5 transverse processes to the iliac crest
questions.x: The iliolumbar ligament runs from the L5 (and L4) transverse process to the iliac crest, stabilizing the lumbosacral junction; its strain causes focal low back pain over the medial iliac crest.

questions.q: Red flags for cauda equina syndrome include all of the following EXCEPT:
o: Bilateral leg weakness and lax anal sphincter tone
questions.x: Cauda equina red flags: urinary retention (later overflow), saddle/perineal sensory loss, bilateral radicular pain and weakness, reduced anal tone and fecal incontinence. Unilateral ankle sprain is unrelated.

questions.q: Suspected cauda equina syndrome requires:
o: Urgent MRI and surgical decompression, ideally within 24-48 hours
questions.x: CES is a surgical emergency: urgent MRI confirms compression (massive disc, tumor, hematoma, abscess), and decompression within 24-48 hours offers the best chance of bladder and motor recovery.

questions.q: The classic triad of spinal epidural abscess is:
o: Fever, back pain and progressive neurological deficit
questions.x: Fever, severe localized back pain and evolving neurological signs form the classic (though often incomplete) triad; Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest organism, and MRI with contrast is the diagnostic test.

questions.q: The most common causative organism of pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis is:
questions.x: Hematogenous vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis is most often staphylococcal (S. aureus), seeding the disc space from skin, urinary or line infections; diabetes, dialysis and IV drug use are risk factors.

questions.q: Pott disease refers to spinal infection with:
o: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, typically sparing the disc early and causing gibbus deformity
questions.x: Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott) begins in the anterior vertebral body, spares the disc relatively early, spreads beneath the longitudinal ligaments to adjacent levels and collapses vertebrae into a kyphotic gibbus.

questions.q: MRI of early discitis/osteomyelitis characteristically shows:
o: T2-hyperintense disc with adjacent endplate marrow edema and enhancement
questions.x: Infection makes the disc bright on T2 with destruction and edema of the adjacent endplates and enhancement after contrast - distinct from Modic 1 degeneration, where the disc itself is typically low signal.

questions.q: The 'bamboo spine' on radiographs is characteristic of:
questions.x: Ankylosing spondylitis fuses vertebrae with thin marginal syndesmophytes, producing the smooth bamboo appearance; fracture risk through the fused, osteoporotic spine is high - extreme caution with neuraxial procedures.

questions.q: DISH (Forestier disease) is distinguished from ankylosing spondylitis by:
o: Flowing ossification of the anterolateral spine over at least four levels with preserved discs
questions.x: Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis shows thick flowing right-sided anterolateral ossification bridging 4+ contiguous vertebrae with preserved disc height and no SIJ erosion - unlike the thin syndesmophytes of AS.

questions.q: Lumbar transverse process fractures are significant mainly because they:
o: Indicate high-energy trauma and possible associated abdominal/retroperitoneal injury
questions.x: Isolated transverse process fractures are stable and treated symptomatically, but they signal significant force; multiple or L5 fractures warrant evaluation for associated visceral, pelvic and other spinal injuries.

questions.q: The Pfirrmann grading system classifies:
o: Lumbar disc degeneration (I-V) on T2 MRI
questions.x: Pfirrmann grades disc degeneration I-V based on T2 signal, disc height and nucleus/annulus distinction; grade III-IV discs are common targets in discussions of discogenic pain, though grades correlate imperfectly with symptoms.

questions.q: Froment's sign, indicating ulnar nerve dysfunction, is elicited by:
o: Asking the patient to grip paper between thumb and index - flexion of the thumb IP joint indicates adductor pollicis weakness
questions.x: In ulnar palsy the adductor pollicis (ulnar-innervated) is weak; the patient compensates by flexing the thumb IP joint with the FPL (median/AIN) during pinch - a positive Froment's sign.

questions.q: Durkan's carpal compression test is positive when:
o: Direct pressure over the carpal tunnel reproduces median nerve paresthesia within 30 seconds
questions.x: Sustained examiner pressure over the carpal tunnel is among the most sensitive provocative tests for carpal tunnel syndrome; paresthesia in the median distribution within 30 seconds is positive.

questions.q: Phalen's test for carpal tunnel syndrome is performed by:
o: Holding the wrists in full flexion for up to 60 seconds
questions.x: Full passive wrist flexion for up to a minute raises tunnel pressure and provokes median-distribution paresthesia; the reverse (extension) prayer position is also used. Sensitivity is moderate and ultrasound CSA adds objective evidence.

questions.q: Finkelstein's test for De Quervain tenosynovitis is performed by:
o: Ulnar deviation of the wrist with the thumb held in the fist
questions.x: With the thumb enclosed in the fist, ulnar deviation stretches the first-compartment tendons (APL/EPB) over the radial styloid, reproducing pain - the classic provocative test, complemented by ultrasound of compartment thickening.

questions.q: A positive Tinel's sign over a peripheral nerve indicates:
o: Percussion-induced paresthesia at a site of nerve injury or entrapment
questions.x: Gentle percussion over a regenerating or entrapped nerve elicits tingling in its distal distribution - Tinel's sign. The most distal point of a positive Tinel tracks regeneration or localizes the entrapment (also elicited sonographically).

questions.q: The cutaneous 'regimental badge' area over the lateral deltoid is supplied by the:
o: Axillary nerve (superior lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm)
questions.x: The axillary nerve's superior lateral cutaneous branch supplies the badge-shaped patch over the lower deltoid; sensory testing there after shoulder injury or surgery screens for axillary nerve injury.

questions.q: Isolated sensory loss in the first dorsal web space of the hand localizes to the:
questions.x: The superficial radial nerve's autonomous zone is the first dorsal web space; sensory change there with normal motor function suggests a distal radial sensory lesion (e.g., Wartenberg syndrome) rather than a posterior cord problem.

questions.q: The recurrent (thenar) branch of the median nerve:
o: Supplies the thenar muscles just distal to the flexor retinaculum and is at risk in carpal tunnel release
questions.x: The recurrent thenar motor branch leaves the median nerve just beyond the retinaculum (variable course: extraligamentous, subligamentous or transligamentous) to the thenar muscles - its variants are at risk during tunnel release.

questions.q: In ulnar neuropathy at the wrist (Guyon), sensation over the dorsal ulnar hand is:
o: Spared because the dorsal sensory branch left the nerve proximal to the wrist
questions.x: The dorsal ulnar sensory branch arises about 5 cm above the wrist; a Guyon canal lesion spares dorsoulnar sensation while affecting the palmar ulnar digits - the localization clue distinguishing wrist from elbow lesions.

questions.q: The medial pectoral nerve, despite its name, arises from the:
o: Medial cord (C8-T1) and supplies pectoralis minor and the sternal part of pectoralis major
questions.x: The medial pectoral nerve (medial cord, C8-T1) pierces the pectoralis minor to reach the lower pectoralis major; it is considered in neurotization and in pectoral muscle spasm after breast surgery.

questions.q: The nerve to subclavius, which can carry accessory phrenic fibers, arises from the:
questions.x: The small nerve to the subclavius (C5-C6, upper trunk) occasionally carries accessory phrenic fibers - one anatomical explanation for incomplete diaphragm sparing in some supraclavicular blocks.

questions.q: The subscapular nerves (upper and lower) from the posterior cord supply:
o: Subscapularis (and teres major for the lower)
questions.x: The upper and lower subscapular nerves (posterior cord, C5-C7) innervate the subscapularis, with the lower also supplying teres major - relevant to posterior cord lesions and shoulder denervation planning.

questions.q: Postganglionic sympathetic fibers release which primary neurotransmitter at most effector organs?
questions.x: Postganglionic sympathetic neurons release norepinephrine at most targets (alpha/beta adrenoceptors); exceptions are sweat glands (acetylcholine) and the adrenal medulla, which secretes catecholamines directly into blood.

questions.q: Sympathetic fibers to sweat glands are unusual because they are:
questions.x: Sudomotor sympathetic postganglionic fibers are cholinergic - the reason anticholinergic drugs cause dry skin, and why sweat testing maps sympathetic function (e.g., QSART) in small-fiber neuropathy and CRPS.

questions.q: The adrenal medulla is unique in the sympathetic system because it is innervated by:
o: Preganglionic sympathetic fibers directly, secreting adrenaline into the bloodstream
questions.x: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla are modified postganglionic neurons innervated directly by preganglionic cholinergic fibers, releasing systemic epinephrine and norepinephrine - the humoral arm of the sympathetic response.

questions.q: Sympathetically maintained pain (SMP) is defined as pain that:
o: Is relieved by sympathetic blockade and rekindled by sympathetic stimulation
questions.x: SMP is the component of pain dependent on sympathetic efferent activity: it improves with sympathetic blocks (stellate, lumbar sympathetic) and can be rekindled by catecholamines or cold - a subset of CRPS and neuropathic pain states.

questions.q: Primary Raynaud phenomenon differs from secondary Raynaud in that it:
o: Occurs without underlying connective tissue disease, with symmetric attacks and no tissue necrosis
questions.x: Primary Raynaud is benign, symmetric vasospasm (white-blue-red) without tissue damage; secondary Raynaud (scleroderma, SLE, vibration injury) is asymmetric, may ulcerate and requires autoantibody screening. Sympathetic block helps severe cases.

questions.q: Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease) is strongly associated with:
o: Tobacco use in young men, causing distal limb ischemia
questions.x: Buerger disease is inflammatory thrombosis of small/medium limb vessels in young male smokers, producing claudication, rest pain and digital gangrene; smoking cessation is the cornerstone, with sympathetic block as an adjunct for rest pain.

questions.q: Acrocyanosis is characterized by:
o: Persistent symmetric bluish discoloration and coolness of the hands/feet without pain
questions.x: Acrocyanosis is benign persistent symmetric cyanosis and coolness of distal extremities from chronic vasospasm, painless and without trophic change - distinguished from Raynaud attacks and ischemia.

questions.q: Intravenous regional sympathetic block with guanethidine (historical Bier technique) aimed to:
o: Deplete norepinephrine from sympathetic terminals in an exsanguinated limb for CRPS
questions.x: Guanethidine (and later bretylium/clonidine) IV regional sympathetic block depletes or blocks sympathetic transmitters in an isolated limb - largely historical evidence for the sympathetic contribution to CRPS, now replaced by ganglion blocks.

questions.q: The phentolamine infusion test historically assessed:
o: Alpha-adrenoceptor-mediated (sympathetically maintained) pain via alpha blockade
questions.x: IV phentolamine (alpha-1/2 antagonist) was used to test whether pain had an alpha-adrenoceptor-mediated SMP component; positive response predicted benefit from sympathetic blockade - a step in understanding CRPS mechanisms.

questions.q: Botulinum toxin for palmar or axillary hyperhidrosis works by:
o: Blocking cholinergic release at sudomotor sympathetic terminals
questions.x: Intradermal botulinum toxin A blocks acetylcholine release from the cholinergic sympathetic sudomotor fibers, abolishing sweating for 4-9 months in treated areas - a non-surgical alternative to sympathicolysis.

questions.q: Iontophoresis for palmar hyperhidrosis uses:
o: A low electrical current through tap water baths to reduce sweating
questions.x: Tap-water iontophoresis passes a mild direct current through water trays holding the palms or soles, reducing sweat production by an incompletely understood mechanism; it is first-line non-drug maintenance for mild-moderate cases.

questions.q: Harlequin syndrome, sometimes seen after upper thoracic sympathetic procedures, involves:
o: Unilateral flushing and sweating of the face with contralateral anhidrosis
questions.x: Unilateral loss of sympathetic outflow (or compensatory overactivity) produces a split-face picture: one side flushed and sweating, the other pale and dry - a striking but usually benign sign of sympathetic pathway disruption.

questions.q: The QSART (quantitative sudomotor axon reflex test) measures:
o: Axon-reflex-mediated sweat production, assessing postganglionic sympathetic sudomotor function
questions.x: QSART applies acetylcholine by iontophoresis and measures the axon-reflex sweat response, testing integrity of postganglionic sympathetic sudomotor fibers - used in small-fiber neuropathy and CRPS work-up.

questions.q: A Hill-Sachs lesion is:
o: An impaction fracture of the posterolateral humeral head after anterior shoulder dislocation
questions.x: Anterior dislocation impacts the soft posterolateral humeral head against the anterior glenoid rim, leaving a wedge-shaped impaction defect; large or 'engaging' Hill-Sachs lesions contribute to recurrent instability.

questions.q: A Bankart lesion involves injury to the:
o: Anteroinferior glenoid labrum and capsuloligamentous complex
questions.x: Anterior dislocation tears the anteroinferior labrum and anterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament (soft-tissue Bankart), sometimes with a glenoid rim fracture (bony Bankart) - the key lesion of recurrent anterior instability.

questions.q: A reverse Hill-Sachs lesion occurs with:
o: Posterior shoulder dislocation impacting the anteromedial humeral head
questions.x: Posterior dislocation (classically from seizures or electric shock) impacts the anteromedial humeral head on the posterior glenoid rim - the reverse Hill-Sachs (trough sign), often missed on initial radiographs.

questions.q: The 'terrible triad' of the elbow comprises:
o: Elbow dislocation with coronoid and radial head fractures
questions.x: Dislocation plus coronoid and radial head fractures renders the elbow grossly unstable (terrible triad), threatening the posterolateral and anterior stabilizers; it usually requires surgical reconstruction.

questions.q: A hook of hamate fracture typically occurs in:
o: Golf, baseball or racquet sports from direct impact of the grip
questions.x: The hamate hook is fractured by the butt of a club, bat or racquet striking the hypothenar palm, causing pain on grip and risking ulnar nerve irritation in Guyon's canal; carpal tunnel or hamate-hookup views and ultrasound/CT detect it.

questions.q: Pisiform fractures are best assessed with the knowledge that the pisiform is:
o: A carpal bone within the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon
questions.x: The pisiform is a sesamoid in the FCU tendon forming the medial wall of Guyon's canal; direct falls fracture it, and it articulates with the triquetrum (pisotriquetral joint, a site of ulnar wrist pain).

questions.q: In the Rockwood classification, AC joint separation type III involves:
o: Sprain of the AC ligaments only
Complete disruption of both AC and coracoclavicular ligaments with marked clavicle elevation
questions.x: Rockwood I = AC sprain, II = AC tear with CC sprain, III = both AC and CC ligaments torn (clavicle elevated, CC distance widened 25-100%); types IV-VI add posterior/superior/inferior displacement. Ultrasound measures the CC distance dynamically.

questions.q: The coracoclavicular ligament consists of the:
questions.x: The conoid (medial) and trapezoid (lateral) ligaments suspend the clavicle from the coracoid, providing vertical stability; their rupture (Rockwood III+) widens the coracoclavicular distance on imaging.

questions.q: The most common clavicle fracture location is the:
o: Lateral third at the AC joint
questions.x: About 80% of clavicle fractures involve the midshaft (middle third) from falls onto the shoulder; the sternocleidomastoid pulls the medial fragment up while the arm weight drops the lateral fragment.

questions.q: Quadrilateral (quadrangular) space syndrome causes pain and deltoid weakness through compression of the:
o: Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery by fibrous bands
questions.x: Fibrous bands or hypertrophy within the quadrilateral space compress the axillary nerve and PCHA, producing poorly localized posterior/lateral shoulder pain, paresthesia and teres minor/deltoid denervation in overhead athletes.

questions.q: Iliopectineal (iliopsoas) bursitis presents with pain:
o: In the anterior groin, communicating with the hip joint
questions.x: The iliopectineal bursa between the iliopsoas tendon and the anterior capsule is the largest hip bursa and often communicates with the joint; distension causes anterior groin pain and may compress the femoral nerve.

questions.q: Avulsion of the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) in adolescents involves the origin of the:
questions.x: Sudden sprinting or kicking avulses the ASIS apophysis at the sartorius origin (the TFL attaches just behind); ultrasound shows the displaced ossific fragment with hematoma in these adolescent apophyseal injuries.

questions.q: A Segond fracture is an avulsion of the lateral tibial rim that is strongly associated with:
questions.x: The Segond fracture - a small lateral capsular (anterolateral ligament) avulsion of the proximal lateral tibia - is nearly pathognomonic of ACL rupture, reflecting the internal rotation pivot mechanism.

questions.q: The 'reverse Segond' fracture, by contrast, is an avulsion of the medial tibial plateau associated with injury to the:
o: Posterior cruciate ligament and deep MCL
questions.x: Reverse Segond is a small medial tibial rim avulsion (deep MCL/medial capsular attachment) associated with PCL tears and medial meniscus injury - the medial counterpart of the Segond mechanism.

questions.q: An arcuate (fleck) fracture of the fibular styloid indicates injury to the:
questions.x: Avulsion of the fibular styloid tip by the arcuate ligament complex (popliteofibular, fabellofibular, arcuate ligaments) signals posterolateral corner injury - easily overlooked, it leads to chronic instability if untreated.

questions.q: On ultrasound of a suspected tibial plateau fracture, the key finding is:
o: Cortical step-off or depression with adjacent lipohemarthrosis
questions.x: Ultrasound shows the cortical break or depressed plateau segment, with lipohemarthrosis (fat-fluid level) indicating intra-articular fracture; CT then defines the split-depression for surgical planning.

questions.q: A patellar sleeve fracture in a child involves:
o: Avulsion of cartilage (sleeve) from the inferior patellar pole with a small bony flake
questions.x: In children the patella is largely cartilaginous; forceful quadriceps contraction avulses a cartilage sleeve from the inferior pole with a tiny visible bone flake - a serious injury easily underestimated on radiographs.

questions.q: A Maisonneuve fracture combines a proximal fibular fracture with:
o: A medial ankle injury (deltoid ligament or medial malleolus) and syndesmotic disruption
questions.x: External rotation forces spiral up the interosseous membrane from the medial ankle to exit as a proximal fibular fracture with syndesmosis disruption - always examine the whole fibula when the medial ankle is injured.

questions.q: A juvenile Tillaux fracture is a Salter-Harris injury of the distal tibia involving the:
o: Anterolateral tibial epiphysis (Salter-Harris III) in adolescents
questions.x: The Tillaux fracture is a Salter-Harris III avulsion of the anterolateral distal tibial epiphysis by the AITFL, occurring in adolescents whose medial physis has already closed; CT defines the intra-articular gap.

questions.q: A triplane fracture of the distal tibia in adolescents involves fracture lines in:
o: The sagittal, axial and coronal planes (epiphysis, physis and metaphysis)
questions.x: Triplane fractures combine a sagittal epiphyseal split, an axial physeal separation and a coronal metaphyseal fragment - Salter-Harris IV-type injuries of the closing physis requiring anatomic reduction.

questions.q: Navicular stress fractures in athletes characteristically cause pain:
o: In the poorly localized 'N spot' of the dorsal midfoot, and heal poorly due to watershed blood supply
questions.x: The navicular's central watershed zone makes its stress fractures insidious, vague dorsal midfoot pain ('N spot') with high nonunion risk; early immobilization in a non-weight-bearing cast is essential.

questions.q: Kohler disease is osteochondrosis of the:
questions.x: Kohler disease is self-limiting AVN of the navicular in children 4-7 years old, presenting with midfoot pain and a dense, flattened navicular on radiographs; it resolves with rest.

questions.q: Sever disease (calcaneal apophysitis) presents in active children as:
o: Heel pain with activity at the calcaneal apophysis
questions.x: Sever disease is traction overload of the calcaneal apophysis (growth plate) in active 8-12-year-olds; squeeze tenderness of the heel is typical, and it is self-limiting with load modification and heel raises.

questions.q: Iselin disease is traction apophysitis at the base of the fifth metatarsal, involving the tendon of the:
questions.x: Iselin disease affects the fifth metatarsal base apophysis where the peroneus brevis inserts, in adolescents - distinguished from a Jones or avulsion fracture by smooth, bilateral, growth-plate-parallel lucency.

questions.q: A calcaneal stress fracture on ultrasound and MRI is typically located:
o: In the posterior calcaneal body/trabecular bone, with heel squeeze pain
questions.x: Calcaneal stress fractures (military recruits, runners, osteoporosis) involve the posterior body trabeculae; the heel squeeze test is positive and MRI shows the fracture line with marrow edema before radiographs do.

questions.q: Tissue harmonic imaging improves the image by:
o: Transmitting at twice the receive frequency
Receiving echoes at twice the transmitted (fundamental) frequency, reducing near-field artifact
questions.x: Nonlinear propagation generates harmonic frequencies (chiefly 2x) within tissue; receiving only the harmonic band suppresses near-field clutter, side-lobe and reverberation artifact, sharpening borders at a small cost in penetration.

questions.q: Spatial compound imaging works by:
o: Steering the beam in multiple directions and averaging the frames, reducing speckle and angle-dependent artifact
questions.x: The beam is electronically steered into several angles and the acquired frames are averaged; speckle is decorrelated and smoothed while real specular reflectors persist, improving margin definition and needle visibility.

questions.q: Aliasing in pulsed-wave Doppler occurs when the:
o: Doppler frequency shift exceeds half the pulse repetition frequency (Nyquist limit)
questions.x: The maximum measurable shift is PRF/2; velocities beyond this wrap around and appear on the opposite side of the baseline. Fixes include lowering the baseline, increasing scale/PRF, or using a lower-frequency probe or continuous wave.

questions.q: The color Doppler 'twinkle' artifact is seen:
o: Behind small rough calcifications or stones, as a mosaic of color pixels
questions.x: A rapidly fluctuating mosaic of color behind a rough strongly reflecting surface (urinary stones, encrusted needles, calcifications) results from machine noise generated by phase jitter at the reflector; it helps localize small stones.

questions.q: Diagnostic ultrasound machines assume a soft-tissue sound speed of:
questions.x: All depth calculations assume 1540 m/s, the average speed in soft tissue. Tissues with markedly different speeds (fat ~1450, bone ~4080) produce speed-propagation artifact with structures mapped to the wrong depth.

questions.q: Speed propagation artifact occurs because:
o: Sound travels slower or faster than the assumed 1540 m/s through a tissue, displacing deeper structures on the display
questions.x: Through a fatty lesion (slower sound), returning echoes take longer and the machine plots the underlying interface too deep; through faster media, structures shift up. The interface appears bent or stepped.

questions.q: Refraction of the beam at the curved edge of a rounded structure causes:
o: Edge (refractive) shadowing and possible duplication of adjacent structures
questions.x: Beam bending at curved interfaces deflects the beam away, leaving a narrow anechoic edge shadow; refraction can also misplace or duplicate small reflectors (ghosting) beside the structure.

questions.q: The mechanical index (MI) on screen estimates the likelihood of:
questions.x: MI = peak rarefactional pressure / square root of frequency; it estimates nonthermal (cavitation) risk. Keep MI as low as practicable, particularly with contrast microbubbles or gas-containing tissue.

questions.q: For an intra-articular injection, probe-related sterility requires:
o: A sterile probe cover with sterile gel (or sterile glove) after skin antisepsis
questions.x: A sterile cover (or sterilized glove) plus sterile single-use gel maintains the sterile field; the uncovered probe is disinfected between patients per its classification, but joint injection demands a sterile field at the needle site.

questions.q: Write zoom (pre-processing zoom) differs from read zoom in that it:
o: Re-acquires the scan lines over the magnified region, genuinely increasing spatial resolution
questions.x: Write zoom resamples the region with new scan-line data, preserving/increasing resolution; read zoom simply enlarges stored pixels and does not add information. Use write zoom before measuring small structures.

questions.q: Lateral resolution is best:
o: In the near field regardless of focus
At the focal zone, where the beam is narrowest
questions.x: Lateral resolution equals beam width, which is minimal at the focus; electronic focusing should be placed at (or just below) the level of interest. Multiple focal zones narrow more of the beam but reduce frame rate.

questions.q: Compared with a low-frequency probe, a high-frequency linear probe provides:
o: Better axial resolution but less penetration
questions.x: Shorter wavelength improves axial resolution but higher frequency is attenuated faster, limiting depth - hence high-frequency probes for superficial nerves/joints and curvilinear low-frequency probes for deep structures.

questions.q: The duty factor of a pulsed ultrasound system is the:
o: Fraction of time the transducer is actually transmitting pulses
questions.x: Duty factor = pulse duration x PRF. Continuous wave has a duty factor of 1.0 (100%); pulsed imaging is typically <1%. Higher duty factor increases temporal-average intensity and heating potential.

questions.q: The 'bayonet artifact' describes the apparent:
o: Displacement or bend of a needle shaft where it crosses tissue layers of differing sound speed
questions.x: Where the beam crosses media with different propagation speeds, echoes from the deeper segment are mapped at a shifted position, so a straight needle can appear bent or offset at the interface - an artifact, not real bending.

questions.q: The FDA derated ISPTA (spatial-peak temporal-average intensity) upper limit for most diagnostic imaging is:
questions.x: Regulatory limits cap derated ISPTA at 720 mW/cm2 for most applications (lower for ophthalmic); displayed MI and TI let the operator track output relative to these limits in line with ALARA.

questions.q: Pregabalin is approved for neuropathic pain and fibromyalgia and acts by:
o: Binding the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing excitatory transmitter release
questions.x: Like gabapentin, pregabalin binds the alpha-2-delta subunit, decreasing calcium influx and release of glutamate, substance P and noradrenaline; unlike gabapentin it has linear pharmacokinetics and higher bioavailability.

questions.q: The maximum recommended daily dose of acetaminophen (paracetamol) in a healthy adult is:
o: 4 g (many experts advise no more than 3 g chronically)
questions.x: Hepatotoxicity from the NAPQI metabolite limits dosing to 4 g/day acutely; lower ceilings apply with liver disease, alcohol use or malnutrition. It is a common hidden ingredient in combination analgesics.

questions.q: NSAID-induced renal impairment results mainly from:
o: Prostaglandin inhibition causing afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction and reduced glomerular perfusion
questions.x: Renal prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2) dilate the afferent arteriole; COX inhibition removes this safeguard, reducing GFR - risk is highest with dehydration, heart failure, cirrhosis, CKD and concurrent ACE inhibitors/diuretics.

questions.q: Tramadol provides analgesia through:
o: Weak mu-opioid agonism plus serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibition
questions.x: Tramadol's dual action suits moderate pain but adds serotonergic and seizure risk - avoid with MAOIs, use cautiously with SSRIs (serotonin syndrome) and in epilepsy; it is a prodrug activated by CYP2D6.

questions.q: Buprenorphine differs from full mu agonists because it is a:
o: Partial mu agonist with a ceiling effect for respiratory depression
questions.x: High-affinity partial agonism gives analgesia with a ceiling for respiratory depression (though not for analgesia); its slow dissociation complicates reversal and it can precipitate withdrawal in patients dependent on full agonists.

questions.q: Methadone requires particular caution because of its:
o: Long, variable half-life, NMDA-antagonist activity and dose-related QT prolongation
questions.x: Methadone's half-life (up to 59+ hours) far exceeds its analgesic duration, risking accumulation and delayed respiratory depression; it blocks NMDA receptors (useful in neuropathic pain) and prolongs QT - check ECG at higher doses.

questions.q: Naloxone reverses opioid overdose by:
o: Competitively antagonizing opioid receptors, especially mu
questions.x: Naloxone is a short-acting competitive antagonist; it rapidly restores ventilation but may need repeating or infusion because its half-life is shorter than many opioids (methadone, modified-release preparations).

questions.q: Intrathecal ziconotide is reserved for severe chronic pain and acts by:
o: Blocking N-type voltage-gated calcium channels in the dorsal horn
questions.x: Ziconotide (from cone-snail conotoxin) selectively blocks N-type calcium channels, inhibiting transmitter release from primary afferents; it is non-opioid, causes no tolerance, but has a narrow window with neuropsychiatric side effects.

questions.q: Intrathecal baclofen is used for severe spasticity because it is a:
o: GABA-B receptor agonist acting at the spinal cord
questions.x: GABA-B agonism hyperpolarizes dorsal-horn neurons, reducing spasticity at microgram doses; abrupt interruption causes life-threatening withdrawal (hyperthermia, rigidity, seizures), so pump integrity is critical.

questions.q: Epidural clonidine added to a neuraxial regimen acts as an:
o: Alpha-2 adrenergic agonist in the dorsal horn, with hypotension and bradycardia as dose-limiting effects
questions.x: Alpha-2 agonism mimics descending noradrenergic inhibition at the dorsal horn, augmenting analgesia and sparing opioids; hypotension, bradycardia and sedation limit dosing, and abrupt cessation risks rebound hypertension.

questions.q: In local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST), symptoms typically appear first in the:
o: Central nervous system (perioral numbness, tinnitus, seizures), followed by cardiovascular collapse
