questions.x: CNS excitation (metallic taste, tinnitus, perioral numbness, seizures) precedes cardiovascular toxicity (arrhythmia, contractile failure); bupivacaine cardiotoxicity may present abruptly with collapse - treat with lipid emulsion.

questions.q: Opioid-induced hyperalgesia is characterized by:
o: Increasing pain sensitivity despite escalating opioid doses, often with allodynia and spreading distribution
questions.x: Chronic opioid exposure can paradoxically sensitize nociceptive pathways (NMDA-mediated central facilitation); pain worsens with dose escalation and improves with tapering or rotation - distinct from tolerance.

questions.q: Botulinum toxin type A relieves muscle-related pain by:
o: Blocking sodium channels in motor axons
Cleaving SNAP-25 (a SNARE protein), preventing acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction
questions.x: The light chain protease cleaves SNAP-25, blocking vesicle fusion and ACh release, causing chemodenervation that recovers over ~3 months as terminals sprout; it also reduces release of nociceptive peptides.

questions.q: Repeated epidural corticosteroid injections may cause:
o: Suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis for weeks after administration
questions.x: Exogenous glucocorticoids suppress CRH/ACTH, lowering endogenous cortisol for up to several weeks; cumulative dose limits, spacing of injections and caution before surgery or in diabetics follow from this.

questions.q: Before a neuraxial procedure in a patient on warfarin, the INR should generally be:
o: Normalized (roughly 1.4 or lower) after adequate drug withholding per ASRA guidance
questions.x: ASRA guidelines require warfarin to be stopped (typically 5 days) with INR normalized (about 1.4 or less) before neuraxial blockade to minimize epidural hematoma risk; similar drug-specific intervals apply to DOACs and antiplatelet agents.

questions.q: In most adults, the spinal cord (conus medullaris) terminates at the level of:
questions.x: The conus usually ends at the L1-L2 disc; the thecal sac with the cauda equina continues to about S2. This anatomy makes lumbar puncture and caudal access safe below L2 and defines levels at risk during procedures.

questions.q: The cervical facet (zygapophysial) joints are oriented approximately:
o: 45 degrees to the horizontal, like shingles of a roof
questions.x: The oblique ~45-degree orientation couples rotation with side-bending and permits the flexion-extension range of the neck; it also dictates probe and needle angulation for cervical medial branch blocks.

questions.q: About half of all cervical rotation occurs at the:
questions.x: The atlanto-axial complex, pivoting around the dens, contributes roughly 50% of cervical rotation; the atlanto-occipital joint instead contributes most flexion-extension (the 'yes' nod).

questions.q: Loss of the normal cervical lordosis on imaging most often reflects:
o: Muscle spasm or positioning and is a common nonspecific finding after whiplash
questions.x: Straightening or reversal of lordosis is usually due to spasm, pain or supine positioning rather than structural disease; it correlates poorly with symptoms and should not alone drive intervention.

questions.q: A C6-C7 disc herniation compressing the traversing root typically causes:
o: C7 radiculopathy with triceps weakness, wrist flexor/finger extensor involvement and reduced triceps reflex
questions.x: In the cervical spine the C6-C7 level affects the C7 root; middle-finger sensory change, triceps and wrist-flexor weakness and a diminished triceps reflex are classic. Cervical roots exit above their same-numbered vertebra.

questions.q: C5 radiculopathy classically presents with:
o: Weak shoulder abduction (deltoid) and elbow flexion, with sensory change over the lateral upper arm
questions.x: The C5 root supplies the deltoid and biceps; pain radiates from neck to the lateral arm, and the biceps reflex may be reduced. Pure C5 lesions spare the hand intrinsics and the triceps jerk.

questions.q: C8 radiculopathy (e.g., C7-T1 disc) typically weakens the:
o: Finger flexors and intrinsic hand muscles, with sensory loss in the ring/little fingers
questions.x: C8 innervates the long finger flexors and hand intrinsics; patients notice a weak grip and clumsiness, with numbness of the medial hand - it mimics ulnar neuropathy but also involves the medial forearm.

questions.q: L4 radiculopathy is best detected by:
o: Quadriceps weakness, reduced patellar reflex and sensory change over the medial leg
questions.x: L4 supplies the quadriceps (femoral nerve) and the medial leg via the saphenous nerve; hip flexion is relatively spared, helping separate L4 from L2-L3 lesions, and the patellar reflex may be depressed.

questions.q: L5 radiculopathy characteristically causes:
o: Weakness of great-toe extension (extensor hallucis longus) and foot dorsiflexion, with sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot
questions.x: EHL weakness is the signature of L5; severe lesions cause foot drop and a steppage gait. The ankle reflex is usually preserved because S1 mediates it - a key discriminator from S1 radiculopathy.

questions.q: S1 radiculopathy typically produces:
o: Weak plantarflexion, a diminished Achilles reflex and sensory loss over the lateral foot/sole
questions.x: S1 supplies the gastrocnemius-soleus and the lateral foot; patients cannot toe-walk normally and the ankle jerk is lost. The S1 root is compressed by the common L5-S1 posterolateral herniation.

questions.q: The femoral nerve stretch test (reverse straight-leg raise) tensions the:
o: Upper lumbar roots L2-L4 and femoral nerve
questions.x: With the patient prone, knee flexion and hip extension stretch the femoral nerve and L2- L4 roots; reproduction of anterior-thigh pain suggests a high lumbar radiculopathy rather than the common L5/S1 lesions.

questions.q: The slump test is used to assess:
o: Neural mechanosensitivity, sequencing trunk flexion, knee extension and ankle dorsiflexion to load the sciatic tract
questions.x: Progressive neural loading (slump, then neck flexion, knee extension, dorsiflexion) reproducing leg symptoms that ease with neck extension indicates adverse neural tension, complementing the straight-leg raise.

questions.q: Neurogenic (pseudoclaudication) leg pain from lumbar spinal stenosis is typically relieved by:
o: Sitting or lumbar flexion, which increases canal dimensions
questions.x: Flexion opens the canal and foramina, easing symptoms - patients walk bent forward or lean on a shopping trolley (the 'shopping cart sign'); extension and downhill walking worsen it, unlike vascular claudication.

questions.q: The Meyerding classification grades spondylolisthesis by the:
o: Percentage of vertebral body slip relative to the vertebra below (grades I-IV, in 25% steps)
questions.x: Grade I is 1-25% slip, II 26-50%, III 51-75% and IV 76-100%; complete displacement is spondyloptosis. Grading guides stability assessment, activity advice and surgical thresholds.

questions.q: Osteoid osteoma of the spine characteristically causes:
o: Night pain in a young patient, relieved dramatically by NSAIDs, usually in the posterior elements
questions.x: This benign osteoblastic tumor of adolescents/young adults involves the posterior elements (often lamina), produces prostaglandin-mediated night pain exquisitely responsive to NSAIDs, and may cause painful scoliosis.

questions.q: An aneurysmal bone cyst of the spine typically appears as an:
o: Expansile, multiloculated lesion of the posterior elements with fluid-fluid levels
questions.x: ABCs are benign but expansile blood-filled cavities of the posterior elements in young patients; MRI/CT shows lobulated expansion with fluid-fluid levels, and neural compression can occur.

questions.q: Multiple myeloma in the spine is suggested by:
o: Punched-out lytic lesions with vertebral collapse and preserved discs, plus Bence Jones proteinuria
questions.x: Marrow-replacing plasma-cell proliferation produces well-defined lytic ('punched-out') lesions, osteopenia and compression fractures; anemia, hypercalcemia, renal failure and Bence Jones protein support the diagnosis.

questions.q: Spinal metastases most characteristically destroy the:
o: Vertebral body and pedicles (the 'winking owl' sign), classically from breast, lung or prostate primaries
questions.x: Hematogenous metastases seed the posterior vertebral body and pedicles; pedicle destruction gives the absent/winking-owl pedicle on X-ray. Red flags include night pain, weight loss, age >50 and cancer history.

questions.q: A burst fracture differs from a simple compression fracture in that the:
o: Vertebral body fragments retropulse into the spinal canal, making it potentially unstable and neurologically dangerous
questions.x: Axial loading shatters the body through the middle column, driving fragments posteriorly toward the cord/conus; canal compromise on CT, >50% height loss or neurological deficit push toward surgical stabilization.

questions.q: Ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL) is important because it:
o: Narrowing the cervical canal, is a recognized cause of myelopathy, particularly in East Asian patients
questions.x: Ectopic ossification along the posterior vertebral bodies progressively stenoses the cervical canal; it may be asymptomatic or produce myelopathy and is a key consideration before cervical epidural or manipulation.

questions.q: The sural nerve is best described as a:
o: Sensory nerve formed by branches of the tibial and common peroneal nerves, supplying the posterolateral calf and lateral foot
questions.x: The medial sural cutaneous (tibial) and peroneal communicating branches unite in the posterior calf; the nerve runs with the small saphenous vein to the lateral foot - a common biopsy and block target.

questions.q: Meralgia paresthetica results from compression of the:
o: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve near the ASIS/inguinal ligament
questions.x: The purely sensory LFCN is compressed as it passes under or through the inguinal ligament medial to the ASIS, producing anterolateral thigh burning and numbness; tight belts, obesity and pregnancy predispose.

questions.q: The genitofemoral nerve, when injured (e.g., after hernia or pelvic surgery), causes pain in the:
o: Inguinal region, scrotum/labia and upper medial thigh
questions.x: Arising from L1-L2 and piercing the psoas, its genital and femoral branches supply the groin, cremaster, scrotal/labial skin and adjacent thigh; entrapment produces groin pain aggravated by hip extension.

questions.q: Post-herniorrhaphy chronic groin pain most commonly involves injury to the:
questions.x: Mesh, sutures or scar can entrap the anterior abdominal wall nerves running through the inguinal canal; diagnostic ultrasound-guided blocks both confirm the culprit and guide neurolysis or neurectomy.

questions.q: Pudendal neuralgia features perineal pain that is typically:
o: Worse with sitting and relieved on a toilet seat, suggesting entrapment in Alcock's canal or at the sacrospinous ligament
questions.x: Pudendal nerve entrapment (between sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments or in Alcock's canal) gives sitting-provoked perineal pain; relief on a toilet seat (ischial pressure offloaded) is a classic Nantes criterion.

questions.q: Superior cluneal nerve entrapment produces:
o: Low back/buttock pain over the iliac crest that may mimic sacroiliac or facet pain
questions.x: The superior cluneal nerves (from L1-L3 dorsal rami) cross the posterior iliac crest through an osteofibrous tunnel; entrapment causes iliac-crest buttock pain, sometimes radiating to the leg ('pseudo-sciatica').

questions.q: A 'Saturday night palsy' from compression of the radial nerve at the spiral groove causes:
o: Wrist and finger drop with preserved (or near-preserved) triceps strength and sensory loss over the dorsal first web space
questions.x: The triceps branches leave the nerve proximal to the spiral groove, so elbow extension is spared while wrist/finger extension fails; the superficial radial branch gives dorsal-web-space sensory loss.

questions.q: Radial tunnel syndrome differs from posterior interosseous nerve syndrome in that it:
o: Presents with lateral elbow/forearm pain without motor deficit, from PIN compression without demyelinating motor block
questions.x: Compression of the PIN within the radial tunnel can produce pure pain (radial tunnel syndrome) resembling resistant tennis elbow; frank extensor weakness of fingers/thumb with preserved wrist extension (radial deviation) defines PIN syndrome.

questions.q: Wartenberg syndrome (cheiralgia paresthetica) involves compression of the:
o: Superficial radial sensory nerve in the distal forearm
questions.x: The superficial radial nerve is compressed where it emerges between brachioradialis and ECRL tendons (tight watch straps, handcuffs); burning/numbness over the dorsoradial hand mimics de Quervain disease.

questions.q: Cubital tunnel syndrome is caused by ulnar nerve compression:
o: Behind the medial epicondyle (retrocondylar groove/arcade of Struthers), worsened by elbow flexion
questions.x: The ulnar nerve passes superficially behind the medial epicondyle; flexion narrows the tunnel and increases pressure. Symptoms: ring/little finger numbness, intrinsic wasting, positive Tinel and elbow-flexion tests.

questions.q: Pronator teres syndrome features median nerve compression at the forearm with:
o: Forearm pain and hand numbness that includes the palm (unlike carpal tunnel, the palmar cutaneous branch is also affected)
questions.x: Compression beneath the pronator produces volar forearm pain, weak flexors and numbness of the thenar palm as well as the digits, because the palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the carpal tunnel.

questions.q: Anterior interosseous nerve (Kiloh-Nevin) syndrome is notable because it:
o: Is purely motor - weak thumb IP and index DIP flexion (abnormal 'OK' sign) with no sensory deficit
questions.x: The AIN is a pure motor branch to FPL, index FDP and pronator quadratus; patients cannot pinch (flattened 'OK' sign). No cutaneous territory exists, so numbness points to a more proximal median lesion.

questions.q: Tarsal tunnel syndrome involves compression of the:
o: Tibial nerve (or its plantar branches) under the flexor retinaculum behind the medial malleolus
questions.x: The tibial nerve divides into medial/lateral plantar and calcaneal branches within the tarsal tunnel; compression (ganglion, tenosynovitis, varicosities, trauma) causes burning plantar foot pain and a positive Tinel.

questions.q: Morton neuroma is best characterized as:
o: A true tumor of the nerve
Perineural fibrosis of the interdigital nerve, most often in the third web space, with a positive Mulder click
questions.x: It is not a neoplasm but fibrotic thickening of the common plantar digital nerve at the metatarsal heads; forefoot burning relieved by shoe removal and a palpable click on web-space squeeze (Mulder) are typical.

questions.q: Common peroneal nerve compression at the fibular head causes:
o: Foot drop with weak dorsiflexion and eversion and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot
questions.x: The nerve wraps superficially around the fibular neck (leg crossing, casts, weight loss); deep peroneal involvement drops the foot while inversion and plantarflexion (tibial) are spared - distinguishing it from L5 radiculopathy.

questions.q: Neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome most often involves the:
o: Lower trunk (C8-T1), causing intrinsic hand wasting and medial forearm/hand sensory loss
questions.x: The lower trunk is stretched/compressed over a cervical rib or fibrous band; the Gilliatt- Sumner hand (thenar and intrinsic wasting), medial forearm numbness and provocation by elevated-arm maneuvers are classic.

questions.q: In the Seddon classification, neurapraxia refers to:
o: Axonal loss with preserved connective tissue
A focal conduction block (demyelination) with intact axons, recovering fully within weeks to months
questions.x: Neurapraxia = temporary myelin dysfunction without Wallerian degeneration; axonotmesis = axonal loss with preserved tubes (regeneration ~1 mm/day); neurotmesis = complete disruption requiring surgery.

questions.q: Wallerian degeneration after nerve injury occurs:
o: In the axon segment distal to the injury, with Schwann-cell tubes guiding regeneration
questions.x: The distal axon and myelin degenerate and are cleared by macrophages; Schwann cells form bands of Bungner that channel regenerating sprouts from the proximal stump at about 1 mm/day.

questions.q: On nerve conduction studies, demyelinating neuropathies typically show:
o: Marked conduction slowing, prolonged latencies and possible conduction block, with relatively preserved amplitudes
questions.x: Myelin loss slows saltatory conduction and can block impulses across the lesion; axonal neuropathies instead reduce CMAP/SNAP amplitudes with near-normal speeds - the fundamental electrodiagnostic distinction.

questions.q: The greater occipital nerve is the medial branch of the:
o: Dorsal ramus of C2 supplying the occipital scalp and implicated in occipital neuralgia and cervicogenic headache
questions.x: The GON pierces semispinalis and trapezius to supply the occiput up to the vertex; entrapment or sensitization produces lancinating occipital pain (occipital neuralgia), treated with ultrasound-guided GON block.

questions.q: The third occipital nerve (superficial medial branch of C3 dorsal ramus) is clinically important as the:
o: Sole innervation of the C2-C3 facet joint - a common source of cervicogenic headache after whiplash
questions.x: The TON crosses the C2-C3 joint and is its only innervation; C2-C3 facet-mediated pain is a leading cause of post-whiplash headache, diagnosed with comparative TON blocks and treated with radiofrequency.

questions.q: Frey syndrome (gustatory sweating) after parotid surgery is mediated by aberrant reinnervation involving the:
o: Auriculotemporal nerve - parasympathetic fibers regrowing into sweat glands of the preauricular skin
questions.x: Severed parasympathetic secretomotor fibers (formerly to the parotid) reinnervate skin sweat glands and vessels, causing flushing and sweating while eating over the auriculotemporal territory; botulinum injection is effective.

questions.q: The sphenopalatine (pterygopalatine) ganglion is a treatment target in:
o: Cluster headache and some trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias
questions.x: This parasympathetic ganglion behind the middle turbinate relays autonomic outflow to lacrimal/nasal glands; blocks (transnasal or infrazygomatic) can abort cluster attacks and are used in some facial pain syndromes.

questions.q: A medial winged scapula after neck or thoracic surgery or heavy load suggests injury to the:
o: Long thoracic nerve, denervating the serratus anterior
questions.x: The long thoracic nerve (C5-C7) runs superficially on the serratus anterior and is vulnerable to traction, surgery and neuralgic amyotrophy; its palsy gives medial winging on wall push (versus lateral winging from trapezius/spinal accessory palsy).

questions.q: In the femoral triangle, the femoral nerve is located:
o: Inside the femoral sheath with the artery
Lateral to the femoral artery, outside the femoral sheath, deep to the fascia iliaca
questions.x: Remember NAVY lateral-to-medial (Nerve, Artery, Vein, Y-fronts); the nerve lies outside the sheath beneath the fascia iliaca over the iliopsoas groove - the target for femoral and fascia iliaca blocks.

questions.q: Calcific tendinitis of the rotator cuff is most painful during the:
o: Resorptive phase, when the calcium deposit liquefies and incites intense inflammation
questions.x: In the resorptive phase macrophages infiltrate the chalky deposit, which swells and becomes exquisitely painful; ultrasound-guided barbotage (lavage/aspiration) is most effective in this phase, usually of the supraspinatus.

questions.q: Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) on ultrasound typically shows:
o: Thickening of the coracohumeral ligament and rotator interval with restricted external rotation
questions.x: Capsular fibrosis thickens the rotator interval and coracohumeral ligament and limits capsular distension on dynamic testing; clinical diagnosis rests on globally restricted passive range, especially external rotation.

questions.q: Long head of biceps tendinopathy is evaluated with the probe over the:
o: Bicipital (intertubercular) groove, assessing fluid, tendinosis, subluxation and the transverse humeral ligament
questions.x: The tendon is scanned in short and long axis within the groove; surrounding fluid (tenosynovitis), medial subluxation with subscapularis tearing, and the 'empty groove' of rupture are the key findings.

questions.q: A glenohumeral joint effusion is best detected on ultrasound over the:
o: Posterior recess with the arm externally rotated
questions.x: The posterior approach shows fluid lifting the infraspinatus off the posterior humeral head/labrum; it is the most sensitive site and the standard route for glenohumeral aspiration and injection.

questions.q: A SLAP tear (type II) involves the:
o: Superior labrum at the biceps anchor, detaching with the tendon
questions.x: Superior labrum anterior-to-posterior lesions peel the superior labrum and biceps anchor off the glenoid (overhead athletes, falls on outstretched arm); type II is the most common surgically treated pattern.

questions.q: Complete distal biceps rupture at the radial tuberosity presents with:
o: A 'reverse Popeye' deformity of the retracted muscle belly and weak supination/flexion
questions.x: The tendon avulses from the tuberosity (eccentric load in middle-aged men); the belly retracts proximally. Intact lacertus fibrosus may limit retraction; ultrasound shows the torn end and retraction distance for surgery.

questions.q: Triceps tendon rupture is recognized by:
o: A palpable gap near the olecranon, weak extension and an avulsed bony flake on ultrasound
questions.x: Rupture occurs at the olecranon insertion (fall, direct blow, or systemic risk - steroids, renal disease, anabolic use); ultrasound demonstrates the retracted tendon end and any avulsed olecranon fragment.

questions.q: Medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow) involves the:
o: Common flexor origin (pronator teres and flexor carpi radialis) at the medial epicondyle
questions.x: Overuse degeneration of the common flexor origin produces medial elbow pain on resisted wrist flexion/pronation - the mirror image of lateral epicondylitis; the adjacent ulnar nerve should also be assessed.

questions.q: Ulnar collateral ligament injury of the elbow (throwing athletes) is assessed at the:
o: Anterior bundle from medial epicondyle to the sublime tubercle, with valgus stress testing
questions.x: The anterior bundle resists valgus load; chronic overload in throwers causes attenuation/tears. Dynamic ultrasound with valgus stress shows joint-line gapping; severe tears may need reconstruction ('Tommy John').

questions.q: Olecranon bursitis most commonly results from:
o: Repetitive trauma/pressure ('student's elbow'), with gout and infection as key differentials
questions.x: The superficial bursa over the olecranon fills with fluid after friction or direct blow; ultrasound distinguishes simple fluid from solid thickening, and aspiration differentiates aseptic, gouty and septic bursitis.

questions.q: Intersection syndrome causes pain where the:
o: First dorsal compartment tendons (APL/EPB) cross over the second compartment (ECRL/ECRB) in the distal forearm
questions.x: Friction at the crossover ~4-6 cm proximal to Lister's tubercle produces pain, swelling and sometimes crepitus ('squeaker's wrist') in rowers and weightlifters; ultrasound shows peritendinous fluid at the crossing.

questions.q: Trigger finger (stenosing tenosynovitis) is caused by catching of the flexor tendon at the:
o: A1 pulley at the metacarpal head
questions.x: A thickened A1 pulley and flexor tendon nodule mismatch cause painful snapping/locking; ultrasound shows pulley thickening (>1 mm) and dynamic catching - treated by steroid injection or ultrasound-guided release.

questions.q: Dupuytren disease on ultrasound appears as:
o: Hypoechoic nodular thickening of the palmar fascia, usually affecting the ring and little fingers
questions.x: Fibroblastic cords in the palmar fascia (distal to the distal palmar crease) progressively flex the ring/little fingers; ultrasound maps nodules relative to the flexor tendons and neurovascular bundles before treatment.

questions.q: Triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) tears cause:
o: Ulnar-sided wrist pain, worse with ulnar deviation and rotation, near the distal radioulnar joint
questions.x: The TFCC stabilizes the DRUJ and cushions the ulnar carpus; traumatic (type 1) or degenerative (type 2) tears give ulnar pain with gripping/rotation, a positive ulnar fovea sign and possible DRUJ instability.

questions.q: Scapholunate dissociation is suggested by:
o: Widening of the scapholunate interval ('Terry Thomas sign') from SLIL rupture leading to rotary subluxation
questions.x: Scapholunate interosseous ligament failure separates the scaphoid and lunate (>3 mm gap) and allows scaphoid flexion/rotary instability; untreated it progresses to SLAC wrist arthritis. Dynamic ultrasound shows the gap widen with clenched fist.

questions.q: Thumb carpometacarpal (first CMC) osteoarthritis is confirmed clinically by the:
o: Grind test - axial load with rotation of the thumb metacarpal reproducing basal joint pain
questions.x: The saddle-shaped trapeziometacarpal joint degenerates with pinch/grip use; axial compression plus rotation (grind) reproduces pain and crepitus. Ultrasound-guided joint injection is a common intervention.

questions.q: Femoroacetabular impingement of the cam type involves:
o: An aspherical femoral head-neck junction (loss of offset) abutting the acetabular rim in flexion
questions.x: A bony bump at the anterolateral head-neck junction (cam) shears the acetabular cartilage during flexion/internal rotation; pincer impingement (overcoverage) often coexists, and both predispose to labral tears and early OA.

questions.q: Hip labral tears most commonly occur at the:
o: Anterosuperior labrum, presenting with groin pain and clicking
questions.x: The anterosuperior labrum bears the highest load (especially with FAI or dysplasia); patients report anterior groin pain, clicking/catching and positive FADIR/FABER tests. MR arthrography is the imaging reference.

questions.q: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome is now attributed mainly to:
o: Gluteus medius/minimus tendinopathy or tearing at the trochanteric facets, with or without bursitis
questions.x: Imaging shows that lateral hip pain usually reflects gluteal insertional tendinopathy (the 'rotator cuff of the hip') rather than isolated bursitis; ultrasound guides CSI or PRP to the tendon and peritrochanteric space.

questions.q: Proximal hamstring tendinopathy produces:
o: Deep buttock pain at the ischial tuberosity worse with sitting and hamstring loading
questions.x: The common hamstring origin on the ischial tuberosity degenerates with repetitive loading (distance runners); sit-provoked deep gluteal pain distinguishes it, and ultrasound shows hypoechoic thickening or partial tears.

questions.q: Quadriceps tendon rupture is suggested clinically by:
o: A palpable suprapatellar gap with inability to maintain extension (straight-leg raise) in an older patient
questions.x: Rupture above the patella (often degenerative, renal disease, steroids) leaves a suprapatellar defect and loss of active extension; ultrasound differentiates partial from complete tears and measures retraction.

questions.q: Patellar tendinopathy ('jumper's knee') affects the tendon:
o: Proximally at the inferior patellar pole, with deep infrapatellar pain on loading
questions.x: Repetitive jumping loads the proximal posterior fibers at the inferior pole; ultrasound shows focal hypoechoic thickening with neovascularity on Doppler - graded loading programs are first-line treatment.

questions.q: Osgood-Schlatter disease is traction apophysitis of the:
o: Tibial tuberosity at the patellar tendon insertion in adolescents
questions.x: Repetitive traction in growing athletes fragments the tibial tuberosity apophysis, causing a tender prominent bump aggravated by running/jumping/kneeling; ultrasound shows fragmentation and distal tendon thickening.

questions.q: Pes anserine bursitis/tendinopathy causes pain at the:
o: Medial proximal tibia at the conjoined insertion of sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus
questions.x: The pes anserinus inserts ~5 cm below the medial joint line; bursitis or insertional tendinopathy (common with knee OA, diabetes, obesity) causes medial knee pain that can mimic medial meniscal pathology.

questions.q: Midportion Achilles tendinopathy on ultrasound shows:
o: Fusiform hypoechoic thickening 2-6 cm above the calcaneal insertion often with neovascularity
questions.x: The relatively hypovascular midportion undergoes degenerative tendinosis with fusiform swelling; Doppler neovascularity accompanies pain. Insertional disease (with enthesophytes/retrocalcaneal bursitis) is managed differently, avoiding loaded dorsiflexion stretches.

questions.q: Increasing the transducer frequency from 5 MHz to 12 MHz will result in:
o: Deeper penetration and better axial resolution
Less penetration and better axial resolution
Deeper penetration and poorer axial resolution
No change in penetration or resolution
questions.x: Higher frequency improves axial resolution but attenuates faster, so penetration decreases. Choose the highest frequency that still reaches the target.

questions.q: The piezoelectric effect at the heart of an ultrasound transducer describes:
o: Conversion of sound energy into heat
Conversion of electrical energy to mechanical (sound) energy and back
Amplification of returning echoes by the receiver
Refraction of the beam at tissue interfaces
questions.x: Piezoelectric crystals deform under voltage (transmit) and generate voltage when deformed by returning echoes (receive).

questions.q: For an ultrasound-guided hip joint injection in an obese patient, the MOST appropriate transducer is:
questions.x: Deep targets need low frequency for penetration; the curvilinear footprint also gives a wider far field. Superficial targets use high-frequency linear probes.

questions.q: A tendon that appears falsely hypoechoic simply because the beam is not perpendicular to its fibers demonstrates:
questions.x: Anisotropy is the key MSK artifact: toggle or heel-toe the probe so the beam is perpendicular and the normal fibrillar echogenicity returns. Do not mistake it for tendinopathy.

questions.q: Posterior acoustic enhancement is typically observed DEEP to which of the following?
o: A fluid-filled cyst or joint effusion
questions.x: Fluid attenuates sound less than surrounding tissue, so the region behind it appears brighter. Bone, calcium and metal produce shadowing instead.

questions.q: Which maneuver is LEAST likely to improve needle visibility during an in-plane approach?
o: Advancing the needle steeply perpendicular to the transducer face
questions.x: Specular reflectors return echoes best near perpendicular incidence of the beam on the needle - a needle inserted steeply toward the probe (perpendicular to its face) reflects echoes away and disappears. Keep the needle as parallel to the probe face as anatomy allows.

questions.q: Compared with color Doppler, power Doppler:
o: Shows flow direction and is less sensitive
Is more sensitive to low-velocity flow but shows no direction
questions.x: Power Doppler integrates the amplitude of the Doppler signal, making it more sensitive for slow flow (hyperemia, small vessels) at the cost of directional information.

questions.q: When optimizing the image for an injection, the focal zone should be placed:
o: At or just below the level of the target
At the deepest part of the image
Anywhere - it has no effect on resolution
questions.x: Lateral resolution is best at the focal zone, where the beam is narrowest. Set depth so the target sits in the middle third of the screen.

questions.q: Before an ultrasound examination begins, AIUM/WAPMU documentation standards require that the recorded study include:
o: Patient and physician identification with machine settings and labeled images
A video recording of the entire session
questions.x: Documentation standards (scored in the CIPS oral exam): patient/physician identification, date, settings, labeled images of target and needle position, and a brief report with relevant measurements.

questions.q: Time-gain compensation (TGC) is used to:
o: Equalize brightness by selectively amplifying echoes from greater depths
questions.x: TGC compensates for attenuation by applying increasing gain to later (deeper) returning echoes, producing uniform brightness with depth.

questions.q: A 55-year-old with burning foot pain and allodynia after surgery is started on pharmacotherapy. Which agent is the MOST appropriate first-line adjuvant for neuropathic pain?
questions.x: Gabapentinoids, SNRIs and tricyclic antidepressants are first-line adjuvants for neuropathic pain; NSAIDs and steroids target nociceptive/inflammatory pain.

questions.q: Before proceeding to lumbar medial branch radiofrequency neurotomy, the accepted standard is to first obtain:
o: A positive MRI showing facet hypertrophy
A concordant response to controlled (comparative or placebo-controlled) diagnostic medial branch blocks
questions.x: Imaging cannot confirm the pain generator. Controlled diagnostic blocks are the gatekeeper before any neurodestructive procedure - a core principle of interventional pain algorithms.

questions.q: During pre-procedure assessment for an epidural steroid injection, which finding is a red flag requiring work-up rather than injection?
o: Progressive lower-limb motor weakness with urinary retention
questions.x: Progressive neurological deficit and sphincter dysfunction suggest cauda equina compression or other serious pathology - image and refer rather than inject.

questions.q: According to the doses quoted in the WIP examiner materials, a typical small-joint (e.g., acromioclavicular) steroid injection contains:
o: 20-40 mg triamcinolone or 3-6 mg betamethasone in lidocaine
questions.x: The examiner manual's model AC-joint answer uses 1-2 mL containing 20-40 mg triamcinolone or 3-6 mg betamethasone in lidocaine.

questions.q: A well-recognized systemic side effect that should be mentioned when consenting a diabetic patient for corticosteroid injection is:
questions.x: Steroid injections transiently raise blood glucose for days. Other quoted side effects: skin discoloration, fat atrophy, pain flare, and tendon weakening with intratendinous injection.

questions.q: In a coronal (transverse) ultrasound scan of the cervical spine, the target for a medial branch block lies:
o: At the peak of the articular pillar
At the waist (groove) of the articular pillar between two facet peaks
questions.x: The cervical medial branch curves around the waist of the articular pillar - the classic sawtooth scan. The bulletin sample answer confirms these dotted-circle structures are the cervical medial branch nerves.

questions.q: The third occipital nerve is blocked at which level?
questions.x: The superficial medial branch of C3 (third occipital nerve) crosses the C2-3 zygapophysial joint and is targeted for cervicogenic headache.

questions.q: On an axial oblique scan of the cervical intervertebral foramen, the two-humped camel sign represents:
o: The superior and inferior articular processes
The anterior and posterior tubercles of the transverse process with the exiting nerve root between them
The carotid artery and internal jugular vein
questions.x: The exiting cervical nerve root sits in the groove between the anterior and posterior tubercles - the landmark for selective nerve root block.

questions.q: During cervical sympathetic trunk block at the C7 level, particular caution is required because the vertebral artery:
o: Is always inside the transverse foramen at C7
Is unprotected (outside the foramen) and anterior at C7, typically entering the foramen at C6
Lies posterior to the longus colli
questions.x: At C7 the vertebral artery has usually not yet entered the foramen and runs anteriorly - always interrogate with Doppler before advancing the needle.

questions.q: Thoracic facet injections under ultrasound guidance have been described using:
o: Sagittal plane, caudal-to-cephalic needle approach, needle in-plane
questions.x: Per the bulletin sample question (Stulic et al., J Ultrasound Med 2011), ultrasound-guided thoracic facet injection has only been described in the sagittal plane with an in-plane caudal-to-cephalic approach.
questions.ref: Stulic et al., J Ultrasound Med 2011

questions.q: After the needle has been placed for a lumbar facet nerve block, the next step is:
o: Placement of the transducer into the long-axis view to localize the transverse process
Placement of the transducer into the long-axis view to localize the pedicle
Injection of saline to visualize spread
questions.x: From the bulletin sample question (Greher et al., Anesthesiology 2004): after needle placement, confirm in the longitudinal plane by localizing the transverse process.

questions.q: According to current literature, the technical success rate for ultrasound-guided lumbar facet joint injection is approximately:
questions.x: Gofeld et al. (Reg Anesth Pain Med 2012) reported 88-96% technical success with fluoroscopic validation - a bulletin sample question.

questions.q: Which statement about the ultrasound-guided lumbar selective nerve root block is TRUE?
o: An out-of-plane approach has never been described
A technical success rate of approximately 90% has been reported
Intravascular injection rates are clearly higher than with fluoroscopy
Nerve stimulation must routinely supplement ultrasound
questions.x: Kim et al. (Clin Orthop Surg 2013) and Gofeld et al. (Spine 2012) report ~90% technical success; published series do not show higher intravascular injection rates, and stimulation is not routine.

questions.q: The sonographic target for a lumbar medial branch block is:
o: The center of the spinous process
The groove at the junction of the transverse process and the superior articular process
questions.x: The medial branch crosses the base of the transverse process where it meets the superior articular process, under the mamillo-accessory ligament.

questions.q: The sacral hiatus, the entry point for caudal epidural injection, is bounded laterally by the:
o: Sacral cornua and covered by the sacrococcygeal ligament
questions.x: Transverse scan shows the two sacral cornua as hyperechoic mounds joined by the hyperechoic sacrococcygeal ligament; the hypoechoic gap beneath is the hiatus.

questions.q: In most adults, the dural sac ends at approximately the level of:
questions.x: The dural sac usually terminates at S2; during caudal epidural injection the needle is advanced only a short distance into the sacral canal to avoid dural puncture.

questions.q: When injecting the sacroiliac joint under ultrasound, the needle targets:
o: The inferior (lower) synovial portion, 1-2 cm above the caudal end of the joint cleft
questions.x: Only the lower third of the SI joint is synovial and accessible; the cleft between sacrum and ilium at the lower pole is the target.

questions.q: The artery of Adamkiewicz, relevant to lumbar selective nerve root block, is most often found:
o: On the left between T9 and L2
questions.x: The dominant radiculomedullary artery usually arises on the left from T9-L2; its injury can cause anterior spinal artery syndrome - use Doppler and keep the needle dorsal in the foramen.

questions.q: In a paramedian sagittal scan of the lumbar spine, the stacked transverse processes produce which characteristic pattern?
questions.x: The transverse processes cast three finger-like hyperechoic lines with shadowing (trident); the horse-head appearance belongs to the laminae at the interlaminar window.

questions.q: The MOST common complication of a thoracic paravertebral block is:
questions.x: Per the bulletin sample question (Naja et al., Anaesthesia 2001), inadvertent vascular puncture is the most common complication of paravertebral block; pneumothorax is the most feared.

questions.q: The stellate ganglion is located:
o: Cephalad to the subclavian artery at the first rib
Anterior to the transverse process of C7 and the neck of the first rib
Posterior to the carotid sheath at the longus capitis muscle
questions.x: Bulletin sample question (Hogan & Erickson, AJR 1992): the ganglion lies anterior to the C7 transverse process and the neck of the first rib; block is performed at C6 over the longus colli for safety.

questions.q: Chassaignac tubercle, the classic landmark for cervical sympathetic trunk block, is the anterior tubercle of:
questions.x: The C6 anterior (carotid) tubercle is palpable and sonographically identifiable; the injectate is placed on the longus colli under the prevertebral fascia at this level.

questions.q: A successful stellate ganglion block is confirmed clinically by:
o: Ipsilateral ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis (Horner syndrome) with hand warming
questions.x: Horner syndrome plus ipsilateral warming of the hand indicates sympathetic blockade; hoarseness signals recurrent laryngeal spread, not success.

questions.q: Which muscle is NOT innervated by the suprascapular nerve?
questions.x: The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus only (bulletin sample question). Subscapularis is supplied by the upper and lower subscapular nerves.

questions.q: At the suprascapular notch, the suprascapular artery usually passes:
o: Below the superior transverse scapular ligament with the nerve
Above (superficial to) the superior transverse scapular ligament while the nerve passes below it
questions.x: Mnemonic: army (artery) goes over the bridge, navy (nerve) goes under. Identify the artery with Doppler before injecting at the notch.

questions.q: On ultrasound near the ASIS, the ilioinguinal and iliohypogastric nerves are found in the fascial plane between the:
questions.x: Scan a few centimeters medial/cranial to the ASIS: three muscle layers are seen and the nerves sit between internal oblique and transversus abdominis.

questions.q: Which artery lies close to the ilioinguinal nerve and should be excluded with Doppler before injection?
o: Branch of the superior epigastric artery
Branch of the deep circumflex iliac artery
questions.x: Bulletin sample question: a branch of the deep circumflex iliac artery accompanies the nerve in the plane between internal oblique and transversus abdominis.

questions.q: Which BEST describes the classic appearance and location where the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is most easily found?
o: Hyperechoic dot over the sartorius under the fascia lata
A cat-eye structure with hyperechoic center and hypoechoic rim over the sartorius muscle
Honeycombed structure medial to the ASIS within the inguinal ligament
Hyperechoic mass over the tensor fascia lata
questions.x: Bulletin sample question: the LFCN classically shows a cat-eye appearance over the sartorius beneath the fascia lata, medial and caudal to the ASIS; anatomy is variable, so compare sides.

questions.q: The median nerve provides motor innervation to all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.x: Bulletin sample question: abductor pollicis longus is supplied by the radial nerve (posterior interosseous branch); the thenar LOAF muscles (lumbricals 1-2, opponens, abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis) are median.

questions.q: The most widely used sonographic cut-off supporting a diagnosis of carpal tunnel syndrome is a median nerve cross-sectional area at the tunnel inlet of:
o: Greater than or equal to 4 mm2
Greater than or equal to 10 mm2
Greater than or equal to 20 mm2
Greater than or equal to 30 mm2
questions.x: A CSA of 10 mm2 or more at the inlet is the common diagnostic threshold; supportive signs include retinacular bowing, flattening ratio, loss of fascicular pattern and hyperemia - compare with the other side.

questions.q: The ulnar nerve can be visualized at all of the following locations EXCEPT:
o: The lateral epicondyle of the elbow
Between the axillary artery and vein in most cases
Along the anterior surface of the medial head of the triceps
questions.x: Bulletin sample question: at the elbow the ulnar nerve lies behind the MEDIAL epicondyle in the cubital canal - there is no ulnar nerve at the lateral epicondyle.

questions.q: Which accessory muscle, when present in the cubital tunnel, can compress the ulnar nerve?
questions.x: Bulletin sample question: the anconeus epitrochlearis overlies the cubital tunnel and is a recognized cause of ulnar compression; look for it during dynamic scanning.

questions.q: In the intercostal space, the neurovascular structures from the superior border of the rib downward are arranged:
questions.x: VAN from above: vein, artery, nerve - the nerve is the lowest, tucked under the inferior rib border between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles.

questions.q: Electrical stimulation of the pudendal nerve will activate which of the following muscles?
questions.x: Bulletin sample question: pudendal stimulation recruits the levator ani and coccygeus; the nerve is found medial to the ischial spine between the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments, beside the internal pudendal artery.

questions.q: When blocking the greater occipital nerve at the superior nuchal line, the safest landmark strategy is to inject:
o: Medial to the occipital artery after localizing it with Doppler
questions.x: The nerve runs medial to the occipital artery at the nuchal ridge; finding the artery with Doppler and injecting medial to it minimizes intravascular injection.

questions.q: The long head of the biceps tendon is found on ultrasound:
o: In the bicipital groove between the greater and lesser tuberosities, under the transverse humeral ligament
questions.x: Transverse anterior scan: the groove lies between the greater tuberosity (lateral) and lesser tuberosity (medial); the subscapularis inserts on the lesser tuberosity and roofs the groove medially.

questions.q: Which vessel, found within or near the bicipital groove, should be identified with Doppler before a biceps sheath injection?
o: Branch of the anterior circumflex humeral artery
questions.x: An ascending branch of the anterior circumflex humeral artery runs in the groove beside the tendon; avoid intravascular injection.

questions.q: The subacromial-subdeltoid bursa is located between the:
o: Deltoid muscle and the supraspinatus tendon
Biceps tendon and the rotator interval
questions.x: In the supraspinatus long-axis view the bursa is the thin hypoechoic interface between deltoid above and supraspinatus below, extending beneath the acromion; inject into it, not into the tendon.

questions.q: The standard ultrasound-guided glenohumeral joint injection uses which approach?
o: Posterior, in-plane from lateral to medial into the recess beside the posterior labrum
questions.x: The posterior approach with the arm across the chest opens the posterior recess; the needle passes through infraspinatus into the joint between humeral head and glenoid.

questions.q: For an anterior ultrasound-guided hip injection, the needle target is the:
o: Anterior synovial recess over the femoral head-neck junction
Joint space at the acetabular rim cartilage
questions.x: Along the femoral neck long axis, the anterior recess drapes the head-neck junction under the iliofemoral ligament; capsular distension confirms intra-articular flow.

questions.q: During the anterior approach to the hip, the structure that must be avoided medially is the:
questions.x: The femoral artery, vein and nerve lie medial to the psoas tendon; map them with Doppler and keep the approach lateral. The LFCN crosses superficially and is also at risk.

questions.q: The subgluteus maximus (trochanteric) bursa is found between the:
o: Iliotibial band/gluteus maximus and the gluteus medius tendon at the lateral facet of the greater trochanter
Greater trochanter and the femoral shaft
questions.x: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome is often gluteus medius/minimus tendinopathy with bursal involvement; the injection plane is between the ITB and the gluteus medius tendon.

questions.q: Before injecting the piriformis muscle, the structure that must positively be identified is the:
o: Sciatic nerve at the infrapiriform fossa
questions.x: The sciatic nerve usually exits the pelvis below the piriformis; confirm its position (typically lateral/deep to the muscle) before advancing the needle into the muscle belly.

questions.q: On a longitudinal suprapatellar scan of the knee, the suprapatellar pouch is seen between the:
o: Prefemoral and suprapatellar fat pads, deep to the quadriceps tendon
Medial meniscus and medial collateral ligament
questions.x: Effusion collects first in the suprapatellar pouch between the two fat pads; this is the preferred (most accurate) in-plane injection route.

questions.q: During an anterior tibiotalar (ankle) injection, the vessel to identify and avoid is the:
o: Dorsalis pedis artery, lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon
questions.x: The dorsalis pedis artery crosses the anterior recess lateral to the EHL tendon; map it with Doppler and enter medial or lateral to it.

questions.q: In the tarsal tunnel behind the medial malleolus, the tibial nerve is found:
o: Anterior to the tibialis posterior tendon
Between the posterior tibial artery/veins and the flexor hallucis longus tendon
questions.x: Tom, Dick ANd Harry: tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, artery/nerve, flexor hallucis longus - the nerve sits with the posterior tibial vessels under the flexor retinaculum.

questions.q: Which dynamic sonographic maneuver is used to assess the acromioclavicular joint during the examination?
o: Cross-body adduction while measuring the acromion-clavicle distance
questions.x: Dynamic cross-body adduction stresses the AC joint, reproduces pain and changes the joint gap; distance is measured against the contralateral side (examiner manual checklist).

questions.q: The sonographic double-contour sign over the cartilage of the first metatarsophalangeal joint suggests:
o: Gout (monosodium urate deposition on the cartilage surface)
questions.x: Urate crystals coating the hyaline cartilage create a hyperechoic line parallel to the bone cortex - the double-contour sign, a classic gout finding.

questions.q: The purpose of dry-needle fenestration (peppering) of a tendinopathic common extensor origin is to:
o: Induce controlled bleeding and a healing response within the diseased tendon
questions.x: Multiple needle passes create microbleeding that stimulates repair; repeated intratendinous corticosteroid is avoided because it weakens collagen and risks rupture.

questions.q: For distal iliotibial band syndrome, the injectate is placed:
o: In the plane between the iliotibial band and the lateral femoral epicondyle
questions.x: The pathology is peritendinous - fluid and thickening between the band and the epicondyle; inject the interface, not the band, and confirm with a test injection.

questions.q: Beam steering on a modern ultrasound machine is used mainly to:
o: Angle the scan lines so the beam meets the needle or tendon more perpendicularly
questions.x: Steering the beam improves specular reflection from needles and reduces anisotropy in tendons and nerves without moving the probe (Bigeleisen ch. 5-6).

questions.q: The mirror-image artifact is most characteristically produced at the:
questions.x: Strong reflectors such as the pleura/diaphragm act like a mirror, duplicating structures on the far side - relevant when scanning intercostal spaces (Bigeleisen ch. 6).

questions.q: Human data on accidental intraneural injection during ultrasound-guided blocks show that:
o: It always produces permanent nerve damage
It can occur without paresthesia or motor response and often without clinical sequelae, but high injection pressure warns of intrafascicular placement
It is impossible with ultrasound guidance
It only occurs at the sciatic nerve
questions.x: Bigeleisen ch. 13 reviews the human data: intraneural injection may be silent and frequently benign, yet it must be avoided - resistance/high pressure and fascicular swelling are warning signs.

questions.q: The EARLIEST clinical features of local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) are usually:
o: Perioral numbness, metallic taste and tinnitus
questions.x: CNS excitation precedes cardiovascular collapse in the classic biphasic presentation (Jankovic ch. 5); lipid 20% emulsion is the specific antidote.

questions.q: The specific antidote and first-line treatment for severe LAST is:
o: 20% lipid emulsion bolus followed by infusion
questions.x: Lipid rescue: 20% lipid emulsion bolus (~1.5 mL/kg) then infusion, with standard resuscitation and avoidance of vasopressin (Jankovic ch. 5).

questions.q: Echogenic needles improve ultrasound visibility primarily because they:
o: Have corner-cube (dimpled) reflectors near the tip that return echoes at steep angles
Are coated with a hydrophilic layer
questions.x: Textured reflectors scatter sound back to the transducer even when the needle is not parallel to the probe face (Bigeleisen ch. 10).

questions.q: Spatial compound imaging improves the image by:
o: Averaging frames acquired at several steering angles, reducing speckle and sharpening tissue planes
questions.x: Compounding merges differently angled frames, smoothing speckle and clarifying boundaries; note it can reduce the contrast of needle echoes (Bigeleisen ch. 5-6).

questions.q: Color Doppler aliasing (color wrap-around) in a small artery is best corrected by:
questions.x: Aliasing occurs when flow velocity exceeds the Nyquist limit (half the PRF); raising the PRF/scale restores accurate display (Bigeleisen ch. 6).

questions.q: Axial (depth) resolution of an ultrasound system is determined mainly by:
o: The length of the scan line
The spatial pulse length - shorter pulses (higher frequency, fewer cycles) resolve better along the beam
questions.x: Axial resolution equals roughly half the spatial pulse length, which is why high-frequency probes resolve superficial structures so well (Peng ch. 1).

questions.q: For a nerve target lying 8 cm deep in the buttock of an obese patient, the most appropriate choice is:
questions.x: Only a low-frequency curvilinear probe provides the penetration for deep targets such as the piriformis region; high-frequency probes are reserved for superficial work (Peng ch. 1).

questions.q: Which practice is REQUIRED for an aseptic ultrasound-guided joint injection?
o: Surgical gown and full draping for every case
Skin antisepsis, sterile gel, gloves and a probe cover or disinfected probe
questions.x: Standard asepsis for percutaneous US-guided injections: antiseptic skin prep, sterile coupling gel, gloves, and a covered or high-level disinfected transducer (Peng ch. 1; Waldman technique templates).

questions.q: Temporal resolution (frame rate) DECREASES when the operator:
o: Increases imaging depth and adds multiple focal zones
questions.x: Each frame needs more scan lines and longer round trips with greater depth, wider sector and extra focal zones - frame rate falls (Peng ch. 1).

questions.q: Platelet-rich plasma used for tendon injection is produced by:
o: Centrifuging autologous whole blood to concentrate platelets above baseline
questions.x: PRP is autologous blood centrifuged to raise platelet (and growth factor) concentration; patients are typically advised to pause NSAIDs around the procedure (Peng ch. 25).

questions.q: Ultrasound-guided barbotage for calcific tendinitis of the shoulder involves:
o: Needle lavage and aspiration of the calcium deposit, usually followed by subdeltoid bursa corticosteroid injection
questions.x: Barbotage breaks up and aspirates the calcific focus under direct vision; the bursa is then treated to limit post-procedure bursitis (Peng ch. 26).

questions.q: Ultrasound-guided hip joint denervation targets the articular branches of the:
questions.x: The hip capsule receives its sensory supply mainly from the obturator (anteromedial) and femoral (anterolateral) articular branches - the radiofrequency targets (Peng ch. 27).

questions.q: For genicular (knee) denervation, the classic three targets are the:
o: Superolateral, superomedial and inferomedial genicular nerves
Medial and lateral patellar retinacular nerves
questions.x: Genicular radiofrequency targets the superolateral, superomedial and inferomedial genicular nerves at the periosteal junctions of femur and tibia (Peng ch. 27).

questions.q: The L5 dorsal ramus, the L5 medial branch equivalent targeted in L5-S1 facet blocks, is found:
o: At the junction of the L5 transverse process and superior articular process
In the groove between the sacral ala and the S1 superior articular process
questions.x: Unlike L1-L4 medial branches, the L5 dorsal ramus crosses the sacral ala beside the S1 superior articular process - the sonographic target (Peng ch. 14).

questions.q: Blocks of the sacral lateral branches (S1-S3) are performed primarily as:
o: A prognostic/diagnostic step before sacroiliac joint radiofrequency denervation
questions.x: The posterior SI joint is innervated by the sacral lateral branches; their block at the posterior foramina predicts response to lateral-branch radiofrequency (Peng ch. 15-16).

questions.q: During an erector spinae plane (ESP) block, the injectate is deposited:
o: Inside the erector spinae muscle belly
In the fascial plane between the erector spinae muscle and the transverse process
Into the thoracic paravertebral space directly
questions.x: ESP targets the interfascial plane deep to erector spinae over the transverse process tips, with cranio-caudal spread to several dorsal rami (Peng ch. 11).

questions.q: The ganglion impar (ganglion of Walther), blocked for sympathetically mediated perineal pain, lies:
o: Anterior to the L5 vertebral body
In the midline anterior to the sacrococcygeal junction
questions.x: The ganglion impar is the solitary midline termination of the sympathetic chains at the sacrococcygeal level (Narouze ch. 18).

questions.q: A diagnostic medial branch block is generally considered POSITIVE when the patient reports:
o: Any pain reduction the same day
Concordant relief (commonly 80% or more) for the expected duration of the local anesthetic
Relief lasting more than one month
questions.x: Controlled blocks are judged by concordant, duration-appropriate relief; a second comparative block raises specificity before radiofrequency (FIPP guide; RAPM Part II).

questions.q: Which interventional procedure carries the HIGHEST bleeding risk category, requiring the strictest anticoagulation management?
questions.x: Neuraxial injections are high-risk procedures in interventional pain anticoagulation guidelines; most peripheral joint and soft-tissue injections are lower risk (FIPP guide).

questions.q: Celiac plexus neurolysis is most commonly indicated for:
o: Chronic pancreatitis and upper abdominal malignancy pain, especially pancreatic cancer
questions.x: The celiac plexus relays upper abdominal visceral pain; neurolysis is standard for pancreatic cancer pain (Narouze ch. 16; Jankovic abdominal blocks).

questions.q: The principal advantage of PULSED radiofrequency over conventional thermal radiofrequency is:
o: Neuromodulation without significant thermal tissue destruction, suitable for dorsal root ganglia and peripheral nerves
questions.x: Pulsed RF delivers brief high-voltage bursts with pauses, keeping tissue temperature sub-destructive while modulating pain transmission (FIPP guide).

questions.q: The third occipital nerve block anesthetizes which facet joint?
questions.x: The third occipital nerve (superficial medial branch of C3) crosses and supplies the C2-3 zygapophysial joint (Narouze ch. 6; Peng ch. 13).

questions.q: To block the C5-6 facet joint with medial branch blocks, the target levels are:
o: C5 and C6 articular pillar waists
questions.x: Each cervical facet joint receives dual innervation from the medial branches above and below; C5-6 needs C5 and C6 blocks (Peng ch. 13).

questions.q: For cervical transforaminal (selective nerve root) steroid injection, the preferred steroid is:
questions.x: Particulate steroids can embolize radicular/vertebral vessels with catastrophic cord or brain infarction; non-particulate dexamethasone is the safety standard (Narouze ch. 8).

questions.q: On a transverse lumbar scan for medial branch block, the L4 medial branch is blocked over which bony junction?
o: L5 transverse process and superior articular process
questions.x: A medial branch is named for its own segment but crosses the NEXT transverse process: the L4 medial branch runs across the base of the L5 transverse process (Peng ch. 14).

questions.q: The sacral hiatus exists because of failure of laminar fusion at:
questions.x: The hiatus is the normal inferior opening of the sacral canal where the S5 (and variably S4) laminae fail to fuse, roofed only by the sacrococcygeal ligament (Narouze ch. 13).

questions.q: The best acoustic window for viewing the lumbar thecal sac and ligamentum flavum-dura complex is the:
o: Midline transverse view over the spinous process
Paramedian sagittal oblique view through the interlaminar space
Transverse view over the transverse processes
Coronal view over the iliac crest
questions.x: The paramedian sagittal oblique (interlaminar) window bypasses the spinous processes and displays the posterior dura, CSF and anterior complex (Narouze ch. 12; Karmakar ch. 8).

questions.q: On the paramedian sagittal oblique lumbar view, the hyperechoic line forming the POSTERIOR boundary of the thecal sac is the:
questions.x: The flavum-dura unit reflects as one hyperechoic line; the anterior dura/posterior longitudinal ligament forms the deep boundary across the anechoic CSF (Narouze ch. 12).

questions.q: Pain referred from the sacroiliac joint most characteristically radiates to the:
o: Buttock, posterior thigh and sometimes groin - below L5
questions.x: SI joint pain maps to the buttock and posterior thigh, occasionally the groin or lower leg; its referral below L5 helps separate it from facet pain (Narouze ch. 14).

questions.q: According to the commonly applied rule, sacroiliac joint pain is supported clinically when at least:
o: One of five provocative tests is positive
Three of five provocative tests (distraction, compression, thigh thrust, Gaenslen, FABER) are positive
questions.x: A cluster of 3 or more positive SIJ provocation maneuvers has diagnostic utility and strengthens the case before a diagnostic block (Narouze ch. 14).

questions.q: The thoracic paravertebral space contains all of the following EXCEPT:
o: The sympathetic chain and rami communicantes
questions.x: The wedge-shaped paravertebral space holds the spinal nerve, rami, sympathetic chain and vessels; the phrenic nerve runs in the anterior mediastinum (Karmakar ch. 11; Bigeleisen ch. 36).

questions.q: The first bifid spinous process palpated/sonographically identified at the upper cervical midline belongs to:
questions.x: C1 has no spinous process; the bifid C2 spinous process is the first midline landmark and the standard starting point for counting cervical levels (Peng ch. 2; Narouze ch. 5).

questions.q: Before performing cervical medial branch blocks, the vessel that must be interrogated with Doppler along the articular pillars is the:
o: Vertebral artery, which courses anterior to the articular pillars within the transverse foramina
questions.x: The vertebral artery lies anterolateral to the pillar waists; confirming its position on Doppler at each level prevents arterial injury or intra-arterial injection (Peng ch. 13; Narouze ch. 7).

questions.q: For an ultrasound-guided genitofemoral nerve block, the nerve is sought:
o: On the anterior surface of the psoas muscle at the L3-L4 level
questions.x: The genitofemoral nerve emerges on the anterior psoas surface in the retroperitoneum; it is scanned there before descending toward the inguinal region (Peng ch. 7).

questions.q: After crossing the ischial spine region, the pudendal nerve enters the perineum through the:
o: Lesser sciatic foramen into the pudendal (Alcock) canal
questions.x: The nerve hooks around the sacrospinous ligament, passes through the lesser sciatic foramen and travels in Alcock canal in the obturator internus fascia (Peng ch. 9; RAPM Part I).

questions.q: A diagnostic block of the inferior cluneal nerve is considered together with the pudendal nerve in the assessment of:
questions.x: The inferior cluneal nerves supply the lower buttock and are blocked in the same interligamentous region for buttock pain syndromes (Peng ch. 9).

questions.q: Entrapment of the suprascapular nerve at the SPINOGLENOID notch produces:
o: Weakness of both supraspinatus and infraspinatus
Isolated infraspinatus weakness with preserved supraspinatus function
Sensory loss over the lateral shoulder
questions.x: Distal to the supraspinatus branch, spinoglenoid entrapment denervates only the infraspinatus; the nerve carries no cutaneous sensation (Peng ch. 4).

questions.q: The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve reaches the thigh by passing:
o: Under the inguinal ligament near the ASIS, over the sartorius origin
questions.x: From the lateral psoas border it crosses the iliacus and exits under the inguinal ligament close to the ASIS - the entrapment point in meralgia paresthetica (Peng ch. 10; RAPM Part I).

questions.q: For complete intercostal analgesia, the block must be placed:
o: Proximal to the origin of the lateral cutaneous branch (near the angle of the rib / posterior axillary region)
questions.x: The lateral cutaneous branch leaves the intercostal nerve near the midaxillary line; blocks distal to it miss the lateral chest wall territory (Peng ch. 5; RAPM Part I).

questions.q: The saphenous nerve becomes subcutaneous at the knee by emerging between the tendons of the:
questions.x: The terminal sensory branch of the femoral nerve pierces the fascia between sartorius and gracilis before descending with the great saphenous vein (Bigeleisen ch. 25).

questions.q: Within Guyon canal at the wrist, the ulnar nerve is accompanied and best localized by the:
o: Ulnar artery, with the pisiform as the ulnar-side landmark
questions.x: The canal is bounded by the pisiform (ulnar) and hook of hamate (radial); the nerve sits beside the pulsatile ulnar artery - map with Doppler (Waldman ch. 68; Jacobson ch. 5).

questions.q: The recurrent thenar motor branch of the median nerve is at risk during carpal tunnel injection because it:
o: Arises on the radial side of the nerve near the distal retinaculum
questions.x: A radial-side approach can spear the thenar motor branch; the ulnar in-plane approach keeps the needle clear (Waldman ch. 68; Peng ch. 21).

questions.q: The stellate ganglion represents the fusion of the:
o: Inferior cervical ganglion and the first thoracic ganglion
C2 and C3 dorsal root ganglia
Middle cervical and vertebral ganglia only
questions.x: Inferior cervical + T1 ganglion = stellate (cervicothoracic) ganglion, which is why it sits at the C7/first rib level (Narouze ch. 24; RAPM Part I).

questions.q: Which is one of the Nantes diagnostic criteria for pudendal neuralgia?
o: Pain that wakes the patient at night
Pain in the territory of the pudendal nerve that is worse with sitting
Objective sensory loss over the perineum
Relief by sitting on a hard surface
questions.x: Nantes criteria include pudendal-territory pain, worse sitting, NOT waking the patient at night, no objective sensory loss, and relief by diagnostic block (Peng ch. 9).

questions.q: In the popliteal fossa, the sciatic nerve components are typically seen on ultrasound as:
o: A single fused trunk in all individuals
Tibial and common peroneal (fibular) divisions sharing a common paraneural sheath, separating at a variable level
Two nerves on opposite sides of the popliteal artery
questions.x: The divisions travel together within a common sheath and split at variable heights; the tibial component continues down the midline while the common peroneal tracks along biceps femoris toward the fibular head (Bigeleisen ch. 26; Jacobson ch. 5).

questions.q: To best expose the supraspinatus tendon footprint on ultrasound, the shoulder is placed in the:
o: Crass or modified Crass position - extension and internal rotation
questions.x: Extension/internal rotation (Crass, or hand-on-buttock modified Crass) rotates the supraspinatus from under the acromion into view (Jacobson ch. 3).

questions.q: Medial subluxation of the long head of biceps out of the bicipital groove most strongly suggests a tear of the:
questions.x: The subscapularis insertion and pulley sling stabilize the groove; their failure lets the tendon displace medially (Jacobson ch. 3).

questions.q: Elevation of the posterior fat pad on an elbow ultrasound or radiograph indicates:
o: Joint effusion - in trauma, an occult fracture
questions.x: Fluid in the olecranon fossa lifts the posterior fat pad; after trauma this is a sensitive indirect sign of fracture (Jacobson ch. 4).

questions.q: The cartilage interface sign on shoulder ultrasound supports:
o: Full-thickness rotator cuff tear - fluid over the exposed humeral head cartilage
questions.x: In full-thickness tears, anechoic fluid outlines the hypoechoic cartilage of the humeral head, sharpening its margin (Jacobson ch. 3).

questions.q: When assessing a suspected hip joint effusion with ultrasound, the measurement is taken at the:
o: Anterior synovial recess along the femoral neck, compared with the other side
questions.x: The anterior capsule-bone distance over the femoral neck is measured bilaterally; capsular convexity and side difference indicate effusion (Jacobson ch. 6).

questions.q: Medial meniscus extrusion beyond the tibial margin greater than approximately how many millimeters is considered abnormal?
questions.x: Extrusion beyond about 3 mm correlates with meniscal degeneration, tears and osteoarthritis progression (Jacobson ch. 7).

questions.q: A popliteal (Baker) cyst on ultrasound characteristically appears between the:
o: Semimembranosus tendon and the medial head of gastrocnemius
questions.x: The fluid neck in the semimembranosus-gastrocnemius recess identifies the Baker cyst and distinguishes it from mimics (Jacobson ch. 7).

questions.q: Plantar fascia thickness above approximately which value supports plantar fasciosis?
questions.x: The normal plantar fascia measures up to about 4 mm; thickening with hypoechogenicity near the calcaneal origin is diagnostic (Jacobson ch. 8).

questions.q: The most frequently injured ligament of the lateral ankle, readily assessed with ultrasound, is the:
questions.x: The ATFL is the first ligament torn in inversion injuries; scan from the fibular tip toward the talus (Jacobson ch. 8).

questions.q: During dynamic ultrasound assessment of subacromial impingement, abduction of the arm is observed for:
o: Pooling of subdeltoid bursal fluid as the supraspinatus passes under the acromion
questions.x: Fluid or bursal thickening bunching at the acromial edge during abduction is a dynamic sign of impingement (Jacobson ch. 3).

questions.q: Which statement about the Achilles tendon is TRUE?
o: It has a true synovial sheath
It is enveloped by a paratenon rather than a sheath, and the retrocalcaneal bursa lies between it and the posterosuperior calcaneus
It is best scanned with the foot in forced dorsiflexion
questions.x: The Achilles has a paratenon (not a sheath - so peritendinitis differs from tenosynovitis), with the retrocalcaneal bursa anteriorly at its insertion (Jacobson ch. 8).

questions.q: External snapping hip on dynamic ultrasound is most commonly caused by:
o: The iliopsoas tendon snapping over the iliopectineal eminence
The iliotibial band or anterior border of gluteus maximus flicking over the greater trochanter
A labral tear producing a deep joint click
Piriformis contraction against the sciatic nerve
questions.x: External (lateral) snapping hip is the ITB/gluteus maximus moving abruptly over the greater trochanter during flexion-extension; iliopsoas snapping is the internal type (Jacobson ch. 6).
